#5720. Average New Car Price Hits New Record High (And Even The Good News Doesn't Sound So Good)

Great news everyone! We just set another new record, and this time it has nothing to do with diesel prices. Sadly, though, it isn't nearly as cool as the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X destroying the Pikes Peak production car record over the summer. No, unfortunately for everyone who still has to work for a living, Kelley Blue Book reports the average transaction price for new cars hasn't just crossed the $50,000 mark. In October, the average transaction price rose to a level never before seen in the U.S. So that's pretty exciting. Aren't you thrilled to be alive right now to experience it?

Using data from its parent company, Cox Automotive, KBB says the average price consumers paid for new cars in the U.S. hit $51,109 in the month of October. That's 1.3% higher than it was in September and a 2.1% increase year-over-year. Higher prices aren't usually a good thing, especially when those higher prices are on things most people need to use every day (cars) instead of luxuries that you don't have to own to participate in society. The average MSRP of new vehicles is also up, reportedly hitting $52,933 in October, up 1.4% versus September and 2.4% higher year-over-year.

That said, it isn't all bad news. There's always a silver lining, and this time around, KBB says, "The Kelley Blue Book ATP estimate marked an all-time high even as vehicle price inflation in October was below long-term averages." Yes, you read that right. The average price people are paying for new cars hit an all-time high in October, but at least the rate of inflation isn't as high as it could be. Don't you feel grateful for that? I know I do. From the sound of it, dealers are also perfectly happy to let customers pay those high prices, as opposed to chasing faster turnover:

The higher ATP – an estimate of the average product prices paid in October before all available incentives, taxes and fees are factored in – was driven in part by both price inflation and strong sales of expensive midsize and full-size SUVs and full-size pickup trucks. Incentive spending increased modestly in October but remains below long-term averages, suggesting automakers and dealers are not aggressively pursuing sales and inventory reduction, despite record prices.

KBB also found that incentive spending accounted for 6.8% of ATP in October. With September 2026 at 6.7% and October 2025 at 6.5%, incentives are trending upward but it's been slow and doesn't appear to have contributed significantly to October's ATP record. Plus, not every car costs the same, and some segments will naturally cost less to buy than others. Once you break pricing out by segment, only one really feels like an outlier. Here's how KBB's breakdown looks:

As you can see, midsize SUVs were number one in sales volume and had an ATP of $50,570, but the people buying compact cars only paid $28,000 for them on average. That probably seems high for a compact, but remember, a 2027 Nissan Sentra without any options has an MSRP of almost $25,000 with destination, and an extra $3,000 to drive something nicer than a stripped-out, base-model Sentra sounds pretty fair to me.

Meanwhile, full-size pickup trucks placed third behind midsize and compact SUVs, but the average transaction price is close to double what people are paying for Honda CR-Vs and Hyundai Tucsons. Yes, on average, full-size truck buyers pay $67,912 for their trucks. Some Ford F-150s will cost more, some Chevrolet Silverados will cost less, but on average a full-size pickup truck buyer spent more than $65,000 to buy their truck.

That said, it's also worth reminding everyone that if you adjust for inflation, the 1997 Toyota Camry cost more than a brand new 2026 Camry does today. Truck buyers' obsession with expensive trucks skews the average, but if raises had kept up with inflation, it wouldn't be nearly as scary to hear the Camry now starts at $30,995. Cars haven't gotten too expensive. Our bosses denying us raises has simply left us too poor to afford these new cars. Meanwhile, they're out there buying $70,000 trucks like its nothing. Or at least they did before Woke 3 arrived. Maybe under Woke 3, we're all getting raises.

#5719. From Fragmentation to Integration: A New Model for Specialty Care

From Fragmentation to Integration: A New Model for Specialty Care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are navigating growing demands with increasingly limited resources. As costs rise and teams are stretched, technology has become essential to helping people work smarter. But technology alone isn’t the answer. Many health systems and specialty care teams are discovering that more tools don’t always mean a more efficient process or better patient outcomes.

Approximately 25% of healthcare spending in the U.S. goes toward administrative expenses. At the same time, 60% of hospitals and health systems use more than 50 software solutions for operations. Yet more technology hasn’t meant less complexity. Care teams still navigate disconnected tools, siloed data, fragmented workflows, and manual handoffs. The opportunity isn’t to add more technology; it’s to make everything work better together.

Health systems want to better manage the specialty patient journey, but administrative burdens get in the way of more coordinated care. What they need is an integrated approach – one that improves patient experiences and outcomes by connecting workflows through technology and adding dedicated human expertise to serve as an extension of existing care teams.

When specialty care teams spend more time navigating processes and technology than focusing on patients, trust erodes, costs rise, and turnover climbs. It also limits teams’ ability to apply the clinical expertise and personalized attention that complex specialty care requires. This friction shows up in three core areas:

The rapid adoption of specialized software and standalone tools for tasks such as scheduling, patient intake, and remote monitoring fragments care delivery. Teams constantly toggle between platforms, manually piecing together a single patient’s record. This can contribute to cognitive overload among care teams, a factor in burnout, and it diverts valuable time and attention from clinical decision-making and personalized patient support that require human expertise.

Point solutions may solve individual challenges, but they often operate in isolation. When systems don’t fully connect, patient information becomes fragmented across applications, leaving specialty care teams without visibility into the full context of a patient’s broader care journey. This can increase the risk of redundant testing, duplicated work, and inaccurate reporting, while making it harder for clinicians to identify when patients may need additional interventions.

The care journey includes multiple critical transitions, from cross-departmental referrals to prescription routing to external coordination. Despite healthcare’s digital process, these transitions still rely too frequently on faxes, phone calls, and manual spreadsheets. The added administrative burden makes it harder for care teams to coordinate timely interventions and provide consistent, personalized support. Without an integrated model that connects the entire care journey, referrals or post-procedure care plans can fall through the cracks.

Complexity comes at a cost: time teams could be spending on patient care. According to AMA research, for every hour physicians spend with patients, they spend nearly two more on EHR and desk work.

For specialty care teams, disconnected technology and fragmented workflows can make it even harder to see the full picture of a patient’s care. Patients with multiple chronic conditions, for example, often see several specialists. When any one of them lacks complete visibility into the patient’s full treatment plan, specialty performance breaks down. The risk of prescribing therapies that shouldn't be combined rises, potentially compromising patient safety and delaying therapy.

Solving today’s specialty care challenges requires more than another point solution. It requires a connected operating model that brings workflows, information and expertise together, giving care teams the visibility and support they need to act with greater confidence and keep patients moving forward.

#5718. Don't Overlook Cancer Risks in People With HIV, Experts Say

— Common cancers should be a key component of HIV care

Preventing and screening for common cancers seen in the general population should be a key component of HIV care, experts said at the recent IDWeek annual meeting.

Given cancer risks, "prevention becomes a key part of HIV care," noted Ma Somsouk, MD, of the University of California San Francisco, during a presentation at the meeting. That includes smoking cessation, treating hepatitis B and hepatitis C infection, managing diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, and screening for cancer.

Of note, AIDS-related cancers, including Kaposi sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, are on the decline with improved therapies, but remain more common among people with HIV compared with the general population.

According to a Swedish retrospective case-control study, people with HIV were significantly more likely to develop human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated anal, penile, vulvar, and cervical cancers. An observational study showed that rates of oropharyngeal cancer among people with HIV have increased since 2000, particularly among heterosexual men ages 50 and older.

Somsouk noted that "the cancer burden is shifting with age in the HIV population." An estimated 70% of all people with HIV are 45 and older, he said, with greater risks of non-AIDS-related cancers like lung and prostate cancer.

Research has shown that people living with HIV have an increased risk for lung cancer, with some studies estimating risk to be 1.5 to 3-fold higher compared with the general population.

Furthermore, in a study of Medicaid beneficiaries, HIV was associated with a higher incidence of lung cancer (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.56-1.96), with Black women at particular risk (HR 2.48, 95% CI 2.09-2.95).

While declining lung cancer deaths in the U.S. are tied to lower smoking prevalence, smoking risk among people with HIV remains "astronomical," said Chyke Doubeni, MD, MPH, of the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center in Columbus, at the IDWeek annual meeting.

A 2016 meta-analysis showed that while 20% of U.S. adults smoked, more than half of people with HIV (54%) smoked -- and that rate rose to 74% among those with HIV and injection drug use.

Lung cancer screening among those with HIV isn't a one-time visit, Doubeni noted. Instead, it's a process that includes prevention, detection, and follow-up care. For clinicians, documenting the smoking history of a patient with HIV is the crucial first step in the prevention process, he said, followed by directing patients to smoking cessation resources.

Understanding how screening recommendations may differ, and how to apply their criteria to patients is also important.

For anyone ages 50 to 80 years with a 20 pack-year smoking history who smokes or quit in the last 15 years, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends annual lung cancer screening with low-dose CT. But Doubeni cautioned that many patients who die from lung cancer don't meet those criteria.

Recent American Cancer Society guidelines dropped the 15-year look-back and widened the potential screenable population. Why? "If you quit 20 years ago, your risk is lower, but it doesn't actually go away," Doubeni explained.

People with HIV are at average risk for colorectal cancer and standard screening recommendations apply. In Somsouk's presentation at IDWeek, he recommended colorectal cancer screening at ages 45 to 75 for those with HIV, with any test recommended by the USPSTF.

"In general, the best test is the one that you can get your patient to complete," Somsouk noted. But patients who have a positive fecal immunochemical test need a colonoscopy within 6 months, he added.

As for other gastrointestinal cancers, Somsouk advised screening for esophageal cancer with upper endoscopy or a capsule test for HIV patients with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease plus three or more risk factors. He also recommended Helicobacter pylori testing for those with dyspepsia, peptic ulcers, or a family history of gastric cancer, as well as in high-risk groups, including immigrants from high-incidence regions. For those with cirrhosis of any cause or chronic hepatitis B virus infection, he advised alpha-fetoprotein testing and ultrasound to screen for liver cancer.

#5716. Staera launches with $4.6M to develop an optical interconnect for chiplets

Staera Semiconductor Inc., a startup that develops technology for linking together chiplets, launched today with $4.6 million in pre-seed funding.

Singaporean fund Openspace Capital led the investment. It was joined by SGInnovate, Black Kite Capital, 28 Holdings, In Group and financial software company Decimus Technologies.

High-end artificial intelligence accelerators comprise multiple chiplets, silicon dies that each perform a narrow set of tasks. They’re linked together by a kind of miniature network that also functions as the host accelerator’s base layer.

That miniature network takes the form of an interposer, an advanced device that sometimes includes computing circuits, or a bridge. A bridge is essentially a small interposer that costs less to make.

Interposers and bridges both use tiny copper wires to move data between the chiplets they connect. San Francisco-based Staera hopes to replace those copper wires with optical links. According to the company, optical technology is faster and uses less power. It can also transmit data over longer distances without slowing down, which enables chipmakers to build bigger accelerators.

“Copper performance plummets over the millimeter-to-meter distances that matter most in AI accelerators, and bolt-on optics add power and complexity.” said Chief Executive Officer Andrew Kim. “We build the light into the chip, the entire optical link inside a chip, so the connection gets smaller, cooler and faster with each generation.”

Staera’s first product is called Lightwire. It transmits data over optical links, or waveguides, made of a transparent material known as silicon nitride. Light beams can only travel through a transparent material if their wavelengths fall within a specific range. Silicon nitride supports a larger range of wavelengths than many alternatives and causes less light loss, which boosts connection speeds.

The light beams into which Lightwire encodes data traffic are produced by miniature LEDs. Those devices are made of gallium nitride, a compound that is widely used in optical systems because it has a direct bandgap.

The electrons that orbit an atomic nucleus have different energy levels known as bands. Light is produced when an electron jumps from one band to one another and then collides with a quasiparticle called an electron hole.

Usually, the process also involves a second quasiparticle known as a phonon. Direct bandgap materials such as gallium nitride don’t require a phonon, which makes the light generation process more efficient.

Staera says Lightwire transmits data between an AI accelerator’s chiplets at a rate of up to 8 gigabits per second. The technology can provide more than 600 optical links per square millimeter. In practice, that means a Lightwire-powered HBM4 memory stack can move up to 24 terabits of data per second instead of the 2.8 terabits supported by current technologies.

Staera’s funding round will advance its commercialization efforts. It will enhance Lightwire, grow its U.S. team and build out a manufacturing supply chain. The company hopes to begin commercial shipments in 2030.

#5715. SpaceX Wants To Build Data Center Powered By Its Newest Product: Natural Gas

SpaceX filed its intention to build a new AI data center at its facility in Starbase, Texas, which will be powered by a new natural gas plant that it will also build. None of that sounds like space, but this is the company that SpaceX has become. The initial phase of this build-out is projected to cost $24 billion, though more phases are to come. Critically, this gives the rocket company, which is also an internet company, which is also an AI company, which is also a social media company, a way to make use of its newest product: natural gas. Again, space!

The company has been moving towards an expansion into fossil fuels for the last few months. In June, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said the company was making plans for "basically mining our own natural gas... to develop our own propellant and bring it to the rocket." The rocket in question being Starship, which SpaceX is essentially betting its future on. That takes a mixture of methane and liquid oxygen to fire up its thrusters; methane can be extracted from natural gas. For that reason, the company has made major moves to ensure its own supply. It hired for its own natural gas trader, normally an oil industry job for buying and selling the stuff, and is building its own pipelines in both Florida and Texas, per Bloomberg.

In addition, SpaceX rapidly spun up AI data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi earlier this year, powered by, you guessed it, natural gas. It spun them up so rapidly that the company is now being sued for ignoring environmental laws. SpaceX is apparently trying to go fast again for this new Texas endeavor, likely trying to get things rolling before a newer, bluer state government takes over. SpaceX wants to grab both the air pollution permits it needs plus a few tax breaks; Texas is expected to make both harder to get early next year, per Politico. To that end, Starbase's city government will convene on the matter in December. There's good reason to think the company will get what it wants: two of the city's three commission members are SpaceX executives. That's handy.

As for the power plant itself, it will feature 35 mobile natural gas turbines and produce around 750 megawatts of electricity. So it's now in the business of building power plants, buying and trading natural gas, and laying out pipelines, all in service of the enough data centers it's putting up. No wonder Vice President of Launch Kiko Dontchev is now saying, "Fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point." You don't say, Dontchev.

At this point, it's not too much of a stretch to say that SpaceX is just the Elon Musk Show, going into whatever industry he feels like at the moment. If his long-desired merger with Tesla goes through, then it will really just be a conglomerate with all sorts of fingers in all sorts of pies. Space will still be a part of what SpaceX does, but now that AI is earning it more revenue than rockets, it may become a smaller and smaller part. Mars has never looked so far away.

#5713. The Perovskite Solar Cell Kraken Has Been Unleashed Upon The US

Perovskite is a relatively inexpensive material that has attracted thousands of researchers since 2009, when a team of scientists in Japan first demonstrated its use in solar cells. They achieved a solar energy conversion efficiency of little more than 3%, but since science loves a challenge, that was just the beginning of the story. In the latest chapter, the US firms Heliene and Caeulux have just introduced a new perovskite-enabled solar module that hits the jackpot at up to 27% efficiency, and it is already in commercial production, no less.

So far in the renewable energy transition, silicon has shouldered much of the heavy lifting due to its excellent solar conversion properties. Still, silicon is relatively expensive material that demands a complex manufacturing process. Perovskite is the reverse. Based on a naturally occurring mineral, synthetic perovskites can be lab-grown and applied to solar cell fabrication in a high volume, high throughput process similar to roll-to-roll manufacturing and other solution-based methods (see lots more perovskite background here).

There being no such thing as a free lunch, “raw” perovskite is challenged by natural conditions, namely, humidity. Tweaking the formula with other, more durable materials can resolve that problem. Researchers have also developed a tandem solution, in which a perovskite layer rests upon a silicon layer, providing an efficiency boost while minimizing the additional cost.

In the US solar market, the sticky wicket is the current state of federal energy, trade, and tax polices. Still, the red-hot demand for solar energy in the US has motivated solar stakeholders to steamroll over those obstacles, attracting overseas investors (here’s one example) as well as new domestic ventures.

On the domestic side, the Corning-backed manufacturer Heliene has been focusing on silicon while the startup Caelux has tackled the perovskite solar cell challenge with a glass substrate that can be layered onto other materials in a solar module. Now the two manufacturers have combined forces, with Caelux’s perovskite-doped glass boosting the conversion efficiency of Heliene’s N-type solar cells by up to 20%.

The Caelux-Heliene mashup comes at a time when Congress has finally put the wheels in motion to streamline the permitting process for energy projects. The two firms already have a running head start. On November 10, the two firms announced that commercial-scale production has already begun on their Hybrid-Tandem™ solar module

“Manufactured by Heliene in Minnesota, the perovskite plus silicon technology combines Caelux’s Energy Producing Glass with Heliene’s established silicon module platform to construct a solar module with two separate power generation layers that deliver higher power density,” Heliene explains.

“One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely new production setup,” added Martin Pochtaruk, Heliene CEO and Founder, in a press statement.

“With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar,” Pochtaruk emphasized.

Stay tuned for the next development. The new modules are now in production at Heliene’s manufacturing facility Minnesota, with deliveries set for 2027. That’s just for starters. Caelux and Heliene have already targeted 29% efficiency and up for their next-generation modules.

The conversion efficiency improvement is the gift that keeps on giving. In the rooftop solar sector, for example, high-efficiency solar cells enable developers to squeeze more electricity out of a given space, making a rooftop array more economical for smaller properties that are otherwise shut out of the market. The cost of a smaller, more effcient array can also ripple downwards in the form of savings on labor, hardware, and transportation expenses.

For rooftop solar in general, the boost in efficiency provides an opportunity to take full advantage of power sharing programs with local utilities, which enable solar owners to earn revenue and qualify for time-of-use discounts. The benefits can ripple into home energy storage systems and home EV charging as well.

On a larger scale, the space-saving angle can help alleviate land use conflicts that otherwise stymie solar development, particularly in the area of farm-to-solar conversion.

Although real estate development is by far the primary factor driving the loss of farmland in the US, solar opponents (looking at you, Brooke Rollins) have played the farm card to gin up resistance to solar development in rural communities. With efficiency improvements, the economic case improves for solar arrays on marginal lands and smaller parcels. That can be partcularly helpful in the community solar field, where solar arrays are typically smaller.

Additionally, the improved efficiency can help accelerate the uptake of agrivoltaic practices that balance energy-producing solar panels with grazing and croplands. These dual-use arrays can enable farmers to continue working their land while guaranteeing a revenue stream from the solar developer.

Furthermore, high-efficiency solar opens up new opportunities in the field of floating solar, where developers can make use of reservoirs and other human-engineered bodies of water instead of taking up space on land. By taking up less room on water for the same power generation capacity, floating solar can also squeeze into reservoirs where recreation and habitat conservation also compete for space.

Perovskite solar cells represent just one key breakthrough area in the US solar industry. Easing the federal energy permitting bottleneck is another. That can be a two-edged sword, enabling more fossil energy resources to flow through the pipeline. However, permitting reform could also prevent the fossil energy industry from running amok through federal energy policy.

Members of Congress are currently negotiating over the particulars of Senate Bill 5653, aka the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. If enacted as envisioned by the solar industry, the reforms will put a crimp in Trump’s “American Energy Dominance” policy, which has placed new and burdensome restrictions on both wind and solar activity in the US while aggressively supporting fossil fuels and nuclear, alongside other renewables including biomass, geothermal, hydropower. Even energy storage has come in for a share of love from the Trump administration, further underscoring the remarkable exclusion of wind and solar from federal energy policy.

The trade organization Solar Energy Industries Association, for one, is urging members on both sides of the aisle to ensure that permitting reform focuses on fairness, predictability, and certainty. In a letter to the House and Senate, SEIA emphasizes that solar and storage developers “cannot finance multi-year, capital-intensive projects without the predictability and certainty needed to build projects and connect them to the grid.”

“According to researchers at Wood Mackenzie, solar and storage represent 70% of the new capacity added to the grid thus far in 2026. Yet $120 billion in clean energy investment is caught up in current permitting delays, let alone the impact of permitting challenges to future deployment,” SEIA adds.

Of course, even if such a bill passes both Houses of Congress, US President Donald Trump could exercise his veto power, and he has already threatened to make copious use of it during his last two years in office. Nevertheless, US Presidents come and go, and this one is scheduled to go in January of 2029 — peacefully this time, one hopes.

It also happens to close just in time to get it home and under whatever shrine you celebrate for the winter solstice.

Originally sold by Propstore in 2016 as part of its Entertainment Memorabilia Auction, this is the bike used in notable "The Dark Knight" moments such as when Batman (Christian Bale) evaded the Joker (Heath Ledger), demonstrating the Batpod's abilities to climb walls and turn around without moving forward thanks to the wheels' ability to flip side-to-side, making the Hummer's crabwalking capabilities look like ancient technology. As of this writing bids sit at around $300,000, with Propstore estimating the sale to range between around $600,000 to $1.2 million. If that's too rich for your taste, maybe you could look into building your own Batpod.

#5710. Assessing and Managing HIV's Higher Heart Disease Risks

— People with HIV are twice as likely to develop cardiovascular disease

Understanding how HIV can shape cardiovascular disease risk may help clinicians tailor care to patients' needs, which starts with statins for most adults with HIV.

"HIV holds its own as a risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease," Virginia Triant, MD, MPH, of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, said in a presentation at the IDWeek annual meeting.

A 2018 meta-analysis showed that people living with HIV were twice as likely to develop cardiovascular disease as those without HIV, Triant observed. Those with HIV also faced greater risks of myocardial infarction and stroke she added, putting HIV nearly on par with the cardiovascular relative risks found in the INTERHEART study for hypertension, diabetes, and smoking.

Traditional factors play a part in the elevated cardiovascular risks linked to HIV. People with HIV have greater rates of hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia than their HIV-negative counterparts, Triant noted. Research also shows an 85% lifetime history of smoking among those with HIV.

That doesn't explain the whole story, Triant pointed out. Antiretroviral therapy brings its own set of cardiovascular risks.

Early protease inhibitors like darunavir were linked with cumulative myocardial infarction risks, and recent use of the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor abacavir was tied to increased myocardial infarction risk. It's not clear whether integrase strand transfer inhibitors also boost cardiovascular risk, with conflicting results from the RESPOND and HIV-CAUSAL studies.

After accounting for traditional risk factors and antiretroviral therapy, there's still a missing piece to the cardiovascular risk puzzle, Triant said. That piece may be the inflammation that comes with HIV.

The SMART study pointed to inflammation's role in cardiovascular disease, she noted. An analysis of data from the REPRIEVE study reinforced inflammation's role, even in people with well-controlled HIV and low to moderate cardiovascular risk.

Despite growing understanding of how HIV uniquely shapes cardiovascular risk, "this has not until very recently translated into differing and tailored clinical guidance for people with HIV," Triant stated. "I really see this as a challenge in delivering equitable care for cardiovascular care for people living with HIV."

Existing cardiovascular risk prediction scores for the general population fall short among people with HIV, incorporating only traditional risk factors without including HIV-related factors, Triant said. Even among those with HIV, cardiovascular risk varies by sex, race, ethnicity, and geographic location.

Among those with HIV, the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) that debuted in 2013 underestimated cardiovascular risk in women and those in low to moderate risk groups. The more comprehensive 2023 PREVENT equations mirrored the PCE risk underestimation for people with HIV, with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) rates greater than PREVENT predictions.

Given underestimated risk, people with HIV have been less likely to receive cardiovascular preventive care that matches guidelines, Triant said. The guidelines for the general population are also less than what's needed for people with HIV, she said.

That began to change with cholesterol guidelines from the American Health Association (AHA) and other groups that added consideration of HIV as a cardiovascular disease risk factor. A 2019 AHA scientific statement that specifically focused on people with HIV highlighted risk-enhancing factors such as prolonged viremia, low CD4 counts, delays in starting antiretroviral therapy (ART), and metabolic syndrome.

Still, "what was really missing from the field was a large trial with robust data to support a recommendation for cardiovascular prevention for people with HIV," Triant said.

Then came REPRIEVE in 2023. That phase III clinical trial included only people with HIV on ART who had low to moderate cardiovascular disease risk and didn't meet general guidelines' thresholds for statin therapy. REPRIEVE showed that statin therapy was linked to a 36% reduction in MACE risk compared with placebo.

These results weren't driven by a subgroup. "It was reduction whether you looked by demographics, or traditional risk factors, or traditional HIV-related factors," Triant explained.

REPRIEVE was the first randomized trial that showed a cardiovascular prevention benefit that was different from the general population. "This is really paradigm-shifting," she noted. A CDC analysis found that full implementation of REPRIEVE's approach in people with HIV and low to moderate cardiovascular disease risk could lead to 7,418 fewer first major adverse cardiovascular events over 5 years.

The REPRIEVE findings have spurred practice-changing guidelines for people with HIV, Triant said.

In 2024, an HHS panel rolled out recommendations calling for daily moderate-intensity statins in people with HIV ages 40 to 75 years with low to intermediate (less than 20%) 10-year risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). In those with less than 5% risk, the HHS panel favored starting at least moderate-intensity statins.

The American College of Cardiology and other societies followed that with a dyslipidemia guideline in 2026 that recommended that everyone with HIV ages 40 to 75 years on ART receive statin therapy to reduce ASCVD event risk and slow coronary atherosclerosis.

"This is really a striking recommendation, and an important one for the field," Triant explained. "Notably, this is regardless of calculated baseline risk, regardless of LDL, for people in this age group."

Clinicians might want to consider starting statins at age 30 for those with HIV, she added. "I would strongly consider HIV to be an ASCVD risk enhancer, even at that age, even though we don't have the trial data," Triant said.

Even with these newly tailored guidelines, implementation will be a challenge, she noted. Statin uptake in people with HIV was suboptimal before REPRIEVE, with 80% of patients eligible for statins under earlier guidelines not getting them.

"Dismantling disparities that we know exist in cardiovascular prevention and care remains a critical challenge," Triant said. "The recent guidelines are likely to be practice-changing for people with HIV, but only if implemented on a broad scale."

#5708. Over One-Third Of Audi Nuvolari Production Will Be Sold In The U.S.

The 2027 Audi Nuvolari isn't a successor to the R8 because whereas that supercar was mass-produced in the tens of thousands over 18 years and two generations, just 499 Nuvolaris will ever be made. Audi has now announced that 182 of those are earmarked for the U.S., which means 36.5% of all Nuvolaris will land stateside, or one in every 2.74 cars.

Each will go for an official starting price of $700,000 before destination or taxes, and U.S. deliveries are scheduled to start in the first half of 2028. That's almost twice as much money as the Lamborghini Temerario on which it's based, but the Lambo isn't limited production or quite as special. Despite the numbered production run and how this sort of car tends to sell out before the public even knows about it, Audi of America says there are still build slots available, as "orders continue to be accepted at authorized Audi dealerships throughout the United States for a limited time."

Sharing its powertrain with the Temerario, the Audi Nuvolari uses a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8 and three axial-flux hybrid electric motors to make 987 horsepower combined. 0 to 60 mph happens in just 2.5 seconds, and its top speed stands at 217 mph. It's said to use Formula 1-derived tech — Audi is in F1 now, in case you forgot — in the hybrid energy management system, by-wire brakes, active aero, and launch control programming.

It's also a new luxury performance car that manages to look good and original without being "polarizing." It's brutalist and a departure from existing Audi styling, but most colleagues I've talked to about it view its design favorably. For what it's worth, I think it's hella cool, particularly from the rear three-quarter view. Audi says there are 50 gloss paint colors and over 10 matte finishes, but you can of course make it look however you want with Audi Exclusive. You can get Audi's first exposed carbon-fiber body on the Nuvolari, and on the inside there's dozens more options.

In any case, if you're in the States and have 700 grand to splash on a German supercar (or, let's be real, almost a million after accounting for options, fees and taxes), there's apparently still time to go to your local Audi dealership and put your name down for a Nuvolari. You'd be joining a small club that only 181 other Americans will be a part of.

#5707. Advocate Health to increase total employee compensation by $846M for 2027

Advocate Health to increase total employee compensation by $846M for 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Nonprofit health system Advocate Health will invest an additional $1.24 billion in its workforce beginning in 2027, with approximately $846 million dedicated towards compensation and $390 million towards incremental benefits.

Advocate will increase its minimum wage to $20 an hour, building on its $18.85 per hour minimum wage established this year.

For a 40-hour workweek, that wage would pay over $26,520 more per year than the federal minimum wage, it said.

Compensation investments will also include merit increases, incentives, pay-range updates and other investments in pay, executives said in the Nov. 5 announcement.

“The most important investment we make isn’t in buildings, technology or equipment. It’s in our people,” said Eugene A. Woods, Advocate Health CEO, in a statement. “Healthcare is a 24/7 calling and every single day our 170,000 teammates bring extraordinary skill, compassion and commitment to the patients and communities we serve. Their dedication is what brings our purpose to life for the millions of people who count on us each year.”

The country’s third-largest nonprofit health system currently covers approximately 83% of employee medical costs, and plans to invest an additional $138 million for what it says will absorb “more than 90% of the projected $149 million increase in medical plan costs.”

Moreover, the health system’s 2027 benefits package extends fully paid parental bonding leave to four weeks enterprise-wide; expands paid bereavement leave; continues coverage for GLP-1 medications for weight loss; provides no-cost mental health support for employees and family members; continues sustained retirement contributions of up to 6% of eligible pay and offers education assistance across more than 1,300 eligible programs.

The package also offers student loan repayment assistance, with lifetime support of up to $21,000 for eligible full-time employees and $10,500 for eligible part-time employees.

“The benefits that matter most are the ones that make a real difference in people’s lives,” said Nakesha Lopez, Advocate Health senior executive vice president and chief people and culture officer, in a statement. “We want our benefits to reflect what teammates need at different stages of their lives, while keeping affordability at the forefront and providing meaningful support for their health, families and financial futures.”

#5706. 1967 Ford Ranchero For Sale With 3,100 Miles Shown Is 351 V8 Swapped, Bright Red And Ready To Roll

I'm known around these parts as a ute fan. Any car you can dream up, I've probably come across it built into a ute, and I've almost certainly liked that version better than the original. Once in a while, though, we have to pay respects to the originators of the ute life — the El Caminos, the Holdens, and of course the ever-gorgeous Ford Rancheros. Take this one, for instance: A 351-swapped 1967 Fairlane Ranchero that's not a hideous restomod.

This Ranchero, while modified and maintained over the course of its life, is gloriously free from any terrible four-spoke steering wheels or gaudy blue LED gauges. It does have an air conditioning system of questionable provenance (the control/vent unit doesn't appear to be either the factory Ford in-dash option available in 1967 nor the period-appropriate round-vented dealer accessory) as well as a modern single-DIN radio, but those are welcome and unobtrusive changes — they don't distract from the classic character of the car. The wheels certainly do, but some five-spoke American Classics will fix that handily.

Under the hood, though, is the mod that really matters: The Ranchero's factory 289ci V8 engine and its associated three-speed manual gearbox have been replaced with a 351 ci V8 and a four on the floor (with a Hurst shifter, even). It's not technically a period-correct swap, as the 351 postdates this Ranchero by a couple of years, but it's close enough that I'll count it. Better than putting a Coyote under there and pretending that the Ford badging maintains the car's character.

This OEM-plus Ranchero is on Bring a Trailer right now at a bidding price of just $2,500, which falls firmly into "Amber wants this" territory. I'm going to need you all to bump that number up until this ute starts to look like more of a bad idea to me, or Jalopnik's local kei car and motorcycle girlie might just end up with a giant hunk of American muscle street-parked outside her apartment. Surely you'll save me from that fate, right?

#5705. The next chapter for Red Hat: AI agents rewrite the cloud-native playbook

Red Hat LLC has spent years making Kubernetes manageable for enterprises that would rather run applications than tend clusters. As AI agents move into production, the company is extending that experience to a new generation of workloads. AI agents don’t just consume infrastructure. They execute commands, call external tools, access enterprise systems and take actions that can affect the business. The next phase of AI agent infrastructure requires enforceable security boundaries alongside efficient resource management.

Red Hat arrives at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City this week with a growing portfolio of technologies addressing those requirements. OpenShift provides the Kubernetes foundation; its work with Nvidia Corp. on OpenShell addresses agent execution and security; and the llm-d project has reached version 1.0 with capabilities for serving the context-heavy workloads agents create. Together, these developments position Red Hat to help enterprises manage agentic AI through open, Kubernetes-based infrastructure.

Unlike conventional applications, autonomous agents can generate commands, invoke tools and delegate work across multiple systems. That flexibility creates opportunities for automation while increasing the importance of consistent access controls and oversight.

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving to support enterprise AI, with Red Hat and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem addressing the security, operational efficiency and scalability requirements of autonomous agents. (* Disclosure below.)

The rapid adoption of OpenClaw has brought renewed attention to agent security. An agent that can read files, run shell commands and make network calls needs clearly defined permissions and isolation to operate safely within enterprise environments.

Red Hat’s response centers on its collaboration with Nvidia around OpenShell, a runtime that places agents inside isolated execution environments and applies policy to their access. Nvidia developed OpenShell; Red Hat is working with Nvidia and the wider community to integrate the technology into Red Hat AI and its open hybrid cloud platform. Red Hat’s announcement describes the work as part of a broader effort to bring security-focused agentic AI capabilities to enterprise infrastructure.

OpenShell uses sandboxing, process-aware policy and controls over network access and credentials. Red Hat has also described how OpenShell can work with OpenShift’s sandboxed containers, adding application-level restrictions inside a virtual-machine boundary. These complementary layers govern agent behavior and isolate the environments in which agents operate, as Red Hat explains in its technical overview of layered sandboxing.

The distinction matters because sandboxing does not make an agent trustworthy. It limits the damage an agent can cause when its instructions, generated code or external inputs lead it somewhere they should not.

In a recent interview with theCUBE, Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, described how OpenShell builds on Kubernetes infrastructure: “The agent sandbox is one of them, so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes native APIs.” His comments get to the central issue: enterprises cannot delegate authority to agents without defining and enforcing its limits.

Red Hat Chief Technology Officer Chris Wright also emphasized the importance of agent isolation in a May interview with theCUBE. Agents that can take real actions in a business need sandboxing and least-privilege protections, he explained.

“You’ve got to give it the right sandboxing. You’ve got to put protections around the agent, give it least privileges so it doesn’t think about read versus read-write — very big difference,” Wright said in SiliconANGLE’s coverage of Red Hat Summit.

Beyond sandboxing, enterprises must manage agent identities, data permissions, tool access and authorization. That distinction is reinforced by Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst for application development, modernization and cloud native at theCUBE Research, whose September analysis of AI agent governance examines the difference between observing what agents do and proving what they were authorized to do. The research identifies runtime enforcement, delegated authority and verifiable audit evidence as requirements that become more important as autonomous systems move into production.

“This creates an opportunity for platforms that can unify application development, infrastructure orchestration, security and observability rather than adding another layer of disconnected tooling,” Nashawaty said.

Beyond security, agents create new requirements for inference infrastructure. An agent may call a model, retrieve information, invoke a tool and return to the model with additional context. Each interaction consumes compute, memory and network capacity, while the system must preserve enough context to continue efficiently.

Red Hat’s llm-d project addresses part of that problem. Founded by Red Hat, IBM Corp., Google Cloud, CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, llm-d uses Kubernetes-native components to distribute inference across accelerators and manage traffic between them.

The project reached version 1.0 on Oct. 20, adding session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, multi-tenant quality-of-service controls and high-availability operations. Those features aim to keep multi-turn requests close to cached context, prioritize latency-sensitive work and reduce disruption during maintenance. The Red Hat release announcement and Google Cloud’s technical overview describe the release.

The architecture provides operators with additional options for coordinating inference workloads and managing accelerator resources within Kubernetes.

Red Hat Senior Vice President and AI Chief Technology Officer Brian Stevens described one of llm-d’s central architectural decisions in SiliconANGLE’s report on Kubernetes inference: “We can independently scale the processing of the input from the production of the tokens.”

Other infrastructure providers are addressing complementary requirements. ScaleOps Labs Ltd. focuses on GPU utilization and resource optimization across Kubernetes workloads. Vultr Holdings LLC offers GPU infrastructure and Kubernetes-based model deployment, while Broadcom Inc. positions VMware Cloud Foundation as a private-cloud platform for Kubernetes and AI workloads. Together, these offerings reflect expanding enterprise choices for resource optimization, accelerator capacity and private-cloud operations.

The operational gap appears in theCUBE Research’s “Day 0 Build, Test Survey Research Report.” Based on a survey of 375 IT, development, operations and platform engineering professionals, the research found that cloud-native adoption is widespread but maturity remains uneven. Inconsistent automated testing, fragmented developer tools and gaps in rollback capabilities continue to complicate production deployment.

“Ninety-two percent of organizations are integrating AI into at least one stage of the software development lifecycle, while 79% expect full-scale AI agent adoption within the next three years,” Nashawaty said, adding that approximately 30% still face operational readiness challenges.

The broader industry is also moving toward production-scale infrastructure. The CNCF’s 2026 annual cloud-native survey found that 82% of container users run Kubernetes in production and that 66% of organizations hosting generative AI workloads use Kubernetes for some or all inference. Those figures reinforce Kubernetes’ expanding role as enterprises adopt AI workloads.

The open-source ecosystem is expanding alongside agentic AI adoption. On Nov. 5, Google announced the donation of Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the CNCF following their acceptance into its Sandbox program in October. The projects address agent execution, isolation and reinforcement-learning workflows. Agent Substrate separates agent sessions and identities from active compute, allowing idle environments to pause and resume; gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary for untrusted code; and OpenRL supports reinforcement-learning post-training on Kubernetes. Google’s announcement describes the projects and their transition into CNCF governance.

These contributions complement broader efforts across the Kubernetes community. Red Hat is a co-founder of llm-d and is integrating Nvidia’s OpenShell into its enterprise AI platform, while Google is contributing technologies related to runtime and training requirements. The common emphasis on open infrastructure creates opportunities for interoperability as enterprise AI systems mature.

Broadcom added another development on Nov. 9, announcing that its VM API project had been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox. The project aims to let organizations manage virtual machines through Kubernetes application programming interfaces across different infrastructure providers. This extends the Kubernetes conversation to managing virtual machines alongside containerized workloads.

Project Lightwell adds another dimension to Red Hat’s enterprise strategy. Announced with IBM in May, the $5 billion initiative aims to use AI-assisted vulnerability identification and validated fixes to strengthen open-source software supply chains. The initiative extends security efforts to the software dependencies supporting production workloads.

Sam Weston, industry analyst for enterprise applications, development and modernization at theCUBE Research, points to the infrastructure mix enterprises already operate.

“With our data showing 61.8% of enterprises run hybrid deployments and an additional 10% operate across multi-cloud environments, Red Hat’s hybrid-first platform strategy aligns closely with where enterprise infrastructure lives today,” Weston said.

Red Hat’s established OpenShift footprint provides a foundation for connecting these developments. As enterprises deploy more autonomous workloads, the company is positioned to combine Kubernetes orchestration, agent isolation and distributed inference within its broader hybrid cloud strategy.

The opportunity extends beyond any individual project. OpenShift, llm-d and OpenShell illustrate how Red Hat is contributing to an open infrastructure model that accommodates both conventional applications and emerging AI agents.

For enterprises, the objective is to make AI workloads secure, efficient and manageable without losing control over how autonomous systems operate. Red Hat’s work across the Kubernetes ecosystem reflects how that foundation is taking shape.

#5704. Novel Glucagon/GLP-1 Agonist Meets Cardiovascular Safety Endpoint

— Survodutide was noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events, trial shows

Survodutide, an investigational glucagon receptor and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, was safe for patients with obesity and either established cardiovascular disease (CVD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), or increased risk of CVD, a randomized trial found.

Among more than 5,500 patients, the primary composite endpoint -- death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemia-related coronary revascularization, or heart failure event -- occurred in 3.7% of those on survodutide versus 4.1% of those on placebo (P<0.0001 for noninferiority).

In the SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT trial, survodutide "met its primary endpoint, establishing cardiovascular safety by demonstrating noninferiority to placebo for MACE [major adverse cardiovascular events]," Biykem Bozkurt, MD, PhD, of Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, said during her presentation at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting in Chicago.

This safety trial provides clinicians with "reassuring data" that treatment with the dual agonist is not associated with increased cardiovascular risk, Bozkurt and colleagues concluded in their report, published simultaneously in The Lancet.

"Given the novelty of this new incretin-based therapy class, establishing cardiovascular safety of glucagon receptor–GLP-1 receptor dual agonists through noninferiority trials is essential," the authors wrote, and has become an expectation by regulatory agencies both in the U.S. and Europe, Bozkurt added.

Treatment with survodutide was also associated with improvements in systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, HbA1C, body weight, lipid levels, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, Bozkurt said.

Gastrointestinal events and treatment discontinuations were more frequent during the dose escalation phase, she added. "Overall, the safety profile was consistent with that observed in the previously reported phase III trials with no unexpected safety findings," Bozkurt said.

AHA discussant Stephen Nicholls, MBBS, PhD, of Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, pointed out that the study design means that while cardiovascular harm can be excluded, "we cannot make any inference about cardiovascular benefit."

The findings raise the question of "what is important to stakeholders when we design our clinical trials?" Nicholls said. "From a regulatory perspective, it would seem it's a relatively low bar to simply show that there's no cardiovascular harm. We need to think more and more about how do we design clinical trials with what's important for our patients and the clinicians that they are working with."

The hope is to eventually triage the right patient to the right treatment at the right time in their disease process, Nicholls added, "and facilitate shared decision-making to achieve more effective personalized prevention of cardiovascular disease and obesity complications."

SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT was a global, phase III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven, cardiovascular safety trial conducted at 524 sites in 34 countries. Adult patients were eligible if they had a body mass index of 27 kg/m2 or greater, and established CVD or at least two obesity complications or CVD risk factors. Participants with CKD were eligible if they had a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater.

A total of 5,530 patients were randomly assigned to a once-weekly dose of subcutaneous survodutide, up-titrated to 3.6 mg or 6.0 mg, or placebo. Of these, 5,507 were actually treated, equally divided between the three dosing arms.

Median time in the study was 22 months. At study close-out, 56.0% of the survodutide 3.6-mg group, 56.6% of the survodutide 6.0-mg group, and 59.0% of the placebo group were still on treatment.

Efficacy and safety analyses included all randomly assigned patients who received at least one dose of survodutide or placebo. The primary analysis, which pooled outcomes for both survodutide doses compared with placebo, was performed according to the treatment-regimen estimand, which assessed treatment effects "regardless of any early discontinuation of survodutide or placebo, temporary stop, the use of protocol-prohibited obesity medications, or a prolonged dose-escalation period," the authors noted.

A secondary three-point MACE endpoint -- death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal stroke, or nonfatal myocardial infarction -- occurred in 2.4% of 3,671 participants in the pooled survodutide group and 2.8% of 1,836 in the placebo group (P<0.0001 for non-inferiority).

Adverse events occurred in 93.0% of the 3.6-mg dose survodutide group, 93.1% of those in the 6.0-mg group, and 85.6% of those on placebo. Gastrointestinal events, including nausea and vomiting, were more frequent in the treated groups, and gastrointestinal events leading to discontinuation occurred in 19.3% of the 3.6-mg group, 20.8% of the 6.0-mg group, and 1.9% of the placebo group.

Serious adverse events and fatal adverse events were similar across treatment groups. Fatal events were primarily due to cardiac disorders, the authors noted.

#5703. AI-enabled virtual mental health startup Siggy launches from stealth

AI-enabled virtual mental health startup Siggy launches from stealth" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Siggy, an AI-enabled virtual mental health provider, has launched out of stealth with $6 million in pre-seed funding.

Siggy aims to build a complete mental health system that delivers continuous, personalized care. It combines therapy, prescription management and AI for intake and between-visits support. Intake is free; patients only pay if they accept treatment. Siggy is backed by Village Global, alongside several angel investors.

Patients begin with a free, anonymous conversation with Siggy’s AI that doesn’t require an account or login. It remembers everything, so patients don’t have to repeat their history when they eventually see a provider. An AI-powered preliminary diagnosis is reviewed by clinicians, and a patient is presented with treatment options. After a call with a human provider, patients log into Siggy to add existing providers or relatives to the system and confirm their treatment goals.

If a patient accepts treatment, they see a human clinician monthly with the option of engaging with Siggy’s AI between visits, which draws on their full history. Siggy’s therapy AI agent does not answer medical questions, instead directing them to human providers. It can help patients work through their goals, remind them of specific exercises and be a general sounding board. There are also safety protocols in place to flag higher-acuity needs to human providers.

Siggy can connect to wearables and offers a one-minute daily check-in on sleep, mood, how the body feels and medication side effects. These data combined form the Siggy Score, a single number out of 100 that patients and their clinicians see every day. When Siggy sees a pattern building, it flags the change to the patient’s clinician with the context behind it. Weekly check-ins in the first two months of treatment let clinicians decide whether to hold a dose, increase it or change a medication.

“It can build a really detailed picture of you rather fast, and the idea is if there are behavior patterns that are recurrent…[Siggy can] begin to help people gain agency and recognize them before they happen,” Siggy co-founder and CEO Jonathan Sabbagh told Fierce Healthcare.

Sabbagh co-founded Siggy with Edvard Engesaeth, M.D., now COO, an early Journey Clinical investor who co-founded Nurx. Siggy’s chief medical officer is Daniel Montville, M.D., a Mayo Clinic-trained psychiatrist. Sabbagh previously worked for two decades in finance before finding out he was living with chronic burnout and undiagnosed PTSD from childhood trauma.

Sabbagh sought psychedelic-assisted therapy and went back to school to study psychology before dropping out to co-found Journey Clinical, a large psychedelic-assisted therapy network in the U.S. with over 3,000 practices. “I saw a real gap where people drop off treatments, they don’t have continuous care,” Sabbagh told Fierce Healthcare.

About 16% of American adults take antidepressants, and a fifth annually drop out before completing the recommended course of treatment. “Prescriptions aren’t the problem … it really is a fragmented system where you don’t have therapists ever speaking with your prescriber,” Sabbagh said.

Siggy can prescribe medications, except controlled substances. Clinicians will taper patients off medications when they are ready. Longer-term, Siggy hopes to be able to identify other conditions through analytics on speech, labs, genetic testing and biomarkers, such as diabetes or ALS. It also hopes to build out neural datasets to support clinical trials for technologies like brain implants.

Siggy is covered by major commercial payers in all 50 states, including Blue Cross Blue Shield, Aetna, UnitedHealthcare and Humana. It also takes Medicaid, Medicare, TRICARE and is free for veterans.

“Our goal is to provide continuous care for life. We don’t really see meds as a feature. It is a combination of building persistent AI identity, being able to track progress and to make essentially personalized decisions that very few could afford,” Sabbagh said.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the company said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination."

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company said.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance said.

"An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans."

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The company said that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement."

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like."

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the company, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company said in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company said in the complaint

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment said in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute."

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment said in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings."

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.

#5701. Impeach and Remove RFK Jr.

— The incoming Congress has several avenues to pursue Secretary Kennedy's impeachment

When the new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, Secretary of HHS Robert F. Kennedy Jr. should be impeached by the House of Representatives and then removed by the Senate.

Can this be done? Yes. Although classically associated with presidents, impeachment applies equivalently to federal officials. The House votes to impeach by a simple majority, which triggers a Senate impeachment trial. Removal occurs if two-thirds of senators agree the official engaged in "...treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors."

Just two cabinet secretaries have been previously impeached, the most recent being Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. Also of note, articles of impeachment already were filed against Kennedy in 2025 by Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.).

Impeachment can serve many purposes even without removal: the personal and professional embarrassment of the impeached official or to bring information to light through document discovery and the compelled testimony. Politicians can also grandstand during impeachments and drive points home for votes. For example, when the House impeached Secretary Mayorkas in 2024, his probability of removal was zero as the Senate was controlled by the other party, which opposed his impeachment. A trial of merits then never even occurred as the Senate voted to dismiss. As a result, the process was arguably performative.

The goal of Kennedy's impeachment would be removal from office because he is dangerous to public health -- because without it, more Americans will needlessly suffer and die. That is the only goal in my mind.

Which Arguments Could Kennedy's Impeachment be Based Upon?

Several options exist to pursue Kennedy's impeachment. All appear valid, and we don't have to select just one, though each also has strengths and weakness, pros and cons.

One avenue is looking at dereliction of duty, particularly in our ongoing measles outbreak. The number of American measles deaths should be zero. It was zero for years, and safe, effective vaccination exists. A single measles death is an unacceptable tragedy laid at the feet of pernicious leaders such as Kennedy. Now, the U.S. is on the brink of losing its measles elimination status, pending the outcome of the Pan American Health Organization meeting.

These arguments mirror those of Mayorkas' impeachment alleging incompetence at managing the southern border, therefore endangering Americans. It's also emotionally resonant as we are all watching the measles outbreak stack caskets in real time.

But "dereliction" and "competence" could prove qualitative rather than explicitly provable. Kennedy, for example, could claim that HHS is doing its best though measles is simply an intractable foe.

A stronger argument may thus lie in his cancellation of $8.9 billion in biomedical research grants. Unlike degrees of dereliction, grant cancellation is an unassailable fact that violates Congress' "power of the purse" as the funds had been earmarked. Regardless of party, if Congress approves funds for an expenditure then the expenditure should be discharged. For congressionally funded programs, the executive branch is executor, not executioner.

The administration's multi-front assault on research draws less attention than deserved given its long-term harm. A generation of medical scientists is being kneecapped, laboratories are shuttering, universities reeling. This magnitude of harm is incalculable because it is unknown -- what are the future cures that are now lost?

Even if impeachment proceeds, Kennedy's removal is a separate question. Removal in the Senate requires 67 votes; an admittedly high bar, never before achieved. The new Senate makeup is still pending narrow races. However, the final party distribution also shouldn't matter, as removal cannot be partisan in the first place. At 67 votes, removal will require both parties, so a politically centered impeachment would end with Kennedy still secretary. But questions of basic competence and our country's health should not be partisan.

Would a sufficient number of senators from both parties vote to remove? One lesson hopefully learned in this midterm election is that, regardless of party, politicians embrace unpopular figures at their peril, and Kennedy is deeply unpopular. The anti-vaccination movement is disproportionately loud, especially with conspiracists now in positions of power, though this fundamentally misrepresents voters' overwhelming support of vaccines. So, an electoral argument could resonate with a senator on either side of the aisle.

Kennedy's anemic support would likely further erode through the discovery process if impeachment proceeds. He's performed dismally during prior congressional testimony, as one would expect from someone with no formal training -- or even real-world work experience -- in healthcare, medicine, or science. The new Congress is on track for a record number of physicians, with doctors who support vaccination sitting on both sides of the aisle in both chambers. How many times have physicians, called before Congress, faced grilling from legislators who are lawyers? Now a lawyer, Kennedy, may face questions from leaders who are doctors.

So, is removal ultimately likely? To be frank, no, it remains definitively uphill. But it's worth pursuing.

Several counterarguments to impeachment exist, including the discretion given to the executive branch in managing agencies and the fact that senators previously voted for instatement while well aware of Kennedy's conspiratorial incompetence. There's also genuine concern for establishing precedent in which future secretaries become routinely impeached by opposing parties. Prior to 2024 there had only been one executive impeachment, and now there could be two in short order. (Meanwhile, the recent effort to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was blocked.) And finally, the effort would be an uphill battle, with the risk of Kennedy emerging stronger should removal fail.

But Kennedy is a historically dangerous individual. How many deaths emanate from his secretaryship and how many more will die if his power is left unchecked? In our work every day, doctors bravely contemplate actions for which we balance risk against the possibility of lives saved if successful. This is no different. Impeachment is fraught, and there are risks, but we have, in the coming months, a window of opportunity with action demanded by the net calculus of consequences.

The views reflected are the author's alone and not those of any organization or employer.
