> Cigna Healthcare, the insurance arm of the Cigna Group, announced that it named Stanley Crittenden, M.D., as its new chief medical officer.

In the role, Crittenden will the lead the insurer's clinical operations, and will be tasked with partnering with other key leaders across the company to support the central goals of improving access and simplifying the healthcare journey for both patients and providers.

Crittenden brings years of experience in managed care, value-based care and population health to the role, Cigna said in an announcement. He most recently served as CMO at Quantum Health, and also held leadership roles at Evergreen Nephrology, Anthem and Humana.

Crittenden is also board certified in internal medicine and nephrology, Cigna said.

“I’m honored to join Cigna Healthcare at this important moment in its transformation toward making health care simpler, more personalized and more affordable,” said Crittenden in the announcement. “I am committed to fostering a collaborative and supportive environment, doing everything we can to improve the experience and outcomes of all those we serve.”

The academic system's board of directors has kicked of a national search for a successor who would hold both titles, according to the March 12 announcement.

A 1990 Vanderbilt graduate himself, Balser spent years as a cardiac anesthesiologist and surgical intensivist at Johns Hopkins before returning to Vanderbilt in 1998. The organization's cash reserves also have also grown from 50 days to more than 110, with total cash on hand plus investments now exceeding $3 billion.

The announcement of his retirement also pointed to his role striking up new strategic partnerships, resetting contracts with commercial payers and heading the implementation of an enterprise resource planning system.

Beth Israel Lahey also notched new partnerships: a teaching relationship with UMass Chan School of Medicine and an upcoming cancer collaboration with the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Tabb will remain in his role while the system's board searches for his successor, a process expected to take about eight to 10 months, according to the announcement.

Stellar said that Smith's experience in the health insurance industry will help the company build out its platform. Stellar supports payers in value-based care by making it easier for providers to engage with these complex environments.

In addition, he'll play a key role in driving the financial evolution of its risk-based portfolio, including the tech-enabled accountable care organization, shaco.

"Stellar is already setting the pace for value-based care, and Raul adds the institutional caliber to match our growing scale," said Michael Meng, CEO and cofounder of Stellar Health. As president, Chinetti will be tasked with leading the insurer's strategy and operations across the state, including a focus on affordability, access and quality for individuals enrolled in TennCare, its Medicaid program.

She brings almost two decades of experience in Medicaid and long-term services and supports (LTSS) to the role, per an announcement from the insurer. Chinetti has held multiple roles within TennCare and most recently served as a staff vice president within Elevance Health's government unit, where she led a center of excellence in LTSS.

Chinetti is also a native of the state who lives in Nashville, with strong community relationships, the company said.

I look forward to working alongside TennCare, providers, advocates, and community leaders to strengthen rural and maternal health, enhance long-term services and supports, and deliver more coordinated, person-centered care that helps our members live healthier, more independent lives.”

> James Downing, M.D., will be stepping down from his role as president and CEO of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital near the end of 2026, the pediatric research hospital announced.

The physician executive has been with the organization for four decades, and has sat at its head for the past 12 years. Under his leadership St. Jude underwent the largest strategic expansion in its history, which included the completion of two separate strategic plans requiring nearly $20 billion of investment and over 2,300 new positions; major expansion to St. Jude's main campus; and greater international collaboration.

Prior to that he served as scientific director for eight years, a period in which he spearheaded the Pediatric Cancer Genome Project.

#5683. Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake."

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance."

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

Materials provided by The Peanut Institute. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5682. Last Batch of New Residency Spots Doled Out by CMS

— But medical societies say more federally funded positions are needed

As the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) doled out the final 200 of an additional 1,000 residency positions created by Congress 5 years ago, medical groups called for more federally funded spots to mitigate workforce shortages.

"While this final distribution represents a meaningful step forward, our country remains in desperate need of additional, permanent residency positions to help alleviate the persistent physician workforce shortage," David Skorton, MD, president and CEO of the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC), said in a statement.

In 2021, Congress passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act, which provided federal funding for 1,000 additional residency programs across the country. It was the first time federal funding for residency slots had been expanded since 1997.

These positions were meant to be awarded to hospitals fitting one of four criteria: being in a rural area, training residents in excess of their current graduate medical education (GME) caps, being in states with new medical schools or branch campuses, or serving areas designated to be in shortage of healthcare professionals.

The first 200 positions were awarded in 2022, and have been rolled out each year since. A second piece of legislation in 2023 created an additional 200 positions, which were awarded in 2025.

In total, 99 hospitals in 31 states received new residency positions, according to AAMC. About 42% of those positions went to primary care and psychiatry residency programs.

Kisha Davis, MD, MPH, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), applauded the additional slots for primary care positions.

"We know that more primary care physicians in underserved communities means better access to care and better health outcomes," Davis said in a statement emailed to MedPage Today. "The AAFP appreciates that CMS awarded 18 new family medicine residency slots in high-need areas" in this latest distribution.

However, while Davis called this "important progress," she added that "we can't lose sight of the fact that our nation does not have enough primary care physicians to meet patients' needs."

"We need concrete policy changes to ensure that more people go into primary care and can practice, and stay, in communities that need it the most," she noted.

AAFP said it is supporting legislation focused on residencies in primary care and rural and high-need areas, as well as funding for graduate programs that can help train primary care physicians to work in community-based settings.

AAMC called on Congress to pass the Resident Physician Shortage Reduction Act of 2025, which would gradually increase the number of Medicare-supported GME positions.

Bryan Carmody, MD, MPH, of Eastern Virginia Medical School in Norfolk, who runs a popular blog on medical education, noted an important caveat -- that hospitals can add residency positions even without federal funding, as long as they meet certain educational standards.

Indeed, hospitals have continued to add residency positions since the 1997 cap, "even without Congress subsidizing the cost," he told MedPage Today in an email.

Carmody said he's not sure that expanding federally funded positions will curb any alleged physician shortage; he also questions whether one exists. Instead, he argued that shortages are "distributional" and the "natural result of the incentives in our system."

"I'm not convinced that subsidizing positions in this way is going to do much of anything to address those problems," he added, noting that there's "no requirement that these newly trained residents will practice in a way that improves access for patients."

They may end up in primary care, or "they might work as a sub-specialist in the affluent suburbs," Carmody said. What they choose is more dictated by the incentives in the current system, he suggested, "and I don't see how those incentives are changed in the least by whether or not the hospital received extra public money to train them or not."

#5681. AI’s future starts to look surprisingly old-school: theCUBE’s KubeCon day one keynote analysis

The cloud-native community that turned Kubernetes into an enterprise standard is now being asked to carry artificial intelligence into production. As the underlying technology looks more alike from one company to the next, the hunt for domain-specific AI value is spotlighting how AI is put to work – and how to do so safely.

That shift is on display this week in Salt Lake City, where the Cloud Native Computing Foundation has added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track to its flagship conference. The plumbing built for microservices is proving to be the substrate for AI factories and agents, along with a renewed focus on tried-and-tested security and business principles, according to John Furrier (pictured, left), co-founder and executive analyst of theCUBE Research.

“The AI-native world that we’ve been covering and following and living — AI factories, the rise of agentic, which involves coding and now tasks — are all based fundamentally on the substrate of cloud-native technologies,” Furrier said. “This community is the heart and soul for the AI generation.”

Furrier spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight (right) as a part of a keynote analysis at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can secure and govern AI agents while turning proprietary knowledge and workflows into measurable business value rather than simply maximizing token consumption. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes has matured from a niche orchestration project into the reference platform for major clouds and neoclouds, and enterprises are now standardizing on it. That maturity is what makes it useful for AI, which needs the same control planes, scalable data layers and telemetry the community already worked out for microservices, according to Furrier.

“Kubernetes got boring, which means it’s working,” Furrier said. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world.”

Those lessons now apply to a pressing question: how much freedom enterprises will give AI agents inside real systems. Agents that cause trouble are usually poorly instructed rather than malicious, and the answer lies in context, identity and guardrails, according to Furrier. Perimeter-style security thinking is expected to make a comeback, along with a move away from token consumption as a measure of value and toward tangible business outcomes.

“We’re gonna get back to an era of, ‘Build something, show me what you built, present it for value,'” Furrier said. “If it’s worth something, there’s an exchange for value.”

#5680. Positive Medicaid signals, open enrollment trends: Recapping major payers' Q3 results

Positive Medicaid signals, open enrollment trends: Recapping major payers' Q3 results" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

While medical cost trend remains a pressure point for health insurers, leading companies cited some positive trends, too, heading into the final months of 2026.

UnitedHealth Group was once again the most profitable company among payers in the quarter, bringing in $4.1 billion in profit for Q3. That's up from a $2.3 billion haul in the prior-year quarter.

Through the first nine months of the year, profits were $15.9 billion at UHG, rising from $12 billion a year ago.

The healthcare giant has been in the midst of a critical financial turnaround since mid-2025, and in the most recent quarter, it highlighted some of the progress that it's logged over the past year at one of its biggest pain centers: Optum Health.

When the company posted an uncharacteristically poor quarter to start 2025, Optum Health was cited as one of the main pressure points. During its most recent call, Optum CEO Patrick Conway, M.D., said that the transition centered on a "continued return to value-based care principles" that sit at the core of Optum Health.

UnitedHealth also led the way on revenue in Q3, posting $112.7 billion. That's down slightly from $113.2 billion the company, reported in the third quarter of 2025.

CVS Health had the second-highest profit and revenue in Q3, bringing in $2.2 billion in earnings for the quarter. This marks a significant reversal from the prior-year quarter, when the company posted a nearly $4 billion loss.

CVS' revenue in the quarter was $108.4 billion, increasing from $102.9 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

The company's financial performance wasn't what dominated the headlines in Q3, however, as CVS shocked the industry in announcing plans to split its pharmacy business off and form two companies. The break-up is expected to close in the first half of 2028, and would establish CVS Pharmacy as its own company while Aetna and Caremark would remain together as CVS Health.

CVS CEO David Joyner said that the shift represents "a structure and plan that are built to win and represent the best path to create value over the long term."

The Cigna Group and Elevance Health were on par with one another in Q3 on profits, both earning $1.4 billion. Cigna wins out on revenue, though, with $73.7 billion, while Elevance reported $51.4 billion.

By comparison, Cigna posted $1.9 billion in profit and $69.7 billion in revenue in Q3 2025.

Core to the third-quarter conversation was the company's newly-unveiled Lead to One healthcare transformation strategy, which puts an emphasis on building a personalized experience for its members and customers.

Cigna said it plans to lean on all the segments under its umbrella to drive toward meeting individual member needs.

Elevance Health, meanwhile, increased its profit slightly year over year from $1.2 billion in Q3 2025. Revenues in the prior-year quarter were $50.7 million.

The company was one of several insurers in the quarter that noted positive signs in its Medicaid plans. While its leaders told investors that 2026 remains a "trough year" for its Medicaid business, improvements are likely in the cards for 2027.

That trend is supported by state rate setting that more fully accounts for the rising cost of care and the acuity of people enrolled in Medicaid, executives said. The member mix is only expected to increase in acuity as states roll out work requirements at the beginning of this year.

Similarly, Centene CEO Sarah London said the company sees an opportunity for "long-term growth" in the Medicaid market as part of its Q3 report. She noted similar trends around rate setting from states.

London added that the insurer has made significant progress on focus areas for improvement, such as behavioral health.

Centene posted a $71 million loss in the quarter, slimming its losses significantly from $6.6 billion in the prior-year quarter. That massive loss a year ago was backstopped by a one-time impairment charge of more than $6 billion.

Revenues in Q3 were $50.6 billion, up slightly from $49.7 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

Humana offered color on early signals in the Medicare annual enrollment period, which suggests that the insurer is poised for further growth in Medicare Advantage for next year. CEO Jim Rechtin said sign-ups through the early parts of the window indicate 2027 membership growth.

The insurer has had momentum around new sign-ups and has also done well in recapturing enrollments that were impacted by market exits, Rechtin said.

Humana posted a $162 million profit in the third quarter, down from $195 million a year ago. Revenues were $41.15 billion, growing from $32.6 billion in the prior-year quarter.

#5679. Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it

Heart disease linked to high cholesterol continues to be the leading cause of death worldwide. Although doctors have more treatment options than ever, many people still struggle to lower their cholesterol to safe levels. Others experience side effects that make existing medications difficult to take.

Researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have now identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why diets high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the body's ability to remove harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the bloodstream. Even more promising, they have identified an experimental drug that has already undergone safety testing in humans and could potentially interfere with this process.

The findings, published in Nature, could open the door to a new approach to treating high cholesterol.

"We've known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver's ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn't fully understand why," said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. "This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle."

The liver plays a central role in controlling cholesterol levels. It removes cholesterol from the bloodstream so it can be processed, broken down, and used by other parts of the body.

To accomplish this, liver cells rely on structures called LDL receptors. Located on the surface of these cells, the receptors work much like docking stations, capturing LDL cholesterol circulating in the blood and bringing it inside for processing.

The number of available receptors matters. When liver cells have more LDL receptors, they can remove more cholesterol from circulation. This is one reason widely used cholesterol medications, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, are effective. They help maintain or increase the number of receptors available to clear LDL cholesterol.

Scientists Uncover a Hidden Cholesterol Pathway

Using experiments involving mice and human cells, the researchers discovered a previously unrecognized process that interferes with the liver's ability to clear cholesterol. Over time, this mechanism reduces the number of LDL receptors, making it harder for the body to keep blood cholesterol under control.

The process begins with a protein known as Ral, which Saltiel had previously investigated in fat cells. The team discovered that consuming high amounts of dietary cholesterol activates Ral, setting off a chain of events that leads to the loss of LDL receptors. As Ral activity increases, fewer receptors remain available to remove harmful cholesterol from the bloodstream.

The researchers then identified another critical piece of the mechanism: an enzyme called cathepsin A (CTSA). This enzyme helps drive the process responsible for depleting LDL receptors.

When scientists used a small molecule inhibitor to block CTSA, the results were striking. LDL receptors became more stable, and levels of circulating LDL cholesterol dropped dramatically in mice.

The discovery is especially significant because the newly identified pathway is different from those targeted by current cholesterol medications. That distinction could make it possible to develop treatments for patients who do not respond adequately to existing drugs.

"There's still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can't get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now," said Saltiel. "This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap."

A Previously Tested Drug Could Accelerate Treatment

Discovering a new biological target is usually only the beginning of a lengthy drug development process. Researchers often need years of additional work to identify a suitable compound and determine whether it can be used safely in people.

In this case, however, the scientists may already have a promising candidate.

A drug designed to inhibit CTSA had previously been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. Although the program was eventually discontinued for strategic reasons, the experimental medication had already progressed through a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully evaluated for safety in humans.

That earlier work could provide an important advantage. Rather than beginning drug development from scratch, researchers believe the existing CTSA inhibitor may be ready to advance into a Phase 2 clinical trial to investigate its effectiveness against high cholesterol.

The findings are still at an early stage, and the drug has not yet been shown to lower cholesterol in humans. Nevertheless, its previous clinical testing could shorten the path toward determining whether this new treatment strategy works in patients.

"Luckily, there's an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that's already been shown to be safe in humans," said Saltiel. "We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial -- which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected."

Co-authors of the study include Xue Feng, Shuo Zhang, Yuqi Wang, Twisha Kurlagunda, Allyssa Sit, Sadatsugu Sakane, Se Yong Park, Churaibhon Wisessaowapak, Kaylee Nguyen, Jamie Yan, Himani Pothulu, Catherine Dinh, Felicia Chu, Yuyao Ren, Bichen Zhang, Patrick Secrest, Chao-Wei Hung, Preethi Veeragandham, Yuliya Skorobogatko, Tatiana Kisseleva, and Amit R. Majithia at UC San Diego; Priya Jaishankar, Pusu Yang, and Adam Renslo at the University of California, San Francisco; Linmeng Han and Peng Zhao at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; and Philip L.S.M. Gordts at the University of Utah.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health (Grants P30DK063491, R01DK117551, R01DK128796, and R01DK135289) and an American Diabetes Association postdoctoral fellowship (1-25-PDF-76).

Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5678. Anticoagulants Reign Supreme in VTE Prevention After Joint Replacement

— Large comparative-effectiveness trial fails to find noninferiority with aspirin

Aspirin didn't prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE) as well as anticoagulants did for patients undergoing elective hip or knee replacements, the randomized PEPPER trial showed.

For the primary composite endpoint of death from any cause or symptomatic VTE over 6 months after 30 days of prophylaxis, 1.26% of aspirin recipients had an event compared with 1.23% of warfarin recipients and 0.94% of rivaroxaban (Xarelto) recipients, reported Vincent Pellegrini Jr., MD, of the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth in Lebanon, New Hampshire, and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine.

In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin, 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban, and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban.

The differences between aspirin and the two anticoagulants did not meet the criterion for noninferiority (P=0.09 and P=0.10), although the comparison between the two anticoagulants did (P=0.01).

Risks of a primary safety outcome event -- bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction -- were 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin; 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin; and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin, none of which met the criterion for noninferiority.

"By providing comparative risk-benefit profiles regarding thrombosis and bleeding for medications used for VTE prophylaxis, these findings can help inform preoperative decision making for patients undergoing elective total hip or knee replacement," the authors wrote.

"Aspirin is widely favored among orthopedic surgeons in the United States and Canada because of low cost, minimal bleeding risk, and the absence of required monitoring, in addition to concerns about anticoagulants with regard to increased risks of bleeding and associated wound complications, readmission, or reoperation," they noted. "However, evidence to confirm the effectiveness of aspirin as compared with anticoagulants [had been] scant."

The results might seem to contradict the findings of the EPCAT III trial published earlier this year, which showed that an aspirin-only approach was as effective and safe as rivaroxaban.

"However, at closer glance, I think they tell two parallel stories," Geoffrey Barnes, MD, of the Frankel Cardiovascular Center at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, told MedPage Today.

"Taken together, these two studies suggest that some component of anticoagulant therapy likely benefits patients after hip and/or knee arthroplasty surgery. As such, it might make sense to employ a short course of anticoagulation (e.g., rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 5 days) followed by aspirin therapy in most hip and knee surgery patients at average risk of postoperative VTE," he argued.

Pellegrini and team noted that EPCAT III and another trial comparing 5 days of rivaroxaban then aspirin versus rivaroxaban alone were much smaller and both had larger noninferiority margins that were equal to the entire projected incidence of VTE and excluded patients at high risk for VTE.

The PEPPER trial randomly assigned patients at 34 centers in the U.S. and Canada who were undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis to receive open-label treatment with aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days.

VTE made up most of the events in the primary effectiveness endpoint. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference in the primary composite effectiveness outcome measure was 0.69 percentage points. Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results to those of the per-protocol analysis.

The trial included 15,317 patients in the primary per-protocol analysis: 7,214 with hip arthroplasty and 8,103 with knee arthroplasty. However, a "very large number of patients [more than 3,500] were excluded from both the warfarin and rivaroxaban groups because of crossover and an inability to stay on the assigned drug," Barnes noted. "While measured covariates were balanced across all three groups, this large difference in exclusions may have introduced unmeasured confounding."

Cost and monitoring affected adherence to rivaroxaban and warfarin, respectively, such that fewer patients crossed over from the aspirin group. Indeed, the per-protocol aspirin cohort (6,090 participants) was 22% larger than the rivaroxaban cohort (4,996 participants) and was 44% larger than the warfarin cohort (4,231 participants), "despite similar initial randomization numbers," Pellegrini and team acknowledged.

The researchers agreed that the crossovers compromised the benefits of randomization "but reflect the pragmatic comparative-effectiveness design."
