#5650. Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds

A major new study suggests that even modest amounts of alcohol may carry serious health consequences. Researchers found that drinking levels many Americans consider moderate are associated with higher risks of premature death, disability, cancer, heart disease, and other long-term health problems.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research challenges the longstanding belief that moderate drinking is harmless or may even provide health benefits. The findings suggest that alcohol's risks begin at relatively low levels of consumption and increase as people drink more.

"This study provides the most comprehensive U.S. estimates to date of lifetime risks of alcohol-attributable mortality and morbidity, showing that even moderate levels of consumption increase the risk of premature death and disability," said study co-author Katherine M. Keyes, PhD, professor of Epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

"No protective effect of drinking was observed even at low levels," added Keyes, whose research examines alcohol and other substance use across different stages of life.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," said lead study author Kevin Shield, PhD, an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

Major Study Examines the Lifetime Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand how drinking affects health over a lifetime, researchers from the United States and Canada conducted an extensive review of existing scientific evidence.

Medical experts evaluated more than 7,200 scientific articles examining diseases and injuries associated with alcohol consumption. They used this evidence to determine how drinking influences the risk of individual health conditions, then combined those findings with large national health data sets.

Using statistical models, the team estimated how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious illnesses or dying prematurely over a lifetime.

The analysis covered a wide range of health problems linked to alcohol, including cardiovascular disease, liver disease, injuries, and several forms of cancer. Among the cancers examined were those affecting the esophagus, mouth, and breast.

By considering these conditions together, the researchers were able to estimate alcohol's overall health burden rather than focusing on individual diseases.

Why Two Drinks a Day May Be Riskier Than You Think

One of the study's most important findings concerns drinking habits that many people would not consider excessive.

Consuming two alcoholic drinks per day, a level often viewed as socially moderate, was associated with a substantially higher risk of premature death attributable to alcohol.

The findings also provide more specific information than the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines, which recommend that Americans "limit alcoholic beverages" but do not identify a particular amount that can be consumed safely.

Earlier dietary recommendations set daily limits of two alcoholic drinks for men and one for women. However, what counts as a single drink depends on the beverage and its alcohol content. A standard drink generally corresponds to 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits, although differences in alcohol concentration can change those amounts.

According to the researchers, the newer guidelines communicate a useful 'less-is-best' principle but lack specific numerical estimates that would help people understand how health risks change with consumption.

Their analysis was intended to fill that gap by measuring risks across a broad range of drinking levels.

Does Moderate Drinking Have Any Health Benefits?

For years, moderate alcohol consumption has sometimes been promoted as beneficial for cardiovascular health. The new findings cast doubt on that idea when the full range of alcohol-related health effects is considered.

The researchers found no statistically significant protective effect on overall health at any level of alcohol consumption.

They acknowledged that relatively low alcohol intake may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. Ischemic heart disease occurs when reduced blood flow deprives the heart muscle of the oxygen it needs, often because arteries have narrowed or become blocked.

However, any potential cardiovascular benefits must be considered alongside alcohol's association with cancer, liver disease, injuries, and other serious conditions.

When the researchers combined these outcomes, the potential benefits were outweighed by the harmful effects, even among people consuming seven alcoholic drinks per week.

This broader assessment helps explain why a drinking habit that appears beneficial when examining one disease may still increase overall health risks.

Although the findings offer a clearer picture of the long-term dangers of alcohol, the researchers emphasize that the estimates describe risks across populations, not the precise likelihood that any individual will develop a particular disease.

The statistical models relied on "the best possible data," according to the research team. Nevertheless, personal health outcomes can differ considerably depending on genetics, lifestyle, drinking patterns, and other individual factors.

To calculate the overall burden of alcohol consumption, the investigators estimated risks for health conditions already known to have a causal relationship with drinking. They then combined those estimates to assess the total impact.

The researchers also acknowledged that scientific understanding of alcohol's health effects continues to evolve. Emerging evidence suggests that drinking may be associated with additional conditions, including pancreatic cancer, that require further investigation.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," said Keyes and Shield.

Despite these uncertainties, the results offer an important reference point: alcohol consumption above one drink per day was associated with increased health risks for both men and women.

The researchers believe that giving people more specific information about these risks can help them make better decisions about how much they drink.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking."

Why the Findings Matter for U.S. Alcohol Guidelines

The research also raises questions about how scientific evidence is considered when federal drinking recommendations are developed.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former associate administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, discussed the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the federal dietary guidance process.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Vincent's comments highlight concerns about whether the research received appropriate consideration during the development of national recommendations.

The study's findings reinforce the importance of understanding alcohol's cumulative health effects rather than assuming that moderate consumption is beneficial or risk-free. Although individual risks vary, the overall pattern was clear: greater alcohol consumption was associated with greater harm, and the researchers found no overall health advantage to drinking.

The research was funded by Synergy Enterprises Inc. and the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

A former Eli Lilly sales rep filed a lawsuit alleging that she was fired after complaining the company was promoting its Mounjaro diabetes drug to combat weight loss before receiving regulatory approval to do so.

Jennifer Mansion, who was hired as a senior territory manager in Dallas four years ago, claimed that she observed other Lilly sales reps promoting the diabetes drug as a salve for obesity. Mansion also contended that a physician touted Mounjaro as a weight loss option during a luncheon sponsored by the drugmaker, according to the suit filed in federal court in Texas.

Such promotions are known as off-label marketing in the pharmaceutical industry. The phrase refers to promoting a medicine for a usage that was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. A physician may prescribe a medicine for an unapproved use, but a drugmaker is not permitted to market its drug for that purpose.

#5648. Carelon agrees to pay $10M to settle ghost network, coverage denial allegations in New York

Carelon agrees to pay $10M to settle ghost network, coverage denial allegations in New York" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Carelon will pay more than $10 million across two settlements in New York over mental health networks and coverage denials.

The company, a division of Elevance Health, will pay $2.35 million in penalties, fees and costs as well as up to $8 million in restitution for members who paid out-of-pocket for out-of-network mental healthcare, to reimburse those whose claims were improperly denied or to overhaul its networks.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said in an announcement that the settlements resolve two investigations from her office that determined the company misled members by directing them to seek care from providers that were out-of-network—through so-called "ghost networks"—and improperly denied coverage for treatment for substance abuse disorder.

James noted that Carelon administers behavioral health benefits for multiple plans, including Anthem Blue Cross, EmblemHealth, Independent Health and the Empire Plan, which covers state and local government workers.

Across these insurers, Carelon manages behavioral health benefits for more than 4 million people in the state, James said.

The alleged behavior also goes against a 2015 agreement with the AG's office, where the company agreed that it would maintain accurate provider networks and "use approved criteria" when denying substance abuse treatments.

"When someone is ready to seek help for a mental health condition or addiction, every day matters," said James. “Carelon left New Yorkers calling provider after provider who could not see them and made it harder for people to get the treatment to which they were entitled."

"These settlements will help people get the care they need and put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets," she said.

Elevance Health said in a statement to Fierce Healthcare that it is committed to ensuring patients have access to the most up-to-date provider information.

"Carelon Behavioral Health is committed to helping people find and access high-quality mental health and substance use disorder care. Accurate, up-to-date provider information is an important part of that effort," the company said. "We continue to invest in tools and processes that support accurate provider information and work closely with providers and other partners to help connect consumers with the care they need."

Carelon was hit with a lawsuit in April over the alleged ghost networks and their impact on the Empire Plan in particular. In the case, plaintiff's attorneys conducted secret shopper calls to analyze Carelon's network, calling 300 providers. Just 17% of those contacted took insurance and were open to new patients.

These "ghost networks" have also drawn concern in other markets, such as for maternal care services in Medicaid and in Medicare Advantage. A study released last month found that commercial plans also routinely have inaccurate provider directories.

#5646. Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch

Drinking tea regularly may offer important benefits for your heart and blood vessels, according to a massive study involving nearly 500,000 adults. Researchers found that people who consumed tea regularly had a lower risk of developing several vascular diseases compared with those who did not drink tea.

However, the findings also revealed some unexpected differences. The type of tea, how strong it was, and even the temperature at which it was consumed were all associated with vascular health. While certain tea drinking habits were linked to a lower risk of disease, drinking tea at extremely high temperatures appeared to have the opposite association.

The research, published in the Journal of Internal Medicine, provides new insights into how an everyday beverage may be connected to long-term cardiovascular health.

Nearly 500,000 Adults Reveal a Link Between Tea and Vascular Health

The study included 485,934 adults in China who were followed for a median of 9.05 years. During that period, researchers recorded 14,863 cases involving several types of vascular disease.

These conditions included cardiovascular disease, which affects the heart and blood vessels, and cerebrovascular disease, which involves blood vessels that supply the brain. The researchers also examined pulmonary heart disease, a condition in which problems involving the lungs or their blood vessels place strain on the heart, and peripheral artery disease, which occurs when arteries carrying blood to areas such as the legs become narrowed or blocked.

Although these conditions affect different parts of the body, they share an important feature: they interfere with the circulation of blood, which delivers oxygen and nutrients to organs and tissues.

When the researchers compared tea drinking habits with the incidence of these diseases, they found that regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of the combined vascular outcomes.

The relationship also appeared to vary with the amount consumed. Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk occurred at approximately six to eight cups per day.

This does not necessarily mean that drinking more tea directly prevents disease or that everyone should consume that amount. Because the research was observational, it could identify connections between tea drinking and health outcomes but could not establish that tea itself was responsible for the differences.

Black Tea vs. Green Tea: Does the Type Matter?

One particularly interesting finding involved the type of tea participants consumed.

Black tea showed more consistent associations with a reduced risk of vascular disease than green tea. This suggests that different varieties of tea may not have identical relationships with cardiovascular health.

Both black and green tea come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, but they undergo different processing methods. Black tea is typically allowed to undergo extensive oxidation, a chemical process that changes the composition of compounds in the leaves, while green tea is processed to limit oxidation.

Tea naturally contains plant compounds known as polyphenols, which have attracted scientific interest because of their antioxidant properties and potential effects on blood vessel function. Antioxidants can help limit certain types of cellular damage caused by reactive molecules.

However, the study does not establish whether these compounds explain the observed differences between black and green tea.

Tea strength also appeared to matter. Participants who drank tea of moderate strength had the lowest associated vascular disease risk, suggesting that stronger tea was not necessarily linked to greater benefits.

Drinking Tea Too Hot May Carry Unexpected Risks

Perhaps the most surprising finding concerned tea temperature.

Although regular tea consumption was generally associated with a reduced risk of vascular disease, drinking tea described as "burning hot" was linked to an increased risk.

The result suggests that the temperature of tea may be an important consideration alongside how much people drink and which variety they prefer.

Very hot beverages can expose tissues in the mouth and digestive tract to high temperatures, but the study did not establish the biological mechanism behind the observed vascular risk. It also did not identify a specific temperature at which tea becomes harmful.

The findings therefore should not be interpreted as proof that drinking extremely hot tea directly causes vascular disease. They do, however, raise questions about whether certain drinking habits could offset some of the favorable associations seen with regular tea consumption.

Tea, Exercise, and Smoking Habits May Work Together

The researchers also examined how tea consumption related to other lifestyle factors, including smoking and physical activity.

Their analysis showed that people who regularly drank tea, were not current smokers, and maintained high levels of physical activity had the lowest vascular disease risk.

"Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk," the authors wrote.

These results highlight the importance of considering overall lifestyle rather than looking at a single food or beverage in isolation.

Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health in several ways, including improving circulation, helping regulate blood pressure, and supporting the function of the heart and blood vessels. Avoiding smoking also reduces exposure to substances that can damage blood vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.

Taken together, the findings suggest that tea drinking may be one component of a broader pattern of habits associated with better vascular health.

Although more research is needed to determine whether tea consumption directly influences disease risk, the study offers encouraging evidence that this widely consumed beverage is associated with cardiovascular health. It also highlights an important distinction: when it comes to tea, the amount, variety, strength, and temperature may all be worth considering.

#5645. BJC Health, St. Luke's reveal plans to merge

BJC Health, St. Luke's reveal plans to merge" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Missouri-based BJC Health and St. Luke's Hospital are planning a merger.

The providers announced on Wednesday that they have signed a letter of intent to come together, bringing the community hospital into the fold with the Show Me State's largest health system. The pair expects the deal to improve access and improve local care in the St. Louis region.

St. Luke's said in the announcement that the letter "follows a deliberate and thorough evaluation process," conducted by its board of directors and leaders "to identify the best path forward for St. Luke’s and the communities it serves."

The providers said they intend to spend the next several months building a definitive agreement to merge and complete the needed regulatory approval process. In the interim, St. Luke's patients can continue to see their regular physicians.

BJC said in the announcement that it is committed to supporting local, community care while also allowing St. Luke's to tap into the resources available across its ecosystem. It intends to provide key support for the hospital's clinical technology and equipment as well as backing infrastructure and facility upgrades and provider recruitment and retention efforts.

St. Luke’s is a well-respected hospital, known for clinical quality, patient experience and the personal attention given to everyone in our care,” said Andy Bagnall, CEO of St. Luke’s, in the announcement. “At the same time, the demands of health care delivery and our communities’ needs are changing rapidly."

We believe that together with BJC, we can strengthen patient care in St. Louis in ways we could not easily do on our own," Bagnall said.

Nick Barto, CEO of BJC Health, called St. Luke's "a trusted leader in our region with a reputation for excellence."

"Together, we will build on that foundation through our aligned clinical strengths and complementary services," Barto said in the announcement. "Our shared goal is to expand access to differentiated, high-quality care while ensuring St. Luke’s can continue serving the growing communities of West St. Louis for generations to come.”

#5643. Financial institutions confront the complexities of scaling AI

AI in financial services is moving beyond the pilot phase as banks, capital markets firms, mortgage lenders and other organizations begin deploying the technology more broadly. The challenge is shifting toward managing AI responsibly at scale while meeting strict requirements for security, compliance and customer trust.

The AWS Financial Services Symposium highlighted that transition in May. As financial institutions expand their use of AI, they have opportunities to test new applications without committing to large-scale deployments, according to Scott Mullins, former general manager of AWS Worldwide Financial Services at Amazon Web Services Inc.

“You can spin this stuff up really quickly; you can experiment with it,” he said during the symposium. “You can show that it actually achieves the things that you want to achieve within specific policy guidelines and frameworks, and you can actually evaluate whether that governance is holding.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s ongoing coverage of the AWS Financial Services Symposium. (* Disclosure below.)

Moving AI from experimentation into production requires financial institutions to address a different set of challenges. Beyond demonstrating that the technology works, organizations must establish the governance and operational safeguards needed to support AI across regulated business processes, according to Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst for application development at theCUBE Research.

“Our AppDev research shows that 92% of organizations now integrate AI into at least one stage of the software delivery lifecycle, yet only about one-third have established the governance, security, and operational maturity required for production-scale AI,” he said. “In banking, capital markets and insurance, the gap is even more pronounced because compliance, explainability, and customer trust are non-negotiable. The next phase of AI adoption will be defined less by model performance and more by platforms that embed policy controls, auditability and security into AI-enabled workflows while improving customer experiences and operational efficiency.”

Infosys Ltd. is addressing those requirements through its AI platform, which incorporates safeguards and controls intended to help financial institutions deploy AI while managing risk, according to Rajaram R.K., vice president and head of sales for financial services at Infosys.

“It has the securities [and] it has the guardrails. It has the token economics … all the capabilities that an organization would need,” he told theCUBE.

Financial institutions face stringent regulatory requirements, making security, auditability and recovery essential to their operations. As banks, insurers and capital markets firms expand their use of AI, those requirements take on additional importance, particularly when automated systems begin influencing business decisions. Despite these challenges, financial institutions are among the sectors leading the way in AI adoption.

“The organizations that treat AI as a regulated business capability, not simply a technology initiative, will be best positioned to accelerate innovation while maintaining resilience and meeting evolving regulatory expectations,” Nashawaty said.

Applying those established risk-management practices to AI requires organizations to consider how automated systems access data, make decisions and operate within existing policies. The challenge is extending governance and operational controls to AI-enabled workflows without undermining the efficiency and innovation those systems are intended to deliver.

Financial institutions are finding practical applications for AI in customer service and employee productivity. At New York Life Insurance Co., reducing routine manual work is giving employees more time to provide personalized service and respond proactively to customers’ needs, according to Kristina Welke, vice president at New York Life.

“We really felt there was a lot of opportunity to support them, remove the manual work they do every day, enable them to provide that consultative support, be proactive versus reactive,” she told theCUBE.

Fifth Third Bank is using conversational AI to improve customer interactions and reduce average call-handling time. The bank is using Amazon Connect to support its customer-service operations, according to Kevin Anderson, product manager on the AI transformation team at Fifth Third Bank.

“Amazon Connect really lays the foundation as it solves for not only messaging but voice as well, allows for AI and automation,” he explained.

For financial institutions, scaling AI depends in part on modernizing the infrastructure that supports data-intensive workloads. Cloud platforms can provide the flexibility to deploy new capabilities while maintaining access to existing systems, making modernization an important consideration as organizations expand their AI initiatives.

Mortgage lender PennyMac Financial Services recently expanded its agreement with Amazon Web Services to accelerate modernization of its proprietary mortgage servicing platform, Plaisse. The partnership also includes plans to deploy enterprise-grade AI capabilities and further develop the platform.

As financial institutions modernize their infrastructure, they also need ways to move and manage data without disrupting existing operations. NetApp Inc. is addressing those requirements through storage and data-management capabilities designed to support migration, resilience and performance in AWS environments, according to Jacob Lim, cloud solutions architect at NetApp.

“We create value for customers by making it simple to migrate and run their data in AWS by combining proven NetApp ONTAP capabilities, such as space-efficient snapshots, near-instant data cloning capabilities with minimal storage overhead and storage performance,” he told theCUBE. “Then, there is also the highly efficient data replication and ransomware detection engine natively built into the operating system directly. Combined with AWS scale and elasticity, customers gained resilience, performance and operational simplicity in the cloud.”

Scaling AI in financial services brings new challenges

As financial institutions incorporate AI into daily operations, managing the complexity of those deployments is becoming an increasingly important challenge. According to PagerDuty’s 2026 State of AI-First Operations report, 59% of surveyed banks were actively incorporating AI into their operations, while another 34% were discussing implementation. As adoption expands, institutions must determine how to govern these systems, maintain data quality and integrate AI into existing workflows.

“I think you’re going to see AI really become: How do we govern, how do we use [and] how do we make sure the data’s clean? How does it become [about] helping us be more efficient in what we’re doing in day-in and day-out operations?” Todd McNabb, chief revenue officer of PagerDuty Inc., told theCUBE.

Technology providers are responding to the demand for faster enterprise AI deployment. AWS’ recently announced $1 billion investment in forward-deployed engineering, for example, is intended to help customers develop and deploy agentic AI applications more quickly. For financial institutions, however, the measure of success will extend beyond deployment speed to how effectively AI can operate within existing systems, regulatory requirements and business processes.

#5642. Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day

Eating mango and avocado every day could offer unexpected benefits for heart health, according to new research. In a study lasting just eight weeks, adults with prediabetes who regularly ate both fruits experienced improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, without gaining weight or consuming more calories.

The findings could be especially relevant to the one in three (98 million) Americans with prediabetes, a condition in which blood sugar levels are elevated but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, the research suggests that incorporating these two nutrient-rich fruits into everyday meals may help support cardiovascular health.

Researchers at Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) investigated the effects of an Avocado-Mango (AM) diet that included one medium Hass avocado and one cup of fresh mango each day. Participants followed this eating plan for eight weeks, while a comparison group consumed a similar diet in which the fruits were replaced with carbohydrate-based foods containing equivalent calories.

The results revealed notable differences between the groups, particularly in how well their blood vessels functioned and how their blood pressure changed over time.

One of the clearest improvements involved the ability of blood vessels to expand as blood flows through them. This flexibility helps maintain healthy circulation and is an important indicator of cardiovascular health.

To evaluate this response, researchers measured flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a commonly used test of endothelial function (blood vessel health). The endothelium is the thin layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, where it helps regulate circulation and the widening and narrowing of arteries.

Among participants eating avocado and mango, the measurement increased significantly to 6.7%. In contrast, it declined to 4.6% in the control group. The difference suggests that regularly consuming these fruits may help blood vessels function more effectively.

Blood pressure measurements also showed encouraging changes, especially among male participants. Men in the control group experienced an average increase of 5 points (mmHg) in central blood pressure, while those consuming avocado and mango saw a reduction of approximately 1.9 points.

Diastolic blood pressure, the lower number in a blood pressure reading, reflects the pressure inside arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Maintaining healthy levels is important because elevated blood pressure can place additional strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers noted that the differences observed in the study could be clinically meaningful if they persist over time.

Importantly, the cardiovascular improvements occurred without significant changes in participants' body weight or total calorie consumption. This suggests that the nutritional quality of the foods people eat may influence heart health even when their weight remains stable.

“This research reinforces the power of food-first strategies to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in vulnerable populations like those with prediabetes,” said Britt Burton-Freeman, PhD, Principal Investigator and Professor at Illinois Tech. “It’s an encouraging message: small, nutrient-dense additions—like incorporating avocado and mango into meals and snacks—may support heart health without the need for strict rules or major dietary overhauls.”

Beyond the improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, participants eating mango and avocado consumed more fiber, vitamin C, and monounsaturated fat. These nutrients are associated with cardiovascular wellness and may help explain some of the observed benefits.

Researchers also identified improvements in certain indicators of kidney health, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a measurement used to assess how effectively the kidneys filter waste from the blood.

However, the fruits did not produce significant improvements in every health measurement. Cholesterol levels, blood sugar, and markers of inflammation remained largely unchanged compared with the control group.

Together, the results suggest that regularly including nutrient-rich fruits in the diet could be a practical way to support cardiovascular health, particularly for people with prediabetes who face an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Although mango and avocado have very different flavors and nutritional profiles, they provide complementary nutrients that support several aspects of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Mango provides dietary fiber (2g/serving, 7% DV, Mango serving size: ¾ cup) and is an excellent source of vitamin C (50% DV). Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage, while fiber contributes to healthy digestion and may help with blood sugar regulation, weight management, and cardiovascular wellness.

Avocado offers another combination of potentially beneficial nutrients. It contains fiber (3g/serving, 11% DV, Avocado serving size: 50 g (1/3 of a medium avocado)), which plays a role in managing cholesterol, blood sugar, and body weight.

It also supplies unsaturated fats (6g unsaturated fats), which can support heart health by helping reduce LDL cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol, when they replace less healthy fats in the diet. Additionally, avocado contains potassium (250mg, 6% DV), a mineral involved in regulating blood pressure.

By providing fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and potassium, mango and avocado offer a convenient way to increase the nutritional value of everyday meals. However, the study did not establish whether eating the two fruits together provides greater benefits than consuming either fruit separately.

Incorporating these fruits into meals does not require a complicated eating plan. Their contrasting flavors and textures make them useful ingredients in salads, smoothies, and grain bowls.

For example, fresh mango can add sweetness to a savory dish, while avocado contributes a rich, creamy texture. Both can be used in recipes such as Mango Avocado Tuna Ceviche or an Avocado and Mango Topper.

Additional recipes and nutritional information are available at Mango.org and LoveOneToday.com.

The investigation included 82 adults between the ages of 25 and 60 who had prediabetes and were classified as having overweight or obesity (BMI 25–35 kg/m2). All participants were generally healthy, did not smoke, were not following specialized diets, and had no major chronic medical conditions.

Over eight weeks, participants followed calorie-controlled eating plans modeled on typical American dietary patterns. One group ate a medium Hass avocado and a cup of fresh mango daily, while the control group received carbohydrate-based alternatives with comparable calorie content.

To make the comparison as consistent as possible, researchers prepared and supplied meals covering 75% of each participant's estimated daily calorie needs. Participants chose their remaining foods independently, allowing some flexibility while helping the researchers limit differences between the two diets and encourage adherence.

The primary measurement was flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a noninvasive method for assessing how effectively blood vessels respond to increased circulation. Researchers also examined blood pressure, blood sugar, and other metabolic indicators, inflammation, kidney function, and dietary nutrient intake.

Despite the additional fruits, the avocado and mango group did not experience significant changes in body weight or overall calorie intake. This finding suggests that incorporating nutrient-dense foods into an otherwise balanced diet may improve certain aspects of cardiometabolic health without necessarily contributing to weight gain.

The study had several strengths, including its carefully controlled feeding approach, two parallel comparison groups, and emphasis on whole fruits rather than isolated nutrients or supplements.

However, researchers also acknowledged important limitations. The intervention lasted only eight weeks, so it remains unclear whether the improvements would persist over months or years. The participants also represented a relatively narrow population of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, meaning the findings may not apply equally to people with different health conditions or dietary habits.

The research measured cardiovascular risk indicators rather than long-term outcomes such as heart attacks or strokes. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the observed changes translate into lasting reductions in cardiovascular disease risk.

Nevertheless, the findings offer an encouraging indication that relatively modest changes in food choices may benefit blood vessel health, even without weight loss or a major dietary overhaul.

#5641. Opinion: Low-income parents can’t afford to take chances with nutritious food their picky eaters might reject

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Priya Fielding-Singh and Darcy Cherlin

Fielding-Singh is the director of policy and programs at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University. Cherlin is the research project manager at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University.

As high food costs and cuts to food assistance squeeze families’ budgets, concerns are growing about whether low-income parents will be able to keep putting food on the table.

But these financial pressures threaten to do more than increase hunger. They also risk harming children’s diets and health in the long run — by making nutritious foods not only harder to afford, but also increasingly risky for parents to buy.

To understand why, consider the most universal of parenting frustrations: picky eating. Most parents experience it, but the stakes vary widely. For well-off parents, watching a child push away a helping of vegetables is annoying but manageable. A carrot left untouched one day can simply mean trying again the next.

But for parents living close to the bone, that same rejected carrot is more than frustrating. It represents money that could have been spent on something their child would have actually eaten.

Simply put: Children’s food refusals come at a cost — one that few cash-strapped families can afford.

Such financial risks profoundly shape how low-income parents feed their kids, as sociologists have documented for years. A decade ago, Caitlin Daniel first showed how the risk of wasting money on rejected nutritious foods led low-income parents to prioritize buying less healthy items they knew their kids would eat. Years later, one of us (Priya) found that catering to kids’ preferences was also driven in part by parents’ earlier bouts of food insecurity: Determined to spare their children those experiences, caregivers often relied on familiar, comforting foods they knew would fill their kids’ stomachs.

Our newest study adds another dimension to this picture. Low-income parents across three states described going to considerable lengths to prioritize children’s nutrition, often at the expense of their own diets.

At the same time, to conserve resources and keep dinnertime from turning into a battle, they paid close attention to their kids’ likes and prioritized buying what they knew their children would eat. As one mother put it, she’d rather her daughter be “happy and fed than sad and hungry.”

Within such severe financial constraints, catering to children’s preferences is strategic. But it can also undermine children’s diets and health over time. That’s because raising kids to be healthy eaters is a long game: Children’s tastes develop gradually as they encounter and become familiar with different foods, and young children often need to try unfamiliar, healthier ones — like bitter vegetables — multiple times before accepting them.

That’s why pediatricians and nutrition experts routinely encourage parents to keep offering fruits and vegetables, even when kids turn them down. It’s smart advice, but it assumes parents can shoulder the costs of following it.

For families with little money to spare, doing so has always been a gamble. And today, it’s becoming an even bigger one. Groceries now cost nearly a third more in dollar terms than they did in 2020. Meanwhile, participation in SNAP — the nation’s largest food assistance program — has fallen by over 5 million people, including an estimated 2 million children, since summer 2025.

These economic pressures are now showing up in parents’ food decisions. A national survey found that more than half of low-income parents reported cutting back on groceries, while over two-thirds worried about having to choose between paying bills and buying healthy food for their children.

Forcing parents into such trade-offs doesn’t just threaten their ability to keep children fed. It also undermines their efforts to help children eat — and learn to enjoy — nutritious foods.

Fortunately, there are ways to address both problems.

First and foremost, we need to ensure children have enough to eat. That means restoring access to food assistance. The next Congress should reverse the cuts to SNAP enacted through H.R. 1 and stop SNAP benefit costs from being shifted to states — a shift that could jeopardize continued access to a program millions of families depend on to put food on the table. To make a bill reversing the cuts veto-proof, it should be a bipartisan effort.

But we also need to invest in programs that support parents’ efforts to feed their children nutritious foods, including incentives that make those purchases more affordable and less financially risky. Protecting and strengthening WIC’s fruit and vegetable benefit and expanding produce incentives like Double Up Food Bucks for SNAP recipients can help families stretch their grocery dollars further, giving them more room to buy nutritious foods their children might not eat the first time around.

Schools and childcare programs must also be critical partners in this work. Beyond providing nutritious meals, they can give kids regular opportunities to encounter and try healthier foods without leaving parents to shoulder the full financial burden. Expanding initiatives like the Department of Agriculture’s Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program and Farm to School programs, which help introduce children to new foods through fresh produce, taste tests, gardens, and other activities, can help.

Nutrition experts are right to encourage parents to keep introducing healthy foods, even when their children refuse them. But advice that families can’t afford to follow simply won’t cut it. We need food policies that not only ensure children have enough to eat, but also give parents the resources and support to help them develop healthy eating habits that last.

Priya Fielding-Singh is the director of policy and programs at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University and the author of “How the Other Half Eats: The Untold Story of Food and Inequality in America.” Darcy Cherlin is the research project manager at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University.

#5640. NYC Property Transfers Show Growing Warning Signs of Deed Theft

More than one-third of New York City transfers of one- to three-family homes from individual owners to companies last year had gaps in their ownership records that researchers say could signal deed theft or other predatory schemes.

The findings come just days after Victor Quimis, 40, became the first person convicted under New York's criminal deed theft law, after admitting to stealing the home of an elderly Queens widow who was receiving hospice care.

Quimis and an accomplice forged Renuka Bherwani's signature to transfer ownership of the Kew Gardens Hills home she had owned for decades, according to prosecutors—first to themselves and then to a corporation controlled by Quimis.

He subsequently obtained a $552,500 mortgage against the property, pocketing more than $300,000 after paying off existing debts. Bherwani's family discovered the theft only after receiving a city notice congratulating Quimis on becoming the home's new owner.

“My mother lived in that house for nearly 40 years, and she was in hospice care in it when her home was stolen out from under her," said Kamal Bherwani, Renuka’s son and the executor of her estate. “Deed theft targets the elderly and the vulnerable, and I urge any family that sees something wrong with a deed to call the Attorney General's Office immediately."

Researchers at New York University's Furman Center are now seeking to better detect potential fraud through patterns in public ownership records, too.

Their latest analysis found that 34.5% of transfers from individual homeowners to companies in 2025 involved a mismatch between the seller on the new deed and the buyer on the previous deed—the highest share in at least a decade.

The share of transactions with mismatched ownership records has climbed from 26.8% in 2021, while an additional 1.4% of transfers in 2025 involved properties with no previous deed on record.

While these discrepancies don’t necessarily indicate fraud—they can also arise through legitimate transactions like foreclosures—researchers say they can help identify properties warranting closer scrutiny.

In New York City, that scrutiny is particularly important. Decades of rising property values have left longtime homeowners and their heirs with a huge amount of wealth that could be vulnerable to exploitation.

Earlier research from the center identified approximately 45,000 homes worth a combined $34.7 billion with at least one indicator of vulnerability to title-related problems or predatory tactics.

The latest report narrows its focus to 2,300 properties at particularly high risk because at least one listed owner is deceased and the property has no recorded deed or one dating back more than 30 years.

That can create difficulties for heirs from establishing their legal rights to the house—an issue that can compound by cutting off access to home equity or financial assistance, or even create difficulties paying necessary bills.

Indeed, nearly 13% of these high-risk properties owed more than $500 in property taxes, compared with fewer than 2% of all individually owned one- to three-family homes. And they were nearly seven times as likely to have appeared on the city's 2025 tax lien sale list.

The findings come as New York City expands efforts to combat deed theft. In April, Mayor Zohran Mamdani established the Mayor's Office of Deed Theft Prevention to coordinate investigations and protections for vulnerable homeowners.

“This is exactly the kind of crime the state's new anti-deed theft law is intended to deter," Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. said in a statement following Quimis' plea. "Queens homeowners can sleep better knowing our Attorney General will be aggressive in using this anti-deed theft law to protect the homes they have worked so hard for.”

The borough accounted for more than half of the city's high-risk properties, according to NYU's latest research. Meanwhile, the Bronx had the highest prevalence relative to its housing stock.

Jamaica and Hollis in Queens also recorded the greatest number of transfers with mismatched ownership records between 2015 and 2025, followed by Queens Village.

Neighborhoods with the greatest numbers of high-risk properties and flagged transfers tended to have larger shares of Black, Asian, and foreign-born residents than the city overall.

The Furman Center has also developed a restricted mapping tool to help government agencies, law enforcement, and legal services providers identify properties that may need intervention.

Researchers say more detailed property records, targeted legal assistance, and estate planning could help protect homeowners before ownership disputes or fraudulent transactions put their homes at risk.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5639. A new tactic in the war over out-of-network bills: Health care providers are suing employers

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Herman examined hundreds of pages of court documents for this story, part of STAT’s Out of Pocket, Out of Reach series.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

This past August, Joe Hancock, a Kentucky plumbing and heating contractor, opened a just-delivered box packed with hundreds of sheets of paper. Leafing through them, he read seven words no small business owner wants to see: “A lawsuit has been filed against you.”

The complaint, from air ambulance firm PHI Health, claimed Hancock was on the hook for almost $27,000 in medical helicopter bills. They were tied to one of his now-retired employees, who needed an emergency flight after a heart attack.

Hancock, who owns Whitehead-Hancock Plumbing, Heating & Cooling, a family-run business in Frankfort, Ky., that has been around for more than a century, didn’t understand why he was being roped into a lawsuit that featured 31 other companies — for medical charges he was never aware of.

“I was terrified,” Hancock said. “I was like, ‘What in the hell is going on here?’”

He’s not alone. The PHI lawsuit highlights an evolving tactic by health care providers in a raging battle over out-of-network bills. Previously, providers targeted health insurance companies to pay outstanding amounts that were awarded through federal mediation. Now, they increasingly are dragging the insurers’ clients — employers — into court, claiming they are responsible for bills that insurers haven’t fully paid or have delayed paying. The practice is introducing a new shock that could further torch the affordability of workers’ health coverage.

“These big suits naming dozens of employers at a time is really an escalation,” said Garrett Hohimer, a vice president at the Business Group on Health. “And it will cause employers to incur expenses that [come directly] out of their health care plans.”

A 2022 law called the No Surprises Act shielded patients from the financial trauma of many types of unexpected medical bills, but it has also given rise to a vast industry that’s driving up costs across the health care system. The law uses an arbitration process to determine how much health care providers should get paid for out-of-network emergency care, like helicopter rides, for people who have some type of commercial health coverage. STAT has reported that providers are winning most of these arbitration awards, which often are far higher than the amounts in-network providers receive for the same services.

Already, high payments tied to this process have added approximately $20 billion in extra costs to the health care system, Georgetown University researchers have estimated. A large portion of those costs inevitably come out of the bank accounts of America’s employers and consequently lead to higher premiums, emphasizing how even well-intentioned health reforms can add to the financial pressure that’s crushing workers and businesses.

PHI Health, a national chain, is arguably the most aggressive company suing employers, which it claims are not “passive” bystanders in insurers’ refusal to fully pay awards. Other regional physician practices have sued some employers as well. But PHI and its army of attorneys have filed lawsuits against hundreds of companies, demanding they collectively pay tens of millions of dollars in unpaid out-of-network claims that it won in the federal arbitration process.

PHI isn’t just suing small, local firms like Hancock’s. It’s also taking legal action against some of the largest corporations — Amazon, Walmart, Eli Lilly, United Airlines, General Motors, PepsiCo, State Farm, and Toyota, to name a few — as well as unions, counties, cities, states, public school districts, and universities.

PHI has sued other health care organizations, including hospitals, nursing homes, and medical billing firms. It also has gone after nonprofits, such as the Catholic Diocese of Cleveland. In each instance, a worker or family member at these companies took an emergency medical helicopter, often at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars per trip.

Unpacking the business — and secretive inner workings — of the U.S. health care industry

In some cases, PHI wasn’t sure what company it should be suing, but sued anyway. Several lawsuits named specific health insurers and employers as defendants, and then added “ABC CORP” or “XYZ CORP” as a placeholder. If the insurer or employer “is not in fact the plan sponsor … that covers the patient transported by PHI, then the identity of the plan sponsor is unknown to PHI, and this action is instead brought against ABC CORP,” one lawsuit reads.

Katie Keith and Ellie DeGarmo are attorneys at Georgetown’s Center for Health Policy and the Law who have tracked No Surprises Act lawsuits, including those filed by PHI. They said the scores of cases reinforce the bloat in the health care system: above-market prices that providers are winning for not participating in an insurance company’s network, attempts from insurers to not pay at all or profit off lowball offers, and a booming revenue stream for arbitrators.

But trying to wring money out of employers — and, ultimately, from their workers — is a stark divergence from the public statements of physician groups and air ambulance companies, which have painted health insurers as the bad guys for not following the rules.

“It kind of undercuts the narrative that this is provider versus insurance company,” Keith said. “In this case, this is about provider versus everyone who pays for health care and is now stuck with the bill for [arbitration] awards that have gone totally off the rails.”

STAT reached out to more than two dozen employers that were listed in PHI’s lawsuits. Most did not respond to inquiries. Of those that did, most declined to comment.

“Because this matter involves pending litigation … we will not be providing any interviews,” said Clint Mitchell, the division superintendent of Spotsylvania County Public Schools in Fredericksburg, Va. PHI Health is suing Spotsylvania County’s school system for almost $28,000.

Jay Litten, the town manager of Bridgewater, Va., told STAT the town’s health insurer, Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, retained counsel and was handling the case. PHI sued Bridgewater in October for more than $37,000 in unpaid awards.

PHI has boasted about its success in the law’s arbitration process. In 2024, it told prospective investors that it was “able to maintain our profitability” by winning more than three out of every four arbitration claims, and it expected “this trend of favorable” outcomes from the process would continue.

The company has some private equity backing, according to financial filings from when the company considered going public in 2023. Its largest shareholder as of 2023 was Q Investments, a family office that has a private equity firm.

PHI declined to make anyone available for an interview. In a statement, CEO Scott McCarty defended the company’s lawsuits, saying the employers PHI has sued “have a duty to their employees and a responsibility to health care providers in their communities to abide by the law and pay for services delivered.”

McCarty said health insurers are asking their employer clients to choose between paying the unpaid arbitration amounts or authorizing the insurer to continue refusing payment.

“Once an employer is on notice of nonpayment and affirmatively endorses that practice, it is no longer a passive bystander,” McCarty said in the statement. “It has made a conscious decision to allow its insurance company not to pay binding federal awards in violation of federal law.”

In PHI’s lawsuits, the company alleges insurers, and now employers, are using an “unlawful scheme to ‘low pay, late pay, or no pay’ providers, including PHI.” All the cases are still pending.

The company also claims insurers float the money from unpaid awards, which are binding decisions, on the stock market as a way to earn extra interest or investment income.

James Gelfand, CEO of the ERISA Industry Committee, a lobbying group that represents large employers, said companies don’t condone insurers delaying payments as a way to make extra money. But he said under the federal law known as ERISA, employers are legally obligated to make sure they spend their health plan assets wisely on behalf of workers. If employers believe the awards are tied to ineligible claims — or are egregiously high compared with what they normally would pay — those payments could violate that obligation.

As a result, the employers’ health insurers “are operating with our blessing when we say, ‘Hey, if the [arbitration] award is inappropriate and wrong, do not pay it,’” he said. “How can we claim to be responsible stewards of people’s money if we’re just like, ‘Oh, here you go!’ That would be crazy.”

Jenny Goins, who is CEO of the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions and used to oversee health benefits for Kentucky state employees, said “slow-walking the payments” to providers is one of the only ways employers can push back if they believe the awards are based on ineligible or incomplete claims. Medical claims are not eligible for arbitration if, for example, the employer or its health plan doesn’t cover a certain service or if there is certain information or data missing.

PHI has frequently named Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, owned by Elevance Health, as a defendant in the lawsuits against employers. Elevance did not make anyone available for an interview. The company said in a statement that PHI is charging prices for air ambulance services that are 700% of what Medicare pays and mileage rates that are 1,500% more than Medicare rates.

“We have already paid PHI substantial amounts for services provided to our members,” Elevance spokesperson Janey Kiryluik said in a statement. “We dispute whether additional amounts are legally owed for claims that were ineligible” for the arbitration process.

PHI said only arbitrators can determine the eligibility of claims. It added that the rates Medicare pays don’t cover the full cost of emergency air care, nor can those prices be considered during the arbitration process.

The bigger issue revealed by the lawsuits, Goins said, is how “broken” the law has become, even though she believed it was well-intended. The issue has now attracted interest in Congress, where lawmakers are proposing various plans to overhaul the arbitration process.

“Greedy people see an opportunity to make more money,” Goins said. “I also see there’s a true opportunity to shine a light on this.”

In September, PHI dropped Hancock’s company as a defendant, one month after its attorneys served him with court papers. Hancock said his heating, cooling, and plumbing business of 30 employees is not self-insured — meaning he buys his health insurance from Anthem, which takes on all the risk of his employees’ medical care.

PHI’s McCarty blamed Anthem in a statement, saying it “does not always receive clear or consistent information from insurers identifying whether a plan is self-funded or fully insured. In this case, after the lawsuit was filed, Anthem’s counsel confirmed that Whitehead-Hancock was fully insured, and PHI promptly dismissed it, without settlement.”

Other businesses are getting released from PHI’s lawsuits, too. It’s unclear if they were wrongfully lumped in, like Hancock’s company, or if they are paying PHI’s demands to clear a costly legal headache.

PHI’s legal team “threw a handful of darts, and they’re going to try to rattle as many cages as they can,” Hancock said. “It’s not right. It shouldn’t be legal.”

STAT’s coverage of the soaring costs of health insurance for workers and employers is supported by a grant from the Commonwealth Fund. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. #5638. Dustin Hoffman Recalls Being Held at Gunpoint in Bed and Early Gritty NYC Days Living With Robert Duvall and Gene Hackman

Dustin Hoffman is opening up about his younger years with the release of his memoir, “Look at Me.”

The actor, who broke into Hollywood with his role in “The Graduate,” appeared on the Nov. 9 episode of the “Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend” podcast and revealed that he had once been held at gunpoint by a man whose wife he was having an affair with during his “youth youth.”

“I was having an affair with a married woman,” Hoffman, 89, admitted. “She thought that once her husband went to asleep, that he stayed asleep.”

Explaining that he had been invited to the woman’s home when her husband had presumably gone to bed, when suddenly it had become clear that the man was well aware of what was going on.

“There we are, having a festival of sorts, and he walked in with a gun,” the “Rain Man” actor shared. “He pointed it at me and he said, I remember what he said, ‘Get out, get out.’”

“When you have a gun pointed at you,” he explained, “You realize how, any second, any second he’s going to pull that trigger. His finger is on the trigger and you think any second he’s going to. You realize, ‘That’s it, I’m gonna die. I’m gonna die, the next second, the next second, the next second.”

The actor recalled that in that moment, he came to the realization that “you will do anything to avoid getting killed.”

At another point in the interview, O’Brien asked the Los Angeles native to detail his move to New York. Hoffman relocated across the country in 1958 at 21, hoping to pursue a career in acting.

As O’Brien put it, Hoffman worked “a lot of absurd odd jobs” at this point in his life, including a role at Macy’s, where he was tasked with selling toys—like foosball and table hockey—to adults.

As an aspiring actor, Hoffman put his own spin on the job, and decided to embody a character of his own making; a retired, injured French hockey player.

“Gene Hackman was right there at adult games, also,” Hoffman said, noting that the fellow actor was his coworker at the time. Decades later, the pair would go on to work together again, starring in the 2003 film, “Runaway Jury.”

Hackman and Hoffman weren’t just coincidental coworkers. They lived together, too.

“You go home to your roommates, and they are Gene Hackman and Robert Duvall. The three of you, I’m picturing a bunk bed with three levels. And you guys are snoring in unison like ‘The Three Stooges.’ That’s what I’m picturing,” joked O’Brien.

Hoffman said that the three men, who eventually each became very famous actors, “didn’t live together quite like that.”

Although he seems to look back on the experience with a sense of humor now, his memoir tells a different story. In an excerpt from the book, Hoffman wrote that he “was so frightened of New York.”

“I didn’t want to go outside. I’d been excited to get there, but once I arrived it scared the hell out of me,” he said. “All these thousands of people who knew what they were doing, whereas I was completely in the dark. It was intimidating.”

At one point, Hoffman lived with Hackman and his first wife, Faye Maltese, in “a little apartment on the East Side.”

“I slept on the kitchen floor next to their refrigerator, which shook and made a lot of noise, like it was having a heart attack once or twice a night,” Hoffman recalled.

Hoffman had originally only planned to stay with Hackman and his wife for a few days, but the arrangement lasted three weeks before “the Hackmans ran out of patience and told me it was time to move on.”

Hackman advised Hoffman to, “go up Riverside Drive and knock on the doors and ask to speak to the superintendent,” to find a new place to live. The actor recalled starting at 60th Street and Central Park West, and knocking on “every door of every building all the way to the Hudson River and back again” until he eventually found a place on 109th street.

He rented a top-floor apartment in a building in Spanish Harlem for $80 a month, and knew he’d “need roommates to afford it,” which is where Duvall came in.

“We had a lot of rowdy nights in that apartment: pizza, unemployed actors, candles in chianti bottles,” Hackman wrote. “I would play the piano. Duvall would sing country music songs. If someone had pointed at Bob and Gene and me at one of our parties and said, ‘Those three are going to be movie stars,” everyone in the apartment would have laughed.”

Even after Hoffman got his first big break, it was a while before he’d find his footing financially. During the podcast interview, he said he was paid $3,000 for his role in "The Graduate," which was released in 1967. But after the film’s premiere, he still needed more funds.

“You didn’t have any money, and so you went back to the unemployment office and someone at Life magazine took a photo of you,” O’Brien said. “The most famous face in America at the time, waiting in the unemployment line to get a check.”

Hoffman confirmed that the story was true, adding that the check was for about $50.

“$55, I think was the most you could get,” he continued, quipping that at that time, people “could live on” about “$200 a month.”

#5637. Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response

Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.

Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.

Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.

"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."

Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain

To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.

The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.

Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.

How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat

By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.

The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.

These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.

"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."

The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.

"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.

There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.

Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.

The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. #5634. A Looming Nor’easter Threatens Millions of Homeowners With First Snow of the Season

A potential nor’easter impacting the Northeast and New England is being forecasted for later this week, with millions of homeowners bracing for possibly the first snow of the season.

Meteorologists are predicting that as early as Wednesday evening, a deep plunge in temperatures combined with a low pressure system moving across the Midwest will make for wet conditions for Louisville, KY, all the way up to Maine.

While snow in these areas this time of year is not unheard of, some locales are prepping for a volatile winter ahead, given the Super El Niño conditions.

So is this just a taste of what’s to come?

Cold air sweeps across the East late in the week, setting the stage for winter weather, according to The Weather Channel.

By Thursday night, a secondary low-pressure system is expected to form off the Eastern Seaboard. As cold air filters in, rain could begin mixing with or fully changing over to wet snow across interior parts of the Northeast.

Friday into the weekend presents the greatest potential for snow, depending on the storm’s exact track, which meteorologists are still unclear on.

If the system tracks close to the coast, it could wrap heavy inland snowfall into the Northeast alongside coastal rain, strong winds, and flooding.

A track farther out to sea would result in much lighter snow accumulations across inland areas.

Homeowners in places like Buffalo, NY, and Burlington, VT, are among those who should prepare for the snow shovels and salt for a snowy weekend.

However, if the temperatures dip low enough, it wouldn’t be unthinkable to see snow in places like Washington, DC, Philadelphia, and New York City as well.

Speaking of New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced ahead of the nor’easter a citywide mobilization to prepare Manhattan for winter weather. This includes a $25 million investment in an expanded Code Blue system and a supercharged snow- and ice-clearing operation.

“We have spent the past year preparing for any challenge winter throws our way. We have trained our workers, readied our equipment and strengthened our protocols because keeping New Yorkers safe can’t begin when the first storm hits,” Mamdani said in a press release.

“This winter, we’re doing things differently—we’re expanding Code Blue to reach more New Yorkers in need, equipping New York’s Strongest to clear snow and ice faster and leaving no stone unturned when it comes to protecting our neighbors from the cold. No New Yorker should face the dangers of winter alone, and no part of our city should be left behind.”

These initiatives come at a time where New York and much of the surrounding states are bracing themselves for the final months of the Super El Nino, which, according to the latest forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization, is projected to be the strongest on record and likely to persist through February 2027.

According to the NOAA, an El Niño system tends to be strongest during the winter months. But because of the strength of the system being tracked this year, there are plenty of variables at play.

“Every El Niño is not the same; each one is unique with its own imprint on our weather,” says Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS). "Advanced monitoring and an improved understanding of El Niño patterns allow the NWS to better predict and better prepare the public and our core partners for what is to come.”

With that in mind, the Farmers' Almanac 2026–'27 winter outlook outlines a season defined by sharp contrasts and volatile conditions across the United States, driven largely by an active El Niño pattern.

In the Northeast, it predicts a season dominated by wet conditions, both rainy and snowy. In fact, much of the country will need to contend with wetter than usual conditions, but whether snow develops will depend largely on the temperatures.
