#5595. What we learned about the hyperscalers from earnings season

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Recently Amazon.com Inc., Google owner Alphabet Inc. and Microsoft Corp. reported earnings within roughly 24 hours of each other, and this earnings season told us more about long-term artificial intelligence strategy than any keynote or press release this year. Beneath the headlines lie three very different strategies.

Here’s what I took away: Amazon will be the long-term winner because its open, platform-first approach gives customers the broadest choice of models and silicon, and it’s showing that size doesn’t limit scale. Microsoft is a solid second, protected less by strategy than by the customers it already has locked in. And Google will be a distant third, with impressive technology built on a fragile business foundation and a closed, Gemini-first strategy that runs counter to where enterprises are heading.

The most remarkable part of the earnings season was that Amazon’s Amazon Web Services business has found a way to buck the law of large numbers. It’s growing 39.3% at its size. AWS revenue reached $46 billion, marking its sixth straight quarter of acceleration and its fastest growth in nearly five years, putting the business at an $184 billion annualized run rate, according to Amazon’s third-quarter release.

To put that in perspective, the last time AWS grew this fast was in the fourth quarter of 2021, when it posted 40% growth on $17.8 billion in quarterly revenue. AWS is now more than two-and-a-half times that size and is growing at essentially the same rate. The roughly $13 billion it added year over year is about three-quarters of what the entire business generated in a quarter back then.

The law of large numbers is supposed to catch every business. The largest cloud provider on the planet is accelerating instead.

Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy projected AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Operating income reached $17.8 billion at a 38.7% margin, and backlog climbed to $578 billion, up from $244 billion at the end of 2025. On the earnings call, Jassy indicated AWS could reach $1 trillion in as little as five years, giving Amazon two businesses that do north of a trillion dollars in revenue.

Bedrock is the most underappreciated piece of Amazon’s strategy and, in the long term, the most important. Microsoft built its AI identity around OpenAI, and Google around Gemini. Both host third-party models, but each has a house favorite that its roadmap and pricing orbit around. AWS made model neutrality the product.

According to an AWS Builder Center guide, Bedrock offers more than 100 models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Google, xAI and Nvidia. In the third quarter alone, Amazon added OpenAI’s GPT-6 family, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, xAI’s Grok 4.7, and Moonshot’s Kimi K3, per Amazon’s quarterly release.

The open-weight wave makes this even more important. Bedrock already runs DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, Kimi, Gemma, Nemotron and OpenAI’s gpt-oss models as fully managed services, as AWS has detailed. As open models close the gap, enterprises will fine-tune smaller, cheaper models for specific tasks and reserve frontier models for the hardest problems. The platform that lets them route across all of them under a single security and governance model wins. A cloud built around a single-model company has a conflict of interest every time an open model gets good enough to replace it.

Customer spending is validating Bedrock’s value, as Fortune 500 spending on Bedrock rose nearly sevenfold year over year and token volume grew nearly 17-fold, Jassy said on the earnings call.

The second advantage is silicon, which is tightly linked to Bedrock. Most of Bedrock’s inference runs on Trainium, which lets AWS keep prices low while protecting margins, according to TIKR’s call coverage. Customers using Amazon’s custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in the third quarter alone, as noted in the call transcript.

The bigger news was Jassy’s commitment to sell Trainium outside AWS starting in late 2027. “We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” he said, according to Yahoo Finance. Training is periodic, whereas inference is a perpetual cost that scales with every agent and transaction. Selling Trainium racks brings AWS’ price-performance to enterprise data centers, sovereign environments and neoclouds, and gives organizations that need on-premises inference a credible alternative to Nvidia.

AWS has the broadest infrastructure footprint, the broadest model selection, and silicon that lowers the cost per token. The downside is the bill: a 2026 capex of roughly $220 billion, per 24/7 Wall St., and negative $33.5 billion in free cash flow, according to TradingKey. That spending is backed by contracted demand. If the growth rate continues, investors should be happy to see Amazon spending ahead of demand, but all eyes will be on free cash flow.

Who builds on AWS: Builders, including digital natives, AI labs, independent software vendors and large enterprises with mature engineering teams seeking model choice, cost control and no dependence on a single model partner.

Of the three hyperscalers, Microsoft’s business is the most predictable because it’s very hard to disrupt and isn’t a disruptor. What it is now is likely what it will be in the future. Azure grew 48% to $33.2 billion, the first time Microsoft has disclosed Azure revenue in dollars, according to CNBC.

But the most notable data point concerned lock-in. Customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold year over year, including Capgemini, Hitachi, Truist and the U.K.’s HMRC, according to Microsoft’s earnings call. That’s Microsoft’s true AI strategy: Upsell AI to the hundreds of millions of workers already living in Office, Teams and Windows. Switching costs are enormous, and Microsoft will capture a large share of enterprise AI spend regardless of how its models compare.

Google and others have tried to disrupt the Office franchise for decades but haven’t posed a serious threat. In the AI era, a company like Canva or Zoom could introduce an entirely new way to create documents and begin to erode that business, but until there is a material loss of share, that installed base seems safe.

Microsoft’s strategy has downsides. The company leans heavily on OpenAI, a partner that increasingly acts like a competitor. On the same earnings call, Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said some third-party capacity deliveries were delayed. Microsoft also didn’t update its total paid Copilot seat count, leaving open how deeply those seats are used.

Who builds on Microsoft: Large, Microsoft-standardized enterprises, especially in regulated industries and the public sector, prioritize knowledge-worker productivity within the tools they already use.

Google Cloud’s headline numbers were impressive. Revenue grew 103% to $30.7 billion, and the operating margin was 36.2%, according to highlights from Alphabet’s earnings call. But a strong quarter doesn’t necessarily signal durability, and the earnings exposed three structural problems.

First, look at what is driving growth. According to Alphabet’s investor relations, CFO Anat Ashkenazi said tensor processing unit system sales were a “meaningful contributor” to cloud revenue. Hardware sales are lumpy and concentrated among a few large buyers, which is a different business from recurring cloud consumption.

Second, the core business funding all of this is showing cracks. Search made up 49.7% of Alphabet’s revenue, below half for the first time in the company’s history. That trend is likely to continue given the diversity of AI platforms. A year earlier, it was 55.3%. Also, Search grew only 12%, down from 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2. YouTube ad revenue grew 9.2% to $11.21 billion, short of analysts’ $11.43 billion expectation. That’s down 15% from a year earlier and 13% from last quarter, adding only $152 million over the last quarter.

Third, spending is outpacing cash. Capex reached $51.4 billion, while free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion. Alphabet expects capex to exceed $300 billion in 2027, according to CNBC. The core business’s decline is becoming significant as the capex arms race continues.

Google has world-class research, Gemini and TPUs. Against that, it has a Gemini-first strategy that sits awkwardly with the open-weight wave, an ad business under AI pressure, and a history of sunsetting products, which remains the biggest objection I hear from chief information officers. Also, Google has always struggled with its enterprise strategy.

In 2018, I wrote this post for CIO.com asking whether Google was ever going to get serious about enterprise, and nothing much has changed. It seems to roll out products that have promise but never makes them best-in-class. As an example, Google Meet is good but not great, and Docs, Gmail and Drive are the same. They’re low-cost, but there are always better alternatives. Why would we expect their AI strategy to be different?

Who builds on Google: AI-native startups, research-heavy organizations,and BigQuery shops willing to accept platform risk. It’s a harder sell to a regulated enterprise making a 10-year commitment.

Neither is likely to make a long-term dent in the hyperscaler market, for one simple reason: They lack the flywheel. Amazon has retail and advertising; Google has search; and Microsoft has Office and Windows, each massive cash-generating businesses that can fund a multiyear compute buildout. The AI infrastructure race is capital-intensive, and IBM and Oracle are running it without that engine.

Oracle’s numbers look impressive on the surface, with cloud infrastructure revenue up 121% to $7.4 billion in its September quarter and RPO at $664 billion. The problem is how it’s financing that growth. Capex hit $28 billion in a single quarter, free cash flow was negative $5.4 billion, and debt has reached $125 billion, according to CNBC. After a $20 billion equity sale, it’s now selling another $10 billion in bonds, as Yahoo Finance reported.

Its database business can’t fund this buildout, so Oracle is relying on borrowed money and customer prepayments. That’s a fragile way to compete with companies that can self-fund.

IBM has largely stayed out of the compute race. Revenue grew 5% to $17.1 billion, led by Red Hat, according to IBM’s earnings release. IBM’s presentation reports $7.8 billion in year-to-date free cash flow, roughly what Amazon or Microsoft spends on capex in two weeks. IBM will matter as a hybrid-cloud integration layer, not a primary AI platform.

The biggest takeaway from earnings season is that the hyperscaler AI race now has a predictable order. Amazon is growing nearly 40% at an $184 billion run rate by doing what it has always done: building an open platform from silicon to agents, offering the broadest shelf of frontier and open-weight models, and preparing to take its inference silicon beyond its own data centers. Microsoft is a strong second, monetizing its existing customer base. Google is a distant third, betting that superior technology can outlast disruption to its core business while asking customers to adopt a closed stack.

To be clear, when I say “distant third,” that’s a forward-looking statement. Currently, Google’s cloud business is only slightly smaller than Azure’s, so my basis for “distant third” is openness, customer trust, enterprise go-to-market and the ability to fund the buildout.

When AI becomes a line item in IT budgets, customers will gravitate toward the platform with the lowest inference costs, the broadest selection of models and the deepest operational track record. Openness wins platform wars.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5594. The 10 Affordable Cities Where Homeowners Are the Least Locked In by Housing Costs

Many homeowners who began the year hoping to move may now be locked in by soaring mortgage rates that threaten to nearly double their monthly payments—but a handful of budget-friendly markets still offer relief.

These rare pockets of affordability are clustered primarily across the Midwest and South, including Pittsburgh; Baltimore; Buffalo, NY; New Orleans; Detroit; Birmingham, AL; San Antonio, TX; Akron, OH; McAllen, TX; and Philadelphia.

Nationally, the typical U.S. mortgage holder pays roughly $1,300 in principal and interest per month. If they were to purchase a home today, that payment would surge by more than 85%, or $1,100, according to a new report on America's "locked-in" homeowners from Realtor.com®.

The market's current predicament can be traced to the COVID-19 pandemic years, when historically low mortgage rates whipped up a buying and refinancing frenzy. As of July 2026, more than a quarter (27%) of all fixed-rate mortgages on record for single-family homes and condominiums were originated in 2020 and 2021 alone.

Once mortgage rates began climbing again in 2022, homebuying and refinancing both hit a wall. Over the subsequent four years, only about 1 in 4 mortgages on record was originated, highlighting the sharp pullback in activity as a result of higher borrowing costs.

"For those who purchased before mortgage rates shot sharply higher, the sentiment of 'I couldn’t afford to buy my home today' continues to ring true in most cases, contributing to historically low mobility and some of the leanest for-sale inventory on record," notes Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

In other words, homeowners who were fortunate enough to secure a sub-4% mortgage rate at the height of the pandemic are reluctant to list. Trading up or downsizing today means taking out a mortgage with a steeply higher rate, gobbling up a much bigger share of their income.

Just how much bigger? Purchasing a median-priced home at the Oct. 22 rate of 7.32%, assuming a 14.3% down payment, would translate into a monthly principal and interest payment of nearly $2,500, almost double the $1,300 typical owners currently pay.

However, in parts of the U.S. where home prices remain accessible, the "lock-in" effect is felt less acutely, keeping inventory—and people—moving and creating a self-reinforcing cycle.

"The affordability of these markets enables mobility, which means the typical outstanding mortgage rate is higher, which helps reduce the payment jump associated with moving, which reinforces affordability," explains Jones.

In the South and Midwest, approximately three-quarters of mortgages carry a rate below 6%, compared to 78% nationally.

Additionally, nearly a quarter of all outstanding mortgages in these two regions were originated within the past four years at 6% or higher, compared with 21.6% in the Northeast and 17.7% in the West.

"That mix means fewer homeowners in these regions are clinging to 3%–4% rates, which lessens the lock-in effect," says Jones.

Across the 100 largest metros, Pittsburgh stands out as the nation's least "locked in" housing market, where a seller purchasing a new home in town would see a 43% increase in their monthly mortgage payment—a modest penalty compared to the 165% in San Jose, CA.

Baltimore is a close second, with a 45% payment gap, followed by Buffalo, at 46.1%.

"A 3% mortgage is a great reason to stay in a house, but it's not always a great reason to stay in a house that no longer fits your life," Colleen Collier, associate broker at Re/Max Plus in Buffalo, tells Realtor.com.

The latest housing data reflects the market's mobility and affordability. In October, Buffalo posted the largest year-over-year increase in active listings (+34.4%) among the 50 largest metros, paired with the largest growth in new listings (+13.1%).

At the same time, the median listing price in the metro registered at $259,999, down 2.8% from a year ago and sitting more than $155,000 below the national median.

Collier notes that while more local homeowners are willing to make a move, it does not necessarily mean they are comfortable giving up their low rates. They are being compelled by life changes.

"They're retiring, downsizing, or relocating to be closer to family," says the broker. "Many are looking to reduce maintenance and their overall living expenses. Others are relocating to a warmer climate. ... They're taking the equity they've built and putting it toward their next purchase."

Collier recently represented clients who sold their home of 30 years to downsize into an apartment. They were able to get a final sale price well above asking, which was enough to cover at least 10 years of apartment living, and fund future travel plans and a new car.

"What made this experience so rewarding was that the homeowner had more equity than they realized," says Collier. "After more than three decades in their home, selling wasn't simply about moving into a smaller space. It was about creating financial freedom and enjoying the next chapter of life."

In Akron, a typical homeowner currently paying just $868 per month should expect to see that figure rise nearly 62% under present-day market conditions—well above Buffalo’s level but still a far cry from the most locked-in coastal markets.

"The financial difference between staying in a home with a low mortgage rate and purchasing another home may be less dramatic here than in higher-priced markets," Mike Valerino, CEO of Akron Cleveland Association of Realtors, tells Realtor.com. "However, that doesn't mean the mortgage rate lock-in effect has disappeared."

According to Valerino, in Summit County, where Akron is located, new listings and closed sales were down in September while the average sales price increased, suggesting that despite the market's relative affordability, homeowners are still weighing the financial implications of moving.

"Life circumstances remain important drivers of housing decisions," he says, echoing Collier's argument. "Growing families need more space, empty nesters may want to downsize, and job changes, retirement, and family considerations can create reasons to move that outweigh the financial benefits of staying put."

At the same time, Valerino says that Akron's relative affordability does not insulate buyers and sellers from the challenges affecting housing markets nationally.

"The mortgage lock-in effect may be less severe here, but the cost of the next home still plays a major role in whether someone decides to move," he says.

In roughly a third of the 100 largest U.S. metros, a move to a median-priced home would more than double the monthly payment. Ballooning borrowing costs disproportionately penalize expensive coastal and fast-growing markets, leaving local homeowners feeling virtually trapped by their lower mortgages.

According to the latest data, the most "locked-in" markets in the U.S. include Portland, ME, San Jose, and Los Angeles, where anticipated monthly mortgage payments surged by more than 140%, grinding mobility to a halt. That friction has severely squeezed inventory and put upward pressure on home prices, sidelining first-time and budget buyers.

"Because homes in these markets are already expensive, buyers typically rely on larger mortgage balances, which amplifies the impact of rising rates," says Jones.

In Portland, for instance, a current owner holding on to a 4% mortgage rate makes a median payment of $1,270 per month. If they were to purchase a home comparable to theirs with a 26.2% down payment and took out a 7.32% mortgage, their payment would jump a staggering 167% to $3,392.

Mortgage rates would have to drop a long way from their current 7.18% level to close the gap between what current owners pay and what a buyer would pay today.

Rates would need to reach 6% before half of U.S. households could afford the median-priced home, and even then a move would still mean a payment about 62% higher than what the typical mortgage holder spends now.

Crucially, however, Jones stresses that falling mortgage rates alone are not enough. Because home values have appreciated significantly over the past few years, buying a median-priced home with a 4% mortgage would still cost about 29% more per month than what existing homeowners pay on their original COVID-19-era loans.

Valerino agrees, maintaining that there is no one "magic number" that will unlock the market.

"Rates in the 5% range could make moving more attractive to some homeowners, but affordability involves more than the interest rate," he says. "Home prices, property taxes, insurance, and accumulated equity all factor into that decision."

The market is poised to loosen gradually rather than all at once as more households buy in to higher rates, softening price growth narrows the gap, and rising incomes boost buying power.

"The lower-priced Midwest and South markets, where the gap is smallest and more loans carry higher rates, are likely to see the most activity first," predicts Jones. "Large coastal markets will need both lower rates and lower prices or significantly higher incomes before sellers feel free to move."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5593. ‘Wake-Up Call’: Trump’s Former Housing Commissioner Says New Congress Must ‘Get Serious’ About Housing Affordability

Democrats and Republicans both understand Americans are broadly worried about the cost of living, and a former Trump administration official says it's time for both parties to take action.

In a bitterly divided Washington, DC, it remains to be seen whether lawmakers will heed that call when the 120th Congress convenes in January, with Democrats back in control of both the House and Senate.

After campaigning hard on affordability concerns, Democratic leaders say they'll use their new majorities to focus on the cost of living. Republican leaders admit they didn't heed voter concerns about the economy. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has threatened to use his veto power freely.

The summer's 21st Century Road to Housing Act, with its dozens of provisions aimed at cutting red tape, was a rare example of bipartisan consensus. What follows that landmark legislation remains an open question.

Republicans want more deregulation while Democrats aim for more support for housing. And each side must now contend with an upswell of hard-liners pushing policies that could radically change the market.

Many of the prominent names in both parties who built the housing bill are returning, including Rep. French Hill (R-AR), Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC). They're likely to return to the House and Senate committees on housing and banking.

"Now is a wake-up call," Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy tells Realtor.com®. "Senate, House, White House. Everyone needs to get serious about tackling and addressing housing affordability. It can't be ignored anymore."

Congress had some bipartisan momentum to provide tax incentives that encourage the buying and selling of homes.

Colin Allen, executive director of the American Property Owners Alliance and a former housing issues adviser to Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), said that could mean some ideas pitched in this Congress could come back as part of larger bills.

"They have good working relationships and have already done some bipartisan work," Allen said.

Take, for instance, the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act, which would create a new tax credit to buy and renovate homes in economically distressed areas. The bill drew 70 sponsors from both parties.

Real estate groups put in significant groundwork this year to update the capital gains tax scheme for the first time in more than 30 years. The More Homes on the Market Act came close to 200 sponsors in Congress. It would double the exclusion for many filers. It's been floating around Congress for several years and has been a target of the National Association of Realtors® and other groups.

Trump expressed some support for changing the capital gains tax scheme, though a specific plan hasn't yet materialized from the White House.

"We've done a lot of legwork to get folks behind it," Allen said. "If we're looking at a larger bipartisan bill, you can see a scenario where a few of those ideas get together. The debt limit is coming up, and there are a few other opportunities to package together."

Hill and Republicans have lobbied for more changes to the financing system. They were able to get several banking reform provisions into the Road to Housing bill. They've also floated new financial reforms to change and rescind banking rules codified in the Dodd-Frank Act and the Basel III accords after the subprime mortgage crisis. Republicans say they've chased smaller banks out of the housing market.

This summer, Hill called Dodd-Frank a "massive overreaction."

"For our smaller banks, the new regulations were a poor fit, burying them in compliance work and bureaucratic red tape," Hill said. "Instead of helping customers, their attention was diverted to filling out forms and satisfying examiners."

Mortgage reform is also a lever Congress can pull. A bipartisan group of six members of Congress pitched the First-Time Homebuyer Affordability Act this summer. It would expand access to low-interest mortgages for first-time homebuyers.

"By expanding access to financing, we can help more hardworking families achieve homeownership, strengthen our communities, and build long-term financial security," said Rep. Darin LaHood (R-IL) said.

Then there's the matter of new construction. Democrats and Republicans found some bipartisan ground in cutting some of the federal red tape that blocks construction of new homes.

Republicans also said they favor rolling back Build America Buy America provisions. Builders, they say, have complained that the sourcing requirements are time-consuming and expensive. But they've also targeted some environmental regulations that Democrats passed.

Dennis Shea, chair of the J. Ronald Terwilliger Center for Housing Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells Realtor.com that some public housing authorities saw costs climb by double digits. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's waiver process is every bit as time-consuming for builders.

"A sentiment exists in both parties to change the rules, but ultimately it takes an act of Congress to exempt housing," Shea said.

Hill and other lawmakers such as Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO) have said that Congress' action should shift some burden onto states to implement reforms at the local and state level. The American Enterprise Institute said this year that state and local policy changes could boost annual homebuilding by six figures. But many of those new homes are accessory dwelling units.

Congress and the White Hose also found common ground on manufactured housing reform. All sides recognize they need to keep eyeing supply-side reforms, says Cassidy.

"Ultimately, the problem in this country is supply," Cassidy adds. "You could lower rates to 2% tomorrow, and all that will do is increase home values. It's not going to solve the underlying issue."

The other big question will be funding of the many provisions created under the Road to Housing Act. While the provisions in the bill were bipartisan, Congress must still approve funding for some of those programs. Some of those discussions are coming in the 2028 fiscal budget and beyond.

Over the months of negotiations on the Road to Housing bill, some Republicans took issue with unfunded mandates in it. Concerns about funding programs, and at what level, could spill over into congressional proceedings in coming years.

Tony Marquez, director of American University's real estate program, who has a long career in real estate and banking, tells Realtor.com that the industry is still amenable to a few different ideas for how to solve housing. It doesn't rely on one side's control of the government.

"My un-professional assessment is we'll have a certain amount of gridlock over a number of years where Democrats may come up with some suggestions," Marquez says. "But the answer to affordable housing is not just one silver bullet. It can have many elements."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5592. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. And that could work in your favor.If you're ready to buy, talk to a local agent about which builders have completed homes sitting on the market in your area see what they're willing to offer to get them sold.

#5591. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.

Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

#5590. Industrial automation startup Path Robotics raises $300M in funding

Path Robotics Inc., a startup working to automate industrial welding workflows, today announced that it has raised $300 million in funding.

Georgian led the Series E round. It was joined by a consortium that included the venture capital arms of Yamaha Motor Co. and Navier Corp., one of South Korea’s largest tech firms. The investment gives Path Robotics a post-money valuation of $2.45 billion.

Welding tasks were historically difficult to automate because of a phenomenon called heat-induced metal distortion. It occurs when the heat produced by a welding torch warps the metal parts being joined together. Furthermore, the parts change shape again when they cool down. Those distortions are often unpredictable, which means they can throw off a robot arm that follows a static, pre-programmed welding plan.

There are also other sources of complexity. Mass produced metal parts that are based on the same blueprint often differ slightly because of manufacturing inconsistencies. In many cases, those variations make it necessary to adjust the way welding is performed. That isn’t always possible with traditional automation software.

Path Robotics has developed an AI model that addresses those challenges. Obsidian, as it’s called, is specifically designed to power industrial robots equipped with welding torches. The company says that the model can observe how metal parts change shape during the welding process and adjust its workflow accordingly. Furthermore, it automatically accounts for unexpected part variations.

Obsidian monitors the welding workflow using four lasers attached to the torch that it controls. The emitters illuminate the parts being welded together and the reflected light is captured by a pair of cameras. According to Path Robotics, Obsidian collects data not only during the welding process but also before and after each run.

The data powers an AI model that the company refers to as a weld world model. Path Robotics’ researchers use it to generate simulated welding projects. Those simulations, in turn, power Obsidian’s training workflow.

Path Robotics originally developed Obsidian for large robotic workstations called welding cells. In April, it introduced a four-legged robot called Rove that uses the model to automate shipbuilding tasks. The company says its software can also be used to make parts for vehicles, power generators, utility poles and other heavy equipment.

“We’re seeing accelerating demand from manufacturers that need to expand production capacity but can’t get there with traditional automation,” said Path Robotics co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Andy Lonsberry. “This capital allows us to scale our welding business alongside our customers while investing further in the data, compute, and model development needed to take on every task before and after welding.”

#5589. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5588. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. Patrick and Brittany Mahomes are expecting their fourth child, and the newest member of the family will have plenty of room to play at their custom-built Missouri mansion.

The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback and his wife, both 31, took to Instagram to share the joyous news that their family is expanding.

"Another blessing from God....& then there were 6," they captioned an image of them and their three kids, Sterling Skye, 5; Golden Raye, 1; and son Patrick "Bronze" Lavon Mahomes III, 3, on a beach.

The couple's growing family means one more child will get to turn their at-home, indoor basketball court into a playground.

The couple's extraordinary property sits on a huge 8-acre parcel they snapped up for just $400,000; however, the dwelling that now occupies it is understood to be worth millions more.

Images have revealed that the home features a stunning swimming pool, complete with its own water slide, as well as a large sports field that has "Mahomes" written across one end.

And Patrick isn't restricting himself to just football as far as his at-home sporting amenities go. In addition to the field, he and Brittany added a putting green and a private pond.

In October 2024, the home was the site of a burglary, an incident that he later described as "frustrating" and "disappointing."

Patrick and his wife are believed to have moved into their home in 2023, having spent close to three years completing their dream abode. At around the same time, they also listed their former Kansas City dwelling—a much more modest house they purchased in 2019.

According to local regulations, home sale prices do not have to be disclosed, meaning that the final sale price is not known. However, they put the abode on the market for $2.9 million. Before the couple purchased the property, it was last listed for $1.99 million.

The expectant mom of four previously shared a very candid glimpse inside the couple's lives at home with their three children, shedding a very entertaining light on the chaos that erupts when the kids are allowed to run loose around the upscale abode.

In a video posted to her Instagram Stories, the entrepreneur and fitness trainer revealed the havoc that her kids had caused inside Patrick's private at-home basketball court, which has, for all intents and purposes, been turned into a makeshift playground.

The clips showed the couple's children crawling around in the space, before panning the camera to reveal the court surface was covered in an array of toys, as well as two bounce houses.

Adding insult to injury, Brittany poked fun at her husband for daring to think that the basketball court would be one space inside the home that he could call his own, saying: "I really think it's hilarious that Patrick wanted this basketball court because he thought it was going to be his."

In the first clip, two of the kids could be seen playing on the ground in front of a "Spider-Man"-themed bounce house—with Patrick III sporting a superhero costume in honor of the Marvel favorite.

His younger sister, meanwhile, holds what appears to be a pickleball racket in her hand as she walks toward her sibling.

As Brittany pans the camera around the room, dozens of other toys are seen littered across the floor—from scooters and ride-on bikes to pink ponies, several of which are covering the NFL quarterback's custom "MAHOMES" logo that runs along one side of the court.

It looks as though the court had, at one point, been set up for all manner of sporting events; a rack of fresh basketballs sits to one side, while a tennis net has been set up on the center line.

But the chaos did not end with the basketball center—with Brittany later revealing that the kids kept the fun going even after they made their way upstairs, where she was greeted by a trail of "Spider-Man" costume pieces laying in a trail on the floor.

“The trail of a kid that had to poop,” she joked.

Despite Brittany joking about their kids taking over the basketball court, Patrick did previously reveal when they were building the house that he had always intended for the space to be "for the kids."

"I’m going to have a half-football field so I can get some work in with some guys out there," he shared during a 2021 interview with NBC Sports. "I’ll have a basketball court ... [but] that’s not for me, that’s for the kids. It’ll have a little golf stuff out there as well."

Then, in 2023, he and Brittany transformed the basketball court into an indoor football stadium in honor of Bronze's first birthday, complete with balloon displays and custom bounce houses for the kids to enjoy.

Luckily, the basketball court is far from the only space inside the palatial property where Patrick can enjoy some peace and quiet at his home, which boasts incredible amenities, both inside and out.

In addition to that primary residence, the couple also owns a vacation home in Texas, where they first met.

The four-bedroom, 7,800-square-foot estate on a half-acre lot comes with lots of baller perks: a wine room, family room with a gas fireplace, and an outdoor space with a gas fireplace, grill grotto, firepit lounge area, large pool, tan deck, and spa.

#5586. Douglas Elliman Goes All-In for AI After Q3’s Flat Earnings

After a middling third quarter, Douglas Elliman CEO Michael Liebowitz told investors that recent changes and efforts to the company are to “modernize” and build a “more efficient platform” by early 2027.

The luxury brokerage’s revenue fell short in the third quarter at $252.1 million for 2026, a $10 million drop compared to 2025’s revenue of $262.8 million.

For the first nine months of the year, revenue also dropped and was reported at $749.9 million. In 2025, that revenue was reported at $787.6 million.

During the Q3 earnings call for Douglas Elliman, Liebowitz claimed that the last quarter was about “technological upgrades” and emphasized the company’s movement toward execution.

“Technology is central to our strategy, and the transformation we introduced last quarter has continued to advance as part of our broader efforts to modernize the business and reduce costs,” he stated.

The company has faced struggles both in the market and internally over the past two years, with C-suite turnover and competition in its home market of New York City.

After the earnings report, the company’s stock jumped 12%, though it is still down 30% this year.

Liebowitz also mentioned multiple additions to Douglas Elliman this past quarter, including Sharon Milz as head of AI technology transformation, Nick Patino as director of AI enablement and Jamie Gagliano as chief operations officer.

“Sharon is overseeing our enterprise AI strategy and deployment as well as the broader technology transformation across the company,” he added. “Nick focuses on making sure these capabilities become part of how we get things done across the company, translating new technology into adoption, productivity and measuring business value. Jamie brings significant experience working with agents and building businesses. She’s already looking across our national operations at how we simplify processes, strengthen support and build a more scalable organization.”

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Aside from a drop in revenue, Douglas Elliman also reported a drop in operating income (loss) annually. For Q3 2026, the company reported an operating income of $6.3 million, while last year’s operating loss clocked in at $10.7 million.

Bryant Kirkland—Douglas Elliman’s CFO—stated on the Q3 earnings call, however, that the year-over-year comparisons lean negatively because of 2025’s data.

“The year-over-year comparisons for the nine months ended Sept. 30, 2026 are impacted by a difficult comparable, due to an unusually strong first quarter of 2025,” he noted.

Adjusted EBITDA—or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization—may signal positive growth for the brokerage, as Q3’s EBITDA was $5.3 million compared to last year’s $1 million.

While the adjusted EBITDA grew for Q3, the company’s adjusted net loss greatly overshadows many gains, as it reported the adjusted net loss at nearly $8 million, compared to last year’s $1.4 million.

Existing-home sales, Kirkland mentioned, were up 1.9% from October 2026, compared to October 2025. But, this result was weighed down. October 2026 had one fewer sales day than last year, Kirkland said. In reality, the receipts from existing-home sales were down 2.7% in October 2026 compared to October 2025.

Liebowitz attributed many of the Q3 losses to changes, and called it a “growth stage.”

Kirkland claimed the company would see returns on its current investments—such as the development marketing pipeline of $26 billion and the additional $11.8 billion scheduled to come to market Dec. 31, 2027—between 2026 and 2032. In particular, Kirkland mentioned Florida’s real estate market and its marketing value.

“We see positive indicators within our development marketing business in Florida, with approximately $19.5 billion gross transaction value, of the $26 billion of gross transaction value that is being actively marketed,” he added. “For most projects in Florida, we receive progress payments during the marketing process and defer the related revenue and commission it spent until the earnings process is complete, which is when the underlying sale closes.”

After investing in an “AI transformation” last quarter, the Q3 earnings release noted that the initiative is expected to gradually drive significant savings in non-commission operating expenses over the next three years.

“Modernizing those systems should make the company more efficient while giving our agents and employees better tools and more time to focus on clients, relationships and growing their businesses,” Liebowitz claimed. “That work is underway, and we remain focused on gradually realizing meaningful efficiencies in our non-commission operating expenses beginning in 2027.”

#5585. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5584. Homebuilders in Fire-Ravaged Altadena Are Using 3D Printing To Rebuild

Residents walking through Altadena, CA, recently were struck by an odd sight this week: A large gantry crane appeared to be "printing" out 11-inch-thick concrete pillars and walls.

The robotic 3D-printed machine, designed by Dutch company COBOD, was being used to rebuild a home that had been destroyed by the Eaton Fire in January 2025, extruding layer after layer of concrete and shaping it into walls.

The home is a project of Emergent Home, a Los Angeles-based builder that's been contracted to produce seven concrete-printed homes in Altadena.

Emergent was actually founded in 2019 to help rebuild after the Carr Fire destroyed more than a thousand homes in Northern California.

3D-printed concrete has gained attention in recent years because of its sturdiness and cost effectiveness—especially in fire-prone areas. The precise nature of the process reduces construction waste and completion time. According to COBOD, homes can be completed twice as fast as conventional construction and at up to 30% less than conventionally built homes.

Most importantly, the homes are fire resistant.

The January 2025 Eaton wildfire ravaged more than 14,000 acres and destroyed more than 6,000 homes. Yet despite the numerous fires and climate risks, the vast majority of homes in the area continue to be constructed with wood.

"Ninety-five percent of this community is rebuilding with wood," Ken Calligar, the CEO of building technology company RSG-3D, previously told Realtor.com®. "It's insane."

"A 6-year-old could have said this wasn't a good idea," he continued. "These towns are so vulnerable, they have no idea. To me, it's so obvious what the solution is."

RSG-3D builds with framing panels made of steel wire and expanded polystyrene wrapped in concrete skins—and is somewhat different from the 3D printed concrete Emergent Construction is using.

The share of 3D-printed concrete homes in the U.S. remains relatively small. So far only a couple hundred homes have been built using the technology. But proponents believe that as climate disasters continue to plague homeowners, and as costs continue to hobble the building industry, the technology will grow in popularity.

Already, one homeowner is getting ready to move into her 3D-printed concrete home. In September, PCI Builders collaborated with RIC Robotics and Stone River Dynamics to produce the first permit-approved 3D-printed concrete house in the area.

The home was for Cindy Lopez, an Altadena resident whose home burned to the ground on Jan. 8, 2025.

“This home represents more than my own recovery, I hope it helps other families see what is possible while encouraging local governments to recognize and invest in 3D-concrete printing as a meaningful option for communities facing increasing wildfire risk," Lopez said in a statement.

#5583. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5582. IBM Quantum announces upcoming Nighthawk r3 processor designed to execute 10,000 operations

IBM Corp. today announced the Quantum Nighthawk r3, its next-generation processor designed to tackle larger, more complex computations at high speed while maintaining quality.

The company also said that in 2027, IBM plans to link two r3 quantum processors into a single system capable of running up to 10,000 quantum operations, scaling to more than 1,000 qubits between them.

“Useful quantum computing hinges on whether results can be delivered with accuracy and speed, both are fundamental,” said Director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta. “IBM Nighthawk is already showing us what that looks like today.”

The new r3 chip follows the introduction of Nighthawk r2 in September, which supports more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 qubits.

Qubits are the fundamental unit of logical information in a quantum computer, similar to a classical computer’s bit. Unlike classical bits, which can be a 0 or 1, qubits can be 0, 1 or a “superposition” of both at the same time. Using this property, quantum processors such as IBM’s Nighthawk can do rapid, complex parallel calculations.

The r2 chip introduced a groundbreaking high-speed qubit reset architecture that lets developers and researchers quickly prime qubits after measurements. Under normal circumstances, after a quantum circuit runs and the result is measured, the qubits must return to the ground state before the next program can run; this process can take hundreds of milliseconds, meaning the chip remains idle during that time. With the new technology, this wait period can be reduced from about 200 milliseconds down to roughly 25 nanoseconds without disturbing neighboring qubits.

Building on lessons learned from Nighthawk r2 and the technology built into it, IBM said r3 will extend the same high-speed architecture to larger quantum systems to support 10,000 operations on 520 programmable qubits with 2,034 physical quantum components.

A physical qubit is the actual, hardware-level quantum device that stores the quantum information. In Nighthawk, the qubits are superconducting and arranged in a square lattice. The programmable qubits are the measurable, active quantum data units, while additional quantum components support them, including couplers and reset elements.

IBM said it has already demonstrated two critical technologies that will make combining two r3 chips. This year, the company connected two Nighthawk r1 processors using four l-couplers, or “long-range” quantum interconnects. These act as a physical bridge between separate processors to create a larger machine.

In the demonstration, the couplers achieved a 99.4% transfer fidelity, progressing towards the target of 99.9% fidelity. The company also connected cryogenic modules into a single system.

In 2027, IBM intends to progress using these modularity advances to scale Nighthawk into a larger quantum system. By connecting two Nighthawk r3 processors into a single 1,040 system, IBM will extend this high-performance architecture to tackle larger and more complex computations.

“As we scale this architecture to larger and more powerful quantum computers, the capabilities of quantum computation will reach new levels as we integrate more closely with classical resources and march ahead to fault tolerance,” added Gambetta.

IBM also announced that its cloud-based service for researchers and developers, IBM Quantum Platform, will bring high-performance classical and quantum computing together in a single managed environment.

Users can now integrate quantum workflows directly with HPC and classical resources on the platform, or with classical compute on their laptop or any number of the world’s most powerful supercomputers.

Integrating quantum and classical computing permits traditional computers to orchestrate algorithms and computations on specialized central processing units and graphics processing units, while the quantum computer runs parallel computations. Users are already seeing promising results, including Cleveland Clinic using the platform to process 2.6 million samples up to three times faster to model biological structures.

Direct integration of quantum and classical systems will also help drive breakthroughs in quantum error correction. Error correction is fundamental to handling the noise that can destabilize individual qubits, creating a high chance of errors rising out of computations. Quantum Platform is launching pulse-level access to give researchers precise control over how they can detect, understand and correct errors within quantum and classical architectures.

IBM recently launched a new quantum error-correction platform that addresses this, in collaboration with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The build physically colocates Nighthawk processors with next-generation AMD GPUs and CPUs.

#5581. Alix Earle’s Feud With Alex Cooper Resurfaces—Inside Her Family’s $4.1 Million New Jersey Home Where She Told Her Side

Social media sensation Alix Earle’s falling-out with Alex Cooper is back in the spotlight after Sofia Franklyn revisited her own split from the “Call Her Daddy” co-founder in her new explosive memoir, "Daddy Issues."

Earle, 25, previously pulled back the curtain on her side of the story from inside her family’s $4.1 million New Jersey home, where Netflix’s "Earle Meets World" cameras captured how the feud took an emotional toll on her.

Now, that drama has been brought to a boiling point after Franklyn shared her own experience with Cooper, 32, in her tell-all book, detailing the experience that took the once-co-hosts from friends to enemies.

Following the release of her book, Earle made it clear whose side she was on when she shared a TikTok video of her reading Franklyn's memoir.

Earle and Cooper were once known to share a close friendship, but their relationship appeared to sour after Cooper dropped Earle's podcast, "Hot Mess," from her Unwell Network in early 2025, sparking rumors that a feud had erupted between the two.

After Earle was publicly seen liking negative comments about Cooper on social media, the latter posted a video urging her online nemesis to air her grievances in public.

Earle responded to Cooper's video with a brief, "On it," but stopped short of sharing her side of the story at the time. Instead, she later teased that fans would finally get answers about what happened between the pair in the Netflix series.

"She's trying to paint it as I'm just like this crazy lunatic who is hating her for no reason. There's a reason," Earle said.

In her Netflix series, Earle opened up about the drama with Cooper, telling her family, “From the start, I didn’t realize things were going wrong because I was obsessed with her. I was like, ‘This is my idol. I’m so happy to work with her,’ and then [I] constantly felt taken advantage of and used and mistreated and manipulated.”

Holding back tears, she said, “What I was thinking—which makes me so sad for me at the time—is I was so happy. I trusted her so much, and all she did was just s--- on it.”

She explained, "We’re filming her podcast, and she’s having us drink before and then asking me really sexual questions I wasn’t comfortable with. But then I’m also answering ‘cause I’m drunk. I’m imagining myself in her shoes, to take someone in college, who’s young, impressionable, you know looks up to you, and then ask them these raunchy questions. It’s stuff that I didn’t necessarily want to live on the internet forever.”

The series, which hit screens on Sept. 4, also offered fans the the most revealing look yet at the behind-the-scenes drama that will be played out on screen for the world to see, including the difficult relationship between Earle's mother, Alisa, and her stepmother, Ashley Dupré, as well as the TikTok star's split from NFL player Braxton Berrios.

"Earle Meets World" take fans inside the star's world as she navigates her booming career, complicated relationships, family dynamics, and the hardships that come with being in the spotlight.

And while Earle has become known for documenting everything from her nights out to her acne struggles, with her millions of followers, the series promises to offer a much more intimate look at what happens when the cameras—or, in her case, the phone—would normally stop rolling.

"There's so much more to my life that people don't get to see,” Earle admitted in the trailer.

The reality series also brings Earle's family firmly into the spotlight, giving viewers a glimpse at the people closest to the influencer as she attempts to balance her increasingly high-profile career with her personal life.

"Every time I step out, there's a story," Earle lamented in the clip.

And among the familiar faces featured in the series is another backdrop that longtime Earle followers may recognize: her family's sprawling New Jersey mansion.

Earle's father and manager, Thomas "TJ" Earle, and her stepmother purchased the property in 2013 for $2.25 million, property records previously reviewed by Realtor.com® reveal.

The pair scored quite the deal on the home, which had previously been listed for $3.35 million. Today, the dwelling is estimated to be worth around $4.1 million, according to Realtor.com.

TJ and Ashley share the home with their three children, Izabel, Penelope, and Thomas, while Alix and her sister, Ashtin Earle, regularly return to New Jersey to spend time with their family.

Over the years, Alix has offered her millions of social media followers glimpses inside the property, revealing that the family has made numerous changes to the dwelling since purchasing it.

Now, the home is poised to serve as one of the backdrops for the family's next chapter as Netflix cameras capture the highs and lows of their lives for Earle's first reality series.

"My family is full of chaos," Earle said in the trailer.

In addition to putting Earle's close-knit blended family front and center, the show will also highlight the TikTok's romantic life, specifically her relationship with former boyfriend and NFL star, Berrios.

In one scene of the trailer, Earle's family can be heard confessing that they are "team Braxton." It then cuts to a clip of the social media icon crying as she admits she struggled to balance both her "break up" as well as the news of her mom's cancer diagnosis—both of which occurred while she was filming "Dancing With the Stars."

Earle's mother, Alisa, can also be seen opening up about the complicated relationship she shares with Dupré, telling the camera: "I'm side by side with someone who had an affair with my husband. You don't forget what happened. It doesn't mean we can't enjoy the people that we love."

Ashtin can then be seen telling her family members that they have "such a special dynamic."

The series also documents the enormous changes that have taken place in the influencer's own life since she first found fame filming "Get Ready With Me" videos from her student housing at the University of Miami.

Since graduating in 2023, Earle has transformed her enormous online following into a sprawling career, complete with lucrative brand partnerships, red-carpet appearances, and business ventures.

"I started sharing a more unfiltered look into my life, and then it just amped up," Earle says in the teaser.

But “Earle Meets World” promises to go beyond the polished snapshots of that success, documenting the more complicated reality of navigating fame, family, friendships, and relationships while millions of people watch.

Earle's sister Ashtin will feature prominently alongside her, as well as several of Earle's close friends.

While Earle's followers are already accustomed to seeing snippets of her family life online—including her visits home to New Jersey—the Netflix series will offer much greater access to the people and places that have played an integral role in her life.

That includes the multimillion-dollar family mansion that has appeared repeatedly in her social media content and will now help set the scene as the Earles invite viewers further into their world than ever before.

The family appears to have made numerous upgrades to the dwelling in the six years since they bought it, with Earle's videos showcasing a much more modern and elegant interior than featured in the original listing images.

Meanwhile, records show that Earle's mother, Alisa, resides in a newly-built dwelling in nearby Point Pleasant.

When they are in New Jersey, the TikTok star and Ashtin, who resides in New York City, split their time between the two dwellings and it is understood that both parents will feature heavily in the Netflix series.

All episodes of “Earle Meets World” are scheduled to premiere on Netflix on Sept. 4.

In a previous press release announcing that Earle would be stepping into the world of reality TV, the TikTok star confessed that partnering with Netflix felt "unreal," adding that she was excited to show fans her life behind the scenes.

"It honestly feels unreal to be partnering with Netflix, and I’m so excited to be creating this show with them," she shared. "I’ve shared my life for years through my own camera, but this felt like the next phase because it’s a chance to go deeper.

"Not just the highlights, but the real moments, too. The vulnerable ones, the hard ones, and the fun, chaotic ones in between. It’s the same authenticity people know me for, but now with a different lens."

The social media mogul revealed that she was most "excited" for her fans to see her "fun" and "modern family."

"People either think we’re insane or they’re like, wait, this is exactly like my life. And honestly, both are true. I’m excited for fans to experience the full picture as it happens. The chaos, the emotional moments, the stressful parts, and all the little things in between that you don’t always see online," she added.

She admitted that the process was a "little scary," adding, "I’m so used to being in control of what I share and what I keep private, so having cameras around in moments I normally wouldn’t post is definitely an adjustment.

"But the real, human moments are what connected me to my audience in the first place. If letting people in even more makes someone feel less alone, or even just makes them laugh, then it’s worth it."
