#5580. How Traton Homes Is Designing for Multigenerational Living

The Presley model's guest suite at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

Today’s buyers are asking their homes to work harder over time. At Traton Homes, main-level guest suites have become an important part of that flexibility, providing space for overnight visitors today and potentially aging parents, caregivers, or other family members in the future.

Director of design Angi Sago explains how evolving household needs are influencing the builder’s approach to floor plans, entertaining spaces, and long-term livability.

Traton offers a variety of floor plans featuring a guest suite on the main. What does that tell you about how buyer priorities are changing?

Buyers are increasingly looking for homes that offer flexibility to accommodate their families’ changing needs. A private guest suite on the main level provides a comfortable space for visiting family and friends, but it also offers the opportunity to accommodate aging parents, whether for extended visits or as a more permanent living arrangement in the future. It’s a feature that adds both immediate convenience and long-term value.

Who are these suites designed for; aging parents, adult children, long-term guests, or a combination?

The Presley model home at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

While these suites certainly provide a wonderful space for overnight guests, we find that many buyers are thinking about aging parents and the possibility of multigenerational living. Having a private guest bedroom with en-suite bath on the main level gives homeowners peace of mind knowing they have a comfortable and accessible space for loved ones, whether they are visiting or eventually become part of the household.

How has demand for multigenerational or guest-friendly living influenced Traton’s floor plans over the past few years?

Traton has recognized the appeal of main-level guest suites for many years, and we’ve incorporated them into our home designs for quite some time. These floor plans have consistently been popular because they offer homeowners flexibility in how they use their space. As families’ needs continue to evolve, we believe this versatility is becoming even more valuable to today’s buyers.

What separates a well-designed guest suite from simply putting an extra bedroom and bathroom on the first floor?

Are buyers looking for spaces that can change purpose over time, such as moving from a guest suite to an aging-in-place bedroom or caregiver space?

Absolutely. Flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a main-level guest suite. A space that initially serves as a bedroom for visiting friends and family can eventually accommodate an aging parent or caregiver. Buyers appreciate knowing their home can adapt to different stages of life without requiring significant changes to the floor plan.

Beyond the guest suite, what design features are becoming more important for homeowners who regularly entertain or host overnight visitors?

Spaces that make entertaining easier and more enjoyable continue to be popular. Butler’s pantries are especially appealing because they can double as a beverage or bar area while providing additional storage and serving space. Keeping rooms are another desirable feature, offering a comfortable, informal gathering area where family and friends can relax and spend time together. Buyers appreciate having spaces that encourage connection while allowing for different types of entertaining.

The Abney model at Linden Grove in Powder Springs, Georgia.

Traton’s floor plans with owner’s suites are offered at various price points. How do expectations for hosting and flexible living differ between by price point, if at all?

Interestingly, we see many of the same priorities across price points. Regardless of price point, homeowners want comfortable, functional spaces where they can welcome family and friends. The primary difference is often the amount of space available for entertaining and the additional features a larger home can accommodate. While buyers of our more expansive homes may have more gathering areas, the desire for a private guest suite and flexible living spaces is equally important to buyers of our more moderately sized plans.

Are buyers willing to give up square footage elsewhere in the home to get a main-level guest suite, larger pantry, loft, or other flexible space?

We find that a main-level guest suite is typically a feature buyers either prioritize from the beginning or don’t necessarily need. Rather than sacrificing square footage elsewhere, buyers tend to gravitate toward floor plans that already incorporate the spaces that matter most to their lifestyle. That’s why offering a variety of thoughtfully designed floor plans is so important. It allows buyers to select a home that best fits their individual needs and preferences.

Looking ahead, how do you expect changing family structures and the way people live together to influence Traton’s next generation of floor plans?

As housing costs continue to put pressure on household budgets, we anticipate that multigenerational living will become an important consideration for home buyers. Sharing a home can offer financial advantages while allowing families to stay connected and support one another. We believe buyers will continue to place a premium on flexible floor plans that provide both shared gathering spaces and private retreats, allowing multiple generations to live comfortably under one roof. At Traton, our goal is to continue designing homes that reflect how families live today while anticipating how their needs may change in the years ahead.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5579. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5577. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5576. Mortgage Demand Jumps 6.2% as Rates Fall for Fourth Straight Week

Mortgage applications rose last week, as interest rates decreased for the fourth week in a row, hitting their lowest levels since mid-September, as a positive jobs report and the results of the midterm election bolster the outlook.

For the week ending Nov. 6 the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index—a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—increased 6.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis from one week earlier.

The Purchase Index, which measures the volume of mortgage applications to purchase a single-family home, increased 8% from one week earlier after seasonal adjustment. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago.

According to MBA calculations, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages with conforming loan balances is 7.21%, a slight decrease from last week's rate of 7.3%. Rates averaged 5.99% a year ago.

Mortgage rates dropped to 7.18% last week from 7.21% the week before, according to a separate survey from Freddie Mac.

“Mortgage rates declined for the fourth straight week,” said Joel Kan, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “The declining trend in rates helped to spur stronger application activity, although the pace of purchase and refinance applications remain considerably lower than a year ago."

In recent weeks, high interest rates had pushed more buyers toward riskier Adjustable Rate Mortgages. However, this past week, ARM applications decreased to 10.9% of the total. applications, down from 11.4% the previous week.

FHA and VA loans saw "particularly strong growth" this past week, said Kan.

The share of FHA loan applications decreased to 15.5% from 16% the prior week. The VA share of total applications increased to 12% from 11.2% the prior week. And the USDA share of total applications decreased to 0.5% from 0.6% the week prior.

The refinance share of mortgage activity remained unchanged at 39.8%, but was 57% lower than the same week one year ago, as homeowners remain locked into their lower interest rates.

October's positive jobs report, which showed that the U.S. economy added 165,000 nonfarm jobs in October, has increased the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates when it next meets in December.

CME Group's FedWatch has the likelihood of an additional rate hike at around 77%.

The positive jobs report news was compounded by broad Democrat wins in the midterm elections. Democrats, many of whom ran on a message of affordability, won the majority in both the House and the Senate. Voters aged 18 to 34 and men aged 18 to 49 had ranked housing costs as a top political issue in a rcent CNBC survey.

Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy called the midterms a "wake-up call."

"Everyone needs to get serious about tackling and addressing housing affordability. It can't be ignored anymore," he told Realtor.com®.

Mortgage rates are calculated based on various factors in the economy, and the length of your loan and credit score will also factor into the mortgage rate you qualify for.

the 10-year Treasury note, because most 30-year mortgages are either paid off or refinanced in roughly eight to 11 years.

That makes the duration on the loans roughly comparable, and mortgage lenders use the 10-year Treasury as a benchmark for setting rates, adding on a risk premium.

Long-term yields for Treasury notes are determined by a number of factors, including the supply of and demand for U.S. government debt, and investor expectations for inflation over the life of the bonds.

#5574. Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC Connect Florida and Indiana Property Data Through RPR View

Business professional using laptop with connected digital document icons, representing document management, data sharing, cloud workflow, file organization, and business automation.

Realtors Property Resource (RPR) has announced that Realtors serving clients with real estate interests in both Florida and Indiana will have access to additional property information through a new data-sharing collaboration between Stellar MLS and MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative (BLC).

According to a release, using RPR View, the MLS data-sharing capability from RPR, eligible customers in both markets will be able to access approved off-market listings, including historical listing data, across MLS boundaries.

RPR says the collaboration reflects a natural connection between Indiana and Florida, where seasonal residents, relocating homeowners and buyers often have real estate interests in both markets. Expanded access to listing history gives Realtors additional context to research properties, understand past market activity and help clients make informed decisions.

“Buyers and sellers deserve informed guidance wherever their real estate goals take them,” said Shayne Fairley, CEO of Stellar MLS. “Often, they don’t stop at market boundaries, and neither should access to trusted listing information for the real estate professionals who serve them. With strong ties between Florida and Indiana, especially among seasonal residents, our collaboration with MIBOR BLC and RPR will provide greater access to property information across both markets, so the professionals who guide their clients can do so with greater confidence.”

He added: “We’re pleased to bring this expanded access to our collective customers, and we look forward to creating similar opportunities with other MLSs and associations.”

A practical approach to cross-market data sharing

Beyond the benefits to Realtors, the release says the collaboration demonstrates how MLS organizations can expand property data access using technology already available through RPR.

With RPR View, participating MLSs determine which listing information to share and which markets can access it. This gives organizations flexibility to expand access while maintaining control over their data-sharing permissions.

For Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC, the arrangement enables reciprocal access to approved off-market listing information, including historical listing data, through an established platform, without developing a separate data-sharing system.

“MLS organizations create the greatest value when we look beyond traditional market boundaries and focus on how real estate professionals actually do business. Our partnership with Stellar MLS reflects that philosophy,” said Shelley Specchio, CEO and President of the MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative in Indiana. “By connecting the Indiana and Florida marketplaces through RPR, we are reducing friction for professionals working in both states and demonstrating what is possible when MLSs collaborate around the needs of brokers, agents and consumers.”

Building connections through existing infrastructure

The release notes that as of October 31, 341 of the nation’s 487 MLSs (70%) participate in RPR View data sharing, representing more than 1 million Realtors. The Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC collaboration demonstrates how this existing infrastructure can support cross-market access while allowing each organization to maintain control over its shared data, RPR says.

“One of the advantages of RPR View is that MLSs can expand data access without having to build a new solution,” said Liz Gunski, vice president of Industry Relations at RPR. “Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC are showing how existing infrastructure can support collaboration while keeping participating organizations in control of their data.”

The expanded data access is scheduled to become available to eligible customers in both markets beginning Nov. 4.

“I think everybody here loves that because that does lead to sovereignty as well,” said Rob Strechay, principal analyst at theCUBE, during the event. “They’re actually building on top of open source and enhancing it in a way that provides more value in supporting it, which is key to their success.”

Deploying and managing AI workloads across hybrid cloud environments presents new operational challenges for enterprises. Red Hat’s answer is Red Hat AI 3.4, an updated version of its enterprise AI platform that supports agentic AI deployments and large-scale inference across hybrid environments.

The company also announced two new managed services: Red Hat AI Inference and Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization Service on IBM Cloud. Red Hat AI Inference is designed to integrate real-time AI inference directly into clients’ production workflows, while OpenShift Virtualization enables clients to migrate and run virtual machines at scale. Both services are intended to accelerate hybrid cloud adoption.

“What’s really going to drive inference demand exponentially is AI agents,” said Joe Fernandes, vice president and general manager of Red Hat AI. “We provide a platform where customers can deploy and manage their AI agents across a hybrid infrastructure environment.”

The next piece of Red Hat’s agentic strategy comes in the form of Ansible Automation Platform 2.7, which connects AI-generated insights to governed infrastructure actions. Its self-service automation capabilities allow authorized users in locations such as branch offices and factory floors to manage servers and networks within established controls.

“Customers are now able to use their own data to calculate savings and efficiencies,” said Sathish Balakrishnan, vice president and general manager of Red Hat’s Ansible business unit. “Every action, whether it’s triggered by humans, an event or an AI agent, passes through the same [access controls], approval gates, audit trails, content signing and credential management.”

AI budgets are booming: according to theCUBE Research, Analysts project that AI cloud spending could approach $2.5 trillion by 2026, growing at roughly 44% year-over-year. However, that investment does not always return concrete value. Research shows that 50.7% of organizations rely on public AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot but only 20.2% report enterprise-wide AI deployments built on a governed framework.

“Most people are token consumers and that is part of the reason they’re trying to figure out how do they get to production,” Strechay said. “How do they get out of these death-by-pilot situations and become token producers so that they can offset the cost or at least lower the cost so they can get to the [return on AI investment] of those applications? You can use [OpenShift] infrastructure along with things like vLLM and some of the other things in Red Hat AI to get and become efficient in how you produce your tokens.”

Part of Red Hat’s strategy for helping customers manage sprawling AI budgets is its partnership with Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. Together, AMD and Red Hat are encouraging enterprises to rethink the financials of AI. Rather than opting for the newest, most expensive hardware, clients might have better results if matching compute resources to the workload, according to John Hampton, corporate vice president of global enterprise technical sales at AMD.

“So many of these enterprises just ran out and bought big [graphics processing unit] clusters because they knew they had to solve for AI,” he said. “Enterprises are coming to us and saying, ‘This is exploding. It’s good that we’re using AI, but we can’t afford this anymore.’”

Red Hat has also joined forces with Intel Corp. to help customers determine which combination of hardware and software best suits their workloads. As enterprises look to reduce inference costs, the companies are emphasizing the value of choosing the right mix of CPUs and GPUs rather than relying on a single approach.

“As we’ve gone through this with our customers in the industry, we’ve seen that people often have just assumed, ‘I’ve got a hammer. I need the nail to hit it with,’” said Bill Pearson, vice president of data center and AI at Intel. “Once they take a step back to say, ‘Wait a minute. I have these [central processing units] in my data center’ or ‘I need to figure out how to balance the right number of CPUs with the right number of GPUs to achieve that outcome I’m looking for,’ they’re actually going to get better results at a better price point for delivering lower-cost tokens.”

Red Hat announced several collaborations at the summit, including Red Hat AI Factory with Nvidia Corp. The partnership includes support for Nvidia’s Blackwell architecture and upcoming Vera Rubin platform, as well as participation in Nvidia’s OpenShell project for AI agent sandboxing and secure execution.

“Moving AI from corporate experimentation to an industrial engine requires a sovereign, consistent foundation across the hybrid cloud,” said Chris Wright, chief technology officer and senior vice president for global engineering at Red Hat, in the announcement. “Through our strategic co-engineering efforts with Nvidia, Red Hat provides the architectural control and open source innovation enterprises need to scale agentic AI with confidence.”

Red Hat’s other partnership announcements focused on agentic AI and edge computing. Boomi LP, which brands itself as a data activation company, is collaborating with Red Hat on a single, integrated stack for deploying agentic AI at scale. The partnerships with Panasonic Connect and Voyager cover edge computing solutions and space edge micro data centers, respectively.

Red Hat’s expanding ecosystem of partnerships reflects the growing range of enterprise applications for agentic AI. The challenge for organizations is determining how those capabilities can address their specific business needs, according to Matt Hicks, president and chief executive officer of Red Hat.

“From the board level down … you have a feeling of, ‘We have to be able to harness what this technology can do,’” said Matt Hicks. “The people that will be the most successful with AI are the people that have the most questions. People that know business, they know their domain. Those are the ones [that] have no barriers to what they can do and change. It’s just about getting started.”

Sovereign AI has become an increasingly important consideration for enterprises seeking greater control over their data and infrastructure. Gartner Inc. forecasts that the sovereign cloud infrastructure-as-a-service market will grow at a compound annual rate of 36% through 2028.

Red Hat is expanding support for sovereign cloud while allowing customers to keep the infrastructure they already invested in. That includes collaborations with Core42, which specializes in sovereign-by-design infrastructure, and Sopra Steria, a longstanding European collaborator on sovereign AI initiatives.

Red Hat is also extending its software security capabilities as enterprises adopt agentic AI. Fedora Hummingbird Linux is a container-native operating system designed for agent-first development, with an automated software delivery pipeline. Meanwhile, Red Hat Hardened Images provides a catalog of minimal container images designed to reduce vulnerabilities and strengthen software supply-chain security.

At this point, sovereign AI and governance play an essential role in giving customers choice and control, according to Ashesh Badani, senior vice president and chief product officer of Red Hat.

“Whether an organization is meeting jurisdictional mandates or reclaiming its data from proprietary silos, we are providing the capabilities and platforms to build a more self-determined future,” he said in a Red Hat press release.

#5572. EXCLUSIVE: Kirk Cousins Cuts $240K From Georgia Mansion’s Asking Price as He Returns to the Minnesota Vikings

NFL quarterback Kirk Cousins has found his way back to the Minnesota Vikings following the Las Vegas Raiders trade—and he's eager to offload his Georgia home as he prepares to make the move.

The trade moved Cousins, 38, his wife, Julie Hampton, and their two kids back to the Land of 10,000 Lakes and allowed the Raiders to acquire Fernando Mendoza as their starting quarterback.

Following the news, Cousins posted, "Thank you Raiders Nation! Go get em @fernandomendoza."

Cousins spent six seasons with the Minnesota Vikings before being traded to the Atlanta Falcons in 2024. While there, he picked up a sprawling $3 million Georgia mansion.

The move to Georgia was an emotional one for the Cousins' family, especially for the athlete's wife, who posted a heartfelt goodbye to Minnesota.

"We came to Minnesota 6 years ago when Cooper was just 6 month old and Turner came shortly after!! Time flies when you’re having fun! I just want to say thank you to everyone who helped us build our life in Minnesota over the past 6 years. We have the most beautiful memories we will cherish forever!" she penned alongside a slew of images of the family.

Then, in April 2026, Cousins was traded to the Las Vegas Raiders. Two days before the news was announced, the NFL pro put his Atlanta property on the market for $2.99 million.

Then, in September, Cousins lowered that asking price to $2.75 million. Now, although the family is looking forward to returning to Minnesota, it appears they are still grappling with a real estate headache in the form of their Georgia home.

The sprawling abode, which was built in 2004, underwent a dramatic overhaul in 2024, likely in anticipation of Cousins and his family moving in. The listing described it as offering "timeless architecture enhanced with sophisticated, modern finishes throughout."

It is located in a gated community known as The River Club, where many Falcons players choose to live because of its impressive communal amenities, top-of-the-line security, and, of course, its enormous mansions.

Cousins' dwelling spans more than 10,000 square feet on a 0.9-acre lot and features six bedrooms and 6.5 bathrooms, providing more than enough room for the quarterback and his family.

Inside, the home features a very traditional aesthetic, starting with an elegant entryway that leads to a soaring double-height great room, complete with a large stone fireplace and patio doors that open to the backyard.

The ground floor is filled with open entertaining spaces, including a formal dining room and a huge "designer kitchen" with a large island and a separate breakfast nook.

Adding a cozy touch to the kitchen is another of the home's three fireplaces, which—according to the listing photos—has been used as a sweet relaxation spot by Cousins and his family, with large armchairs currently flanking the stone addition.

A pantry provides an incredible amount of storage, complemented by the kitchen's many built-ins and cupboards.

The third fireplace in the home is located in the stunning wood-paneled office, which overlooks the backyard and features beautiful built-in shelves, as well as a stately mantelpiece.

All six of the bedrooms in the home boast their own en suite bathrooms. However, the primary suite also features an enormous seating area with bay windows that overlook the surrounding landscape.

A finished basement provides an ideal spot for a game room, media center, or gym, while also housing another bedroom, bathroom, and a small office space.

The newly renovated screened-in deck at the back of the property can be used year-round as a dining or relaxation spot, the listing notes. An outdoor fireplace also adds another cozy spot for guests to gather.

#5571. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5570. Jester Lands in Court: Florida Woman Accused of Stealing Properties With Forged Deeds

A Florida woman has been accused of perpetrating a brazen deed fraud scam and illicitly transferred ownership of three properties in a scheme to fund her lavish lifestyle.

Melissa Jester, 41, of Bunnell, FL, is facing criminal charges after authorities say she forged a property owner's signature on deeds, transferred the land to a company she controlled, and pocketed the proceeds from one of the sales. She was arrested Nov. 6.

The victim, who owned three vacant lots in Florida for nearly two decades, recently discovered that the properties were transferred out of her name without her knowledge—and that one had been sold for nearly $30,000, according to the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office.

The victim contacted the authorities on Aug. 27 and said she had never authorized the sale or transfer of the properties. The three lots are located in the coastal city of Palm Coast, about 30 miles north of Daytona Beach.

An investigation was launched, and detectives uncovered what they described as a paper trail of forged documents, suspicious financial transactions, and a property sale that ultimately helped lead them to Jester.

Detectives traced a trail of forged documents and fraudulent financial transactions to Jester.

According to investigators, paperwork transferring ownership of all three lots to Florida Ohana Homes LLC, a company owned by Jester, was mailed to the Flagler County Clerk of Courts on June 29, 2026.

The paperwork appeared to have the property owner's signature on it. It was forged, investigators say.

Jester took further steps to hide her involvement by purchasing a money order on June 18 to pay the filing fees for the property under a different name, according to the affidavit.

The money order was purchased at the Amscot location on Palm Coast Parkway. The transaction did not require identification.

But the alleged scheme did not end there.

According to the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office, Jester, acting as managing member of Florida Ohana Homes LLC, then sold one of the stolen lots for $29,970 to an unsuspecting buyer on Sept. 10.

Surveillance video from the UPS Store on Belle Terre Parkway showed Jester signing the warranty deed and having it notarized. The money was transferred to the Bank of America account for Florida Ohana Homes LLC.

Authorities also allege that Jester transferred $8,000 from the business account into her personal account at VyStar Credit Union, where the money was spent on hotel stays and purchases throughout Flagler County.

By following the financial transactions, detectives were able to trace the money and recover a substantial portion of the proceeds from the alleged illicit sale.

More than $14,000 was seized from the company's Bank of America account and another $6,000 from Jester's personal credit union account. A total of $20,000 was recovered.

On Nov. 6, deputies located Jester driving in Bunnell, FL, and arrested her on charges of grand theft and obtaining property valued between $20,000 and $50,000 by swindle.

She is being held at the Sheriff Perry Hall Inmate Detention Facility on a $45,000 bond.

Flagler County Sheriff Rick Staly said the case stood out because, unlike many property fraud schemes involving suspects operating from distant locations, the alleged perpetrator lived nearby and conducted the transaction in person.

“Most of the deed fraud we see is run by scammers hiding in another state or another country. This one lived in Bunnell and signed the closing papers in front of a security camera in Palm Coast,” Sheriff Staly said. “Our detectives followed the trail of forgeries and money and recovered most of it for the victim.”

#5567. Andersen Partnership Helps Build Accessible Homes for Wounded Veterans

Since 2018, Andersen has worked with Jared Allen's Homes for Wounded Warriors, a nonprofit organization that builds injury-specific, accessible mortgage-free accessible homes for veterans who sustained severe injuries during their military service.

Since 2018, Andersen has partnered with Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors to help provide accessible, mortgage-free homes designed around the individual needs of severely injured military veterans.

Through the partnership, Andersen has donated windows and doors to 12 veteran families and home projects across the country. The manufacturer also supports the nonprofit through financial contributions and company matches of employee donations.

Most recently, Andersen contributed to a custom home for Marine Lance Corporal Josh Wege in Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin. Josh Wege, who sustained life-changing injuries while serving in Afghanistan, received the keys to the mortgage-free home alongside his family.

The residence was designed around Wege’s accessibility and mobility requirements, with the broader goal of providing greater independence, comfort, and quality of life.

“Building a home that meets the needs of a critically wounded veteran and their family takes a team of people who believe in our mission,” says Jared Allen, founder of Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors since 2009. “Andersen is an important part of that team, and we’re grateful for their support and commitment to the veterans we serve.”

Jared Allen, a Pro Football Hall of Famer and former Minnesota Vikings defensive end, added that the partnership helps create homes “where veterans can live more independently, and families can make memories together for years to come.”

For Andersen, the partnership also provides an opportunity to apply product selection and design considerations to the specific mobility needs of each homeowner. Depending on the project, those considerations can include wider openings, low- or zero-threshold transitions, accessible hardware placement, and patio door configurations intended to make movement easier between indoor and outdoor spaces.

Charlie Jackson, an account sales manager at Andersen, has helped project teams identify window and door solutions based on individual veterans’ accessibility requirements.

“My father was a World War II Marine, so supporting veterans has always been personally meaningful to me,” Jackson shares. “These projects bring Andersen’s work into focus because you can see how thoughtful product choices and accessible design come together to make everyday life easier for a veteran and their family.”

“As a 10-year Andersen employee, I’m proud to contribute my experience to help identify the products and solutions that best support each homeowner’s accessibility, comfort, and long-term needs,” he adds.

The homes are completed through collaboration among Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors, manufacturers such as Andersen, local businesses, tradespeople, and other supporters.

#5566. Agents may soon be the main workload, and most of the time they’re doing nothing

As AI agents take on more enterprise work, agent sandboxing has become a basic requirement rather than an afterthought. Every agent that writes code, runs tools or drives a browser needs hard walls around it. Those walls also can’t come at the cost of runaway compute bills.

Google LLC’s answer is Agent Substrate, an open-source project built on Kubernetes that the company donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation alongside its gVisor sandbox. Customers have raised the same problem for the past 18 months: They need to run agentic workloads securely and efficiently on the infrastructure they already have, according to Brandon Royal (pictured, left), product manager, AI agents and infrastructure, at Google Cloud.

“Any agent needs to be fully isolated,” Royal said. “Whether it’s accessing tools or using a computer or a browser, there needs to be some level of isolation, period, full stop.”

Royal and Benjamin Elder (right), staff software engineer at Google, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how agent sandboxing is central to Google’s open-source Agent Substrate. (* Disclosure below.)

Agent Substrate starts with hardened sandbox runtimes densely packed on Kubernetes clusters. All traffic passes through a layer that applies policy and understands identity, so an agent can reach nothing it hasn’t been explicitly granted, Elder explained. The project also keeps secrets out of the agent’s hands by injecting credentials on the wire.

“Don’t expose credentials to the sandbox,” Elder said. “Don’t let the agent touch the credentials. Instead, when it requests to do something, you can make a decision about outside the sandbox.”

Security is only half the equation. Agents in a swarm spend much of their time blocked, waiting on a large language model call or on a human to follow up. Agent Substrate snapshots those idle agents out of memory and CPU, stores them offline and restores them when they’re needed, freeing resources across the cluster, according to Elder.

“Should you be holding compute while you’re getting coffee? Because you might come back in five minutes. You might come back in five hours or five days,” Royal said. “We don’t know.”

Google is already building on the project. Gemini Managed Agents now runs on Agent Substrate and gets the same density, efficiency and security guarantees, Royal noted. Google Cloud also recently introduced Agent Compute Engine to host AI agents.

“Agents are going to become the predominant workload in the future,” Royal said. “Maybe it’s six months, maybe it’s 12 months, but we see this as a really big area of growth.”

#5565. Invitation Homes Invests in HBI Training for Veterans

The Home Builders Institute (HBI) and Invitation Homes have launched a partnership aimed at helping transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families build careers in construction, property maintenance, and the skilled trades.

The partnership will expand Invitation Homes’ existing Invitation to SkillUp initiative through an investment in HBI’s Military Services program, which provides hands-on, instructor-led skilled trades training, industry-recognized certifications, and job placement assistance.

Through the partnership, HBI and Invitation Homes will connect HBI-trained veterans, military spouses, and family members with career opportunities in the build-to-rent and single-family rental sectors. The organizations also plan to expand recruitment at HBI Military Services locations, including Fort Stewart, Georgia, and Jacksonville, Florida.

Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group will participate in mentorship and career guidance efforts.

“Veterans and their families have dedicated themselves to serving our country, and we are proud to support them as they transition into rewarding civilian careers,” Invitation Homes president and CEO Dallas Tanner says. “Through our Invitation to SkillUp initiative, we are investing in talented individuals whose dedication and service strengthen our communities, while helping create meaningful opportunities in the skilled trades.”

HBI has spent a decade training, certifying, and placing transitioning service members, veterans, and their families in skilled trades careers. According to HBI president and CEO Ed Brady, nearly 90% of graduates from the organization’s military program find jobs, earning an average of more than three times the federal minimum wage.

“We know this model works, and with this important investment from Invitation Homes, we can help more veterans enter the skilled trades every year because the people who served this country deserve a career as strong as their service,” Brady said.

Invitation to SkillUp is Invitation Homes’ national skilled trades development initiative, which works with trade schools and organizations to expand trades education and increase awareness of career opportunities.

Invitation Homes joins other companies supporting HBI’s military programs. The Home Depot Foundation and DEWALT were early supporters, while Google recently provided a $1 million contribution to the effort.

The partnership comes as the housing industry continues to look for ways to strengthen its skilled labor pipeline. For transitioning service members and military families, the effort offers a pathway from military service into construction and housing careers while providing the industry with another source of trained workers.

#5564. Lennar, Operation Finally Home Surprise Two Military Families With New Homes

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier with their families.

Two military veterans and their families received life-changing news ahead of Veterans Day when Lennar and Operation Finally Home surprised them with the gift of new homes.

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier were surprised with the announcement during the inaugural Operation Finally Home Golf Classic reception in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 9.

Neither family knew about the plans beforehand and attended the event as guests of Operation Finally Home.

The announcement followed a live performance by country music artist and Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan. Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath and Lennar San Antonio division president Brian Barron then revealed that each family would receive a new Lennar home.

The partnership builds on Operation Finally Home’s mission of providing mortgage-free homes and home modifications to wounded, ill, and injured veterans, first responders, and their families.

Gallmeier served in the Marine Corps from 2005 to 2015 after being motivated to enlist by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. During his service, he deployed twice to Iraq in support of combat operations and later deployed to Okinawa, Japan, as part of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit.

Gallmeier sustained a traumatic brain injury following a grenade blast during combat operations in Iraq. He also developed post-traumatic stress disorder and continues to manage PTSD, amongst other conditions, according to Operation Finally Home.

Following his military career, Gallmeier earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in divinity from Biola University and became a pastor. He currently lives in California with Tatiana Zaragoza and their three children, Alyssa, Caspian, and Everett.

A formal groundbreaking for the family’s new Lennar home is scheduled for Nov. 10 in the Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas.

Taylor enlisted in the U.S. Army in August 2004 shortly after graduating from high school in Washington state. He served as an infantryman and filled roles including Squad Automatic Weapon gunner, driver, and team leader.

From June 2006 to September 2007, Taylor deployed to Baghdad in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom. His unit lost 21 soldiers during the deployment.

After completing his military service in December 2007, Taylor continued serving his community as a firefighter and emergency medical technician.

A serious back injury in January 2024, combined with the lasting physical and emotional effects of his military service, ultimately forced Taylor to medically retire from firefighting in March 2025.

Following the injury, Taylor and his wife, Aylynn, and their four children faced financial uncertainty and eventually sold their home and moved in with relatives. The family’s new Lennar home will provide a fresh start. A groundbreaking for the Taylor residence is slated in December.

#5562. Attached Housing Stands Out in Baltimore’s Housing Market

Annualized new-home sales declined 5.2% in September to 2,613 units. Attached housing accounted for 1,951 sales versus 662 detached sales during the period. However, the Baltimore market is sending mixed signals as 2026 winds down. By comparison, the market’s average new-home sales rate of 2.4 homes per project matched Maryland and remained above the national rate of 2.0.

That aforementioned product split is one of Baltimore’s defining characteristics. Annualized attached sales fell just 0.9% year over year compared with a 16% decline for detached homes as of September data. The strongest sales activity also sits toward the more attainable end of the new home market, with attached homes priced from $350,000 to $450,000 experiencing the most closing activity over the past year.

Related, affordability remains a constraint. As of July, the median new-home closing price stood at $555,337, down 2.9% year over year, compared with $420,000 for existing homes.

The economic backdrop adds another layer. Total nonfarm employment in the Baltimore metro declined 0.6% year over year in August, while the unemployment rate was 4.1%. Households are estimated to decline 0.1% in 2026 and post flat annual growth through 2028.

One potential longer-term catalyst comes from defense manufacturing. Anduril Industries announced a $3.7 billion investment in a high-tech shipyard at Baltimore County’s Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center. The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs, while generating more than $2 billion in annual economic output.

Baltimore’s opportunity is therefore less about broad based growth and more about positioning. Ideal locations, attainable price points, and disciplined starts stand out in a market where buyers are still active but increasingly selective.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.

#5561. Kim Kardashian’s Former Beverly Hills Tuscan Villa From Early Seasons of ‘Keeping Up With the Kardashians’ Hits the Market for $8.5 Million

Kim Kardashian’s former Beverly Hills home has hit the market, with an asking price of $8.495 million for a piece of reality television history.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom home was featured heavily in the earliest seasons of “Keeping Up With the Kardashians.” Remember when Kris Jenner and Khloé Kardashian went out on the town, and after a few too many margaritas, decided to toilet-paper the Tuscan-style villa?

Fortunately, the defaced rose bushes have been cleaned up since that 2013 episode.

Kim purchased the 4,027-square-foot home for $3.4 million in 2010. Three years later, she sold it fully-furnished, and it went for $5.12 million after a bidding war, according to Robb Report.

Later, in 2024, Kim visited the property with Khloé and celebrity broker Josh Altman, to find that it was still nearly exactly as she’d left it. Recognizable details such as a “KK” logo on the wall of her iconic glam room and her custom bedding were still there, prompting the star to share a tour of the time capsule on her Snapchat profile.

Today, the famous family’s connection to the estate is more of an “if you know, you know” situation. It’s undergone a complete transformation by AD100 designer Sebastian Zuchowicki, and now boasts a more sleek, contemporary look.

With that said, many of the structural features that made the home a gem in the first place are still present.

The gourmet kitchen has been redone in a European country style, with custom cabinetry and a spacious center island. Charming windows line one wall, while a double-sided fireplace connects the breakfast room and lounge. New, top-of-the-line appliances have also been added.

The primary suite is certainly luxurious, with a fireside seating area, two fabulous and generously-sized walk-in closets, and a spa-inspired Italian-tiled bathroom that features double vanities, a soothing shower, and a unique soaking tub.

Additionally, the second floor also includes three more en suite bedrooms, which each have a distinct personality. From floral wallpaper to chic striped walls, these rooms manage to be neutral and statement-making at the same time.

The home is perfectly primed for entertaining, especially considering the private theater.

Indoor-outdoor living is encouraged, with a covered fireplace lounge and a fully equipped outdoor kitchen.

The resort-style pool and spa makes the backyard feel like a true getaway. There’s also a tranquil fountain, a hillside sun terrace, a dedicated bathroom, and a fire pit. A gazebo and cabana serves as a spot to watch television without being cooped up inside.

The gourmet kitchen is appointed with custom cabinetry, premium appliances, a spacious center island, and a double-sided fireplace connecting the breakfast room and lounge. A private theater provides an additional space for entertainment.

Today, Kim holds an impressive collection of properties in California and Idaho. Most notably, she’s spent years renovating her $60 million Hidden Hills home. The home has been undergoing major construction since 2024, and during a recent episode of “The Kardashians,” it was revealed that the Skims founder is creating an 8,000-square-foot closet.

Kim continues to share her real estate updates with viewers, and during the Nov. 5 episode of the family’s Hulu show, she purchased a new Palm Springs, CA, estate on what appeared to be a whim.

The Kardashian-Jenners have a series of homes in La Quinta, with hidden pathways connecting the properties. When Kim realized the house located next door to Kylie Jenner’s abode was up for grabs, she sneaked onto the property to see if she liked it better than her existing home.

Later in the episode, Khloé confirmed that her older sister had, in fact, made the purchase.

#5560. Spec Versus Built-to-Order: Builders Navigate a Changing Market

For builders, the push and pull between speculative homes and built-to-order (BTO) homes is a classic struggle, reflecting the desire to balance operational efficiency against market demand. A favorable mix directly dictates a company’s profit margins, inventory risk, and customer satisfaction.

Spec homes allow builders to more directly compete with resale inventory, offering faster move-ins that can capture demand from buyers looking to move quickly. In strong markets, heavier spec exposure can increase sales velocity. In slower markets, builders with large levels of spec inventory are exposed to carrying costs and pricing risk.

A built-to-order approach reduces that inventory risk and offers buyers greater personalization in their final purchase. Built-to-order homes typically carry higher sales prices and translate into healthier margins while requiring buyers to wait longer to move in.

While several companies are steadfast in their approaches, such as the 100% spec commitments of Meritage Homes and CBH Homes and the 70% BTO target set by KB Home, the spec-BTO balance often shifts over time.

In the immediate post-pandemic period, many builders leaned more heavily into spec production. Unprecedented levels of demand and rapidly rising home prices set a backdrop for many large builders to offer more spec and quick move-in (QMI) homes because homes were absorbed at record levels. Similarly, the standardized production and simplified SKU packages helped builders guard against pandemic-related supply chain disruptions and labor shortages.

When mortgage rates began to spike in late 2023, a go-to-market approach with spec production remained prevalent to help buyers with certainty of price and move-in timing. Public builders at the time noted buyers were less willing to commit many months ahead given rate uncertainty and favored move-in ready homes. Builders favoring a heavier spec production mix were able to lean into financing incentives in the form of price cuts and rate buydowns to capture demand as economic uncertainty began to mount.

At the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026, one of the more notable themes to emerge is a more concentrated shift toward a higher built-to-order mix. KB Home began sharing its goal of a 70% BTO mix in the second quarter of 2025, noting the approach is customer-centric and that a design-forward, personalized approach is a differentiator in a market where incentives were prevalent.

“Our buyers choose their lot, floor plan, and personalized finishes. The result is a home that has a real specific value to the people who will live in it,” president and CEO Rob McGibney said during an earnings call with investors. “Homes built to customer specifications do not require heavy incentives to sell.”

Similarly, in the past couple quarters PulteGroup has highlighted its efforts to skew production more toward BTO homes, targeting a 60-40 mix.

“Our decision to build more spec homes once supply chains collapsed and build cycles effectively doubled was the right one at the time, but we much prefer having a growing backlog of sold homes,” PulteGroup president CEO Ryan Marshall shared during a recent earnings call.

The shift is not just occurring among large public builders, with Texas-based Stylecraft Builders reporting a shift toward the BTO model. After carrying essentially no to-be-built volume as recently as 12 to 18 months ago, the company is targeting a goal of 20% to 25% of sales from BTO orders.

Spec-heavy, BTO-heavy, and hybrid operators are all succeeding in the current challenging market. Rather than converging toward a single model, many builders increasingly view spec and BTO homes as complementary tools that can be adjusted based on market conditions, buyer behavior, and community characteristics.

For many builders, spec homes and BTO homes are not an either-or strategy, and a flexible approach that puts buyers front of mind yields the most successful results.

“They serve different customer needs and we want to execute both approaches well,” David Weekley Homes chief operating officer Ladd Fargo tells BUILDER. “The approximate mix depends on the market, buyer behavior, product type, and price point.”

The by-market approach is one that resonates strongly with Trumark Homes. As a private builder that serves as the western hub for Daiwa House, Trumark Homes leans into the local expertise of its division operators to meet the market with the best approach across its operating platforms in California, Colorado, and Washington.

“We know that we have strong operators in all our markets, and we trust our division teams to understand their buyer profiles, have a pulse on the competition, and utilize the data and tools available to plan accordingly,” Trumark Homes chief operating officer Steve Kalmbach says. “We will continue to be nimble and make the best strategic decisions for each community along the way.”

Fred McConnell, vice president of brand and performance marketing at Risewell Homes, tells BUILDER the company has become more intentional about creating built-to-order opportunities while maintaining a strong offering of quick move-in, spec homes. The mixed approach allows Risewell to be both consumer-led and market-responsive while aligning the company’s core brand platform, Built Well to Live Well.

“Our goal is to maintain the flexibility to respond to both the consumer and the dynamics of each individual market and community,” McConnell says.

Huntsville, Alabama-based Davidson Homes has seen a shift toward more BTO homes, but the company’s core strategy has not changed. CEO Brandon Jones says the company continues to meet buyers where they are, offering a solution for those who need to move in 45 days or those who want to choose every detail from homesite to interior finishes. He says the market has not picked a winner between spec or BTO and has instead rewarded builders who are disciplined about using both approaches.

“We start with the buyer, not the model. A lot of our industry has moved to one way of building,” Jones continues. “We’ve kept real personalization on the menu because buyers still want it, and we keep inventory on the ground because some buyers can’t wait. If we get the buyer right, the mix takes care of itself.”

CBH Homes has been a 100% spec builder since 2019, placing high value on the efficiencies gained in the building process and the simplification it provides to the buyer experience. The efficiencies gained early, from purchasing to scheduling trade partners, provide consistency and synergy that allows real value to be passed on to the buyers.

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable,” CBH Homes president and owner Corey Barton explains. “Our buyers can walk through a home, see the finishes, know the price, and know when they can move in. There are fewer unknowns.”

In the current market, where some builders are shifting approaches back toward a heavier BTO mix, Barton says CBH Homes still sees value in its 100% spec approach.

“When rates move or the right opportunity presents itself, our buyers don’t have to wait months for their home to be built,” Barton says. “On top of that, we know if a buyer has the option, they will want to make changes. Not allowing change orders allows us to keep costs down and construction efficiency high. Our goal isn’t to give the buyer a thousand decisions to make. It’s to do the work up front and create a beautiful, professionally designed home they can walk into and say, ‘This is it.’”

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable.”

Meritage Homes made a similar transition to an all-spec approach in 2016, focusing on the entry-level segment and leaning into competition with resale inventory. The builder’s shorter cycle times allow it to start homes later while also maintaining its 60-day closing guarantee. CEO Phillippe Lord says that its trade relationships and limited SKU counts set it apart from other builders and provide greater certainty to its vendor partners. While the builder has been market responsive and has increased its portfolio of move-up product given market conditions, Meritage Homes remains committed to its 100% spec approach.

Houston-based David Weekley Homes has leaned more heavily into move-in-ready spec homes to respond to a buyer that is placing more value on speed and certainty. Fargo says the shift has been driven by changes in buyer preferences rather than operational considerations.

“In a more uncertain market, many buyers are less willing to commit far in advance. They want to know what they’re buying, what it will cost, and when they can move in,” Fargo explains. “With quick move-in homes, the goal is not simply to build more inventory. It’s to be thoughtful about which homes we start, where we build them, the price points we target, and when the homes will be available.”

Similarly, Kalmbach notes Trumark Homes is seeing more contingent buyers in the current market. For these buyers, knowing what homes are available within a given time frame can be an important factor when they are looking to move but still must sell their previous home. Spec homes represent a solution for this buyer.

For builders that have leaned more heavily into a BTO approach, most cite personalization, design, and customer centricity as core factors. By allowing buyers to choose lots, floor plans, and personalized finishes, says KB Home’s McGibney, the company is best able to serve its customers.

“Buyers are already invested in and feel a connection to the homes they created,” McGibney said. “This is in contrast to a speculative business model where incentives are used to create value. In that model, the builder increases the incentives to the point at which the buyers believe they have been adequately compensated for features and finishes they did not choose.”

Erlanger, Kentucky-based Fischer Homes has seen an increase in interest in BTO homes in 2026, with the builder noting many buyers are placing an emphasis on personalization. BTO homes utilize Fischer Homes’ Design Studio, giving buyers the opportunity to select finishes and details that bring a unique vision to life and allowing the builder to deliver a home that reflects the specific needs and preferences of a particular buyer.

“The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

Beyond design, KB Home’s McGibney said a BTO-forward approach provides visibility, predictability, and limits risk. When a buyer commits and the company locks in a price, the direct costs can be established before a shovel hits the ground and KB Home knows the margin it will achieve at delivery before a home is started.

“We view this as a fundamentally lower risk profile than a speculative model, where a builder starts a home with an assumption for the future sales price and then finds later, at the time of sale, that market conditions may require price reductions or heavy incentives,” McGibney said. “The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

PulteGroup’s shift toward increasing built-to-order homes reflects the preferences of move-up and active-adult buyers. The builder’s lower cycle time allows it to selectively use rate buydowns to facilitate BTO sales while still achieving higher margins than on spec sales.

“[Move-up and active-adult buyers] are individuals who expect choice, and our operating model allows them to choose their preferred lot and select the options and upgrades they desire,” Marshall said.

For luxury builder Toll Brothers, the company can provide a design-forward experience even to spec buyers given its timing and approach to sales. The builder is focused on selling specs as early as possible in the construction cycle to allow personalization through its design studios, providing an experience that is like the BTO experience in all but name.

Several builders say the spec-versus-BTO decision is often less about philosophy and more about the product being sold and the customer buying it.

Decisions are closely tied to what different buyer segments prioritize in the purchase process. For entry-level buyers, value is often concentrated in price, payment certainty, and speed, characteristics that favor a spec approach. Move-up buyers, by contrast, are often purchasing for the home itself and have greater flexibility to prioritize personalization and design choices over speed.

“A first-time buyer is usually solving for payment and timing. A move-up buyer is solving for the home itself,” Jones of Davidson Homes explains. “Spec answers the first. Built-to-order answers the second.”

Kalmbach of Trumark Homes adds that buyers who are seeking customization in the home buying process are more likely to have the resources and time to engage earlier in the purchasing process, beginning with lot selection and continuing through the full design process. Fargo of David Weekley Homes echoes this distinction: standardized, higher-density, and entry-level products generally lend themselves more naturally to move-in-ready construction while higher-priced, customizable homes are better positioned for BTO.

“In general, building from the ground up allows customers the opportunity to personalize their home and participate more fully in the home building process,” says Fargo. “The longer timeline also gives our team members more time to understand the customer, build a relationship with them, and help create a home that is right for them. That relationship and the experience we provide the home building process are things we value.”

Vincent Salandro is an editor for Builder. He earned a B.A. in journalism and a B.S. in economics from American University.

#5558. Christmas Lights Are Squeezing Homeowner Budgets More Than Ever, but There’s a Way To Pay Less and Still Be Festive

Christmas lights can bring holiday cheer to your home and neighborhood, but they don’t come cheap.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects the national average residential electricity price at about 18 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2026—roughly 37% higher than in 2020. This translates to the highest utility bills some homeowners have ever seen, made worse during times of the year when more electricity is needed.

According to a recent study by Payless Power, running a full display throughout December costs $15.36 with LED lights and $92.03 with incandescent lights at the typical electricity rate. That’s a $76.67 difference.

Where you live can affect your electric bill, too.

Hawaii is the most expensive state for holiday lighting, at $42.53 for a full LED display and $254.84 for the incandescent version. Rhode Island ($31.85), Massachusetts ($31.47), Maine ($30.98), and New Hampshire ($26.81) also make the list of the five most expensive states for a full LED display.

Meanwhile, homeowners in North Dakota ($11.25), Nebraska ($11.49), and Missouri ($12.02) pay the least.

The good news is there are ways to lower your electric bill without sacrificing curb appeal or holiday spirit, regardless of where you live. All it takes is a bit of planning and creativity.

A variety of factors are contributing to high electric bills these days.

“The grid is outdated. Infrastructure is old, and utility companies need to replace and upgrade equipment,” says Brandon Young, CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX.

Extreme weather plays a huge role as well, as the lines and equipment can’t always handle conditions like freezing temperatures and high winds.

Increased electricity demand adds to the problem.

“Demand is growing, and the grid can’t always keep up. Data centers and industrial use are large consumers of energy, and it takes a lot to power those facilities,” Young explains.

Fuel costs also fluctuate and affect how much it costs to generate electricity.

“Prices for residential customers in 2025 went up more than twice the rate of inflation,” says Young.

These high costs are particularly noticeable during the holiday season. Young points out that many homeowners often forget that a higher utility rate doesn’t take December off.

“The higher rate is there all year, and every kilowatt-hour is more costly. The oven and lights for holiday gatherings all cost more to use,” Young adds.

Fortunately, you don’t have to forgo Christmas lights altogether.

These tips can help you enjoy them while keeping your electricity costs in check.

While you don’t get to choose your utility rates, you do get to choose your light bulbs. And LEDs are much cheaper than incandescent bulbs.

“One hundred bulb C9s cost about $19.57 in December to run, and if they're swapped with LEDs, you’ll pay $2.80,” says Young.

LED lights aren’t hard to find either. You'll notice a variety of options at just about any home improvement store.

You don’t have to keep your lights on all day, every day.

Consider displaying them only from 5 to 10 p.m., for example. You could use a timer or smart plug that allows you to turn them on or off manually when you want to.

Also, if you plan to leave town, keep them off until you return.

Lighting every bush in your yard will cost you. Instead, be selective about where you hang lights.

Highlighting your front door, roof line, and a tree in your yard can make just as big of an impact.

If you have inflatables, there’s no reason to keep them on 24/7.

“Unplugging inflatables when you go to bed saves a few dollars. The cost to leave one up for the month is about $1.68, which is a lot to pay [compared with] a 100-bulb LED light strand at 14 cents,” says Young.

In addition, you don’t have to use inflatables for your home to stand out. A light projector can do the trick at a fraction of the cost.

The study says that a projector costs only 17 cents per month to run, compared to $1.68 for an inflatable.

#5557. NAR Board Approves 2027 Budget, Installs New Leadership

At its Nov. 9 meeting during NAR NXT in New Orleans, the National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) board of directors approved a 2027 budget and installed new leadership.

The board approved an operating budget projecting approximately $280 million in revenue and $247 million in expenses. Under the new approach, NAR departments were required to evaluate expenditures from the ground up rather than simply carry forward previous spending levels, prioritizing initiatives and identifying measures of success.

NAR Treasurer Craig Sanford described the approach as a significant step in the association’s financial modernization efforts. The board approved the budget by an overwhelming majority.

Directors also approved the following financial recommendations:

In his final board of directors meeting as NAR president, Kevin Brown highlighted progress on initiatives aimed at protecting members’ business interests, expanding housing opportunities and helping members adapt to a changing industry.

He also highlighted progress on MLS collaboration, including outreach to nearly 500 MLS executives and the formation of a work group to address emerging challenges and modernize policies. That work helped inform four policy recommendations approved by NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee during NAR NXT, aimed at strengthening copyright protections for listing content, giving MLSs greater flexibility in setting local data feed requirements and clarifying permitted uses of MLS data.

For Realtor® members, the changes address business concerns, including protecting the time and money invested in marketing properties, preserving access to their own listing information and establishing clearer rules for how listing data can be used and shared.

Brown also pointed to NAR’s advocacy surrounding the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a housing package aimed at increasing supply, improving affordability and expanding homeownership opportunities. NAR’s attention is now turning toward implementation, including working with federal agencies and supporting state and local associations.

Other initiatives highlighted during the meeting included six “modernized” Center for REALTOR® Development courses scheduled to launch Dec. 1, more broker summits (on track for 85-plus by the end of the year) and continued advocacy, including for the bipartisan More Homes on the Market Act, which would increase the capital gains tax exclusion for homeowners selling their primary residences (something the Trump administration previously floated as well).

New NAR President Christine E. Hansen’s priorities include advancing NAR’s three-year strategic plan, improving awareness of member tools and resources, and restoring pride in the Realtor® brand.

The association’s 13 regional vice presidents were also installed.
