#5556. AI agents carry memory and storage like people, so their data needs guarding while in use

As AI agents move into production on Kubernetes, cloud engineering teams at financial companies face a security problem that encryption alone can’t solve. Container orchestration has become the default foundation for AI workloads, and the data those agents use is now the main target.

Payment networks feel that pressure more than most because every transaction carries customer data and regulatory exposure. Protecting data while it is being processed, and not just while it is stored or moving, has become central to running agents at scale, according to Krishna Mayuram (pictured), senior principal engineer and vice president of cloud engineering at Mastercard Inc.

“What we call confidential computing is when you are launching these applications in a highly secure, virtualized secure environments or confidential environments or confidential containers, you are able to protect the data in use,” Mayuram said. “We have protected data at rest, data in motion. Now, what is happening to the data in use?”

Mayuram spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed cloud engineering, security problems and the challenges of protecting data in use. (* Disclosure below.)

Mastercard runs its platforms on Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift, a Kubernetes platform that Red Hat is extending to support AI agents. Red Hat has also brought confidential containers to OpenShift on bare metal. Agents act much like microservices and need the same elastic infrastructure, Mayuram explained.

“We need to scale the platform, that’s Kubernetes which gives horizontal scaling, vertical scaling, if you will, and also the agents, just like applications, require all the elastic capabilities of Kubernetes,” Mayuram said.

Scale increases the risk, especially for a company that operates under many countries’ laws. Mastercard recently added trust services for agentic commerce. Internally, the same idea applies, with guardrails at every step from development to deployment, according to Mayuram.

“The business is distributed, the industry is very distributed, and we have different laws of the land. So all these things need to be encompassed with guardrails,” Mayuram said. “Whether agents or regular, the guardrails remain the same. The enterprise security remains same.”

#5555. For Every Condo Buyer in the U.S., There Are More Than Two Sellers. That Gives Condo Buyers Strong Negotiating Power.

Condo buyers today have more negotiating power than they’ve had in at least 13 years. There were an estimated 123% more condo sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the largest gap in records dating back to 2013. The gap widened from 95.5% a year earlier.

Redfin estimates the number of buyers using proprietary data on the typical time between a buyer’s first home tour and the closing of a purchase, along with MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers is based on active listings in the MLS. The figures in this report are national estimates. See the full methodology and explore the interactive dashboard.

Redfin defines a buyer’s market as one with more than 10% more sellers than buyers, and a seller’s market as one with more than 10% more buyers than sellers. A market is considered balanced when the difference between sellers and buyers is within 10%. Other housing-market statistics, including median sale price, are based on Redfin’s analysis of MLS data.

A buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily mean condos are affordable for buyers.

The condo market has undergone a dramatic reversal since the pandemic-era homebuying boom. In September 2021, there were 25.1% fewer sellers than buyers.

Five years later, the number of buyers fell 54%, while the number of sellers rose 36%. The shift has left sellers competing for a much smaller pool of potential buyers.

The number of condo buyers fell to an estimated 88,460 in September, down 2.5 % from August and the lowest level in at least 13 years. Meanwhile, condo sellers totaled 197,248, up 0.9 % from the prior month.

Several factors are weighing more heavily on the condo market than on the single-family home market. Rising insurance premiums, HOA fees and special assessments are making condos increasingly expensive to own, particularly in Florida and Texas, where hurricane risks and other natural disasters have contributed to higher insurance costs. That’s a problem for first-time buyers, who often turn to condos as a more affordable entry point into the housing market but lack equity from a previous home sale.

While the condo market is challenging for buyers, those who can afford housing costs will have more power in negotiations.

“For renters who have saved for a down payment and are ready to build equity, these buyer-friendly conditions are an opportunity,” said Asad Khan, a senior economist at Redfin. “Buyers have more options and a better chance of finding a place they like. Although condo prices and HOA fees remain relatively high, buyers have more room to negotiate price cuts, and condos are still generally more affordable than single-family homes.”

The single-family market saw a similar trend in September, with the number of buyers dropping to a record low since 2013. Sellers outnumbered buyers by 53.7%–a wide gap, but less than half as wide as what we’re seeing in the condo market.

The huge surplus of condo sellers over buyers is contributing to the record-breaking buyer’s market in the overall housing market, which encompasses condos, townhouses and single-family homes

The national median condo sale price fell 0.8% to about $339,000 in September, the first year-over-year decline in five months.

House hunters should keep in mind that the costs of buying and owning a condo extend beyond its purchase price, and those ongoing expenses can put additional pressure on buyers’ budgets. Rising homeowners association (HOA) fees and insurance premiums can push up the total monthly cost of ownership. Buyers should also consider the possibility of special assessments to cover major repairs or improvements to a building’s common areas.

But for buyers who can afford the upfront costs of a condo and plan to stay put for several years, today’s buyer’s  market may offer an opportunity.

“Find a motivated seller and there are a lot of them,” said Cecilia Cordova, a Redfin Premier agent in Miami, who lives in a condominium herself. Researching the buildings you’d like to live in is the key to finding a financially healthy community and avoiding surprise assessment bills later, she said.

Condo buyers have more options than they did years ago. “We have enough inventory for the next three to four years,” said Cordova.

For prospective sellers? Cordova suggests considering renting their condo out for the time being. “If you really need to sell, the strategy is to list it lower than anybody else in the same building. It’s not time for you to try to experiment with a higher price,” she said.

Today’s home prices and mortgage rates have made it harder for first-time homebuyers to enter the market, reducing demand for condos, which have traditionally served as an entry point to homeownership. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.18% as of November 5, and home prices remain near historic highs.

Sellers are increasingly dropping their asking prices to attract buyers, Redfin data shows. About 37% of condos that sold in September had a price reduction, compared with 16% during the pandemic-era housing boom five years earlier.

The typical condo that sold in September spent 63 days on the market before going under contract, up from 35 days five years earlier.

Condo buyers in Texas had more negotiating powers than anywhere else in the country in September. San Antonio had the widest seller-buyer gap among the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas, with an estimated 459% more sellers than buyers. Houston followed with 322% more sellers than buyers, then came Austin, with 258% more.

Miami also had one of the nation’s widest gaps, with an estimated 274% more condo sellers than buyers in September, ranking third.

“San Antonio condos may have an attractive purchase price, but buyers are looking at the total monthly payment. Because we have so many affordable single-family homes available, many buyers choose a house when the payments are close,” said Derrell Skillman, a Redfin Premier agent in San Antonio, TX.

Skillman added San Antonio has a large military community, and its housing market tends to follow the military’s permanent change-of-station (PCS) season.

“We usually see more military-related activity during the spring and summer when families are transferring in and out of the area. Once that period slows down, the drop in demand can be more noticeable, especially in a smaller segment like condos,” he said. “HOA costs, financing restrictions, builder incentives, softer investor demand and the slowdown after the military PCS season are all contributing to the buyer’s market for condos,” said Skillman.

Meanwhile, new construction is adding to the softness in Sun Belt markets. The Sun Belt is home to nine of the 10 metros where condo sellers outnumber buyers most.

Nassau County, NY, was the only metro area among the 50 analyzed that was a seller’s market for condos in September. There were 32% fewer sellers than buyers, with an estimated 1,545 buyers compared with 1,052 sellers.

“Condo buyers are mostly people who want maintenance-free living,” said William Ortiz, a Redfin Premier agent in Long Island, NY. “They want to have an easier lifestyle as opposed to all the maintenance and upkeep that comes with a house. Common charges are expensive, but they’re willing to pay for that convenience.”

According to Sandra Glaser, a Redfin senior agent in Long Island, condo demand is coming from three main groups: first-time buyers priced out of single-family homes, particularly those moving from the city to the suburbs; downsizers seeking less upkeep; and investors looking for rental income from properties that require minimal maintenance.

Five other metros — Chicago, Milwaukee, New Brunswick, Newark and San Francisco — had balanced condo markets, where the difference between buyers and sellers was within 10%.

San Francisco’s condo market, for example, is heating up, with the median sale price jumping 20% year over year to nearly $1.2 million in September. Khan, the Redfin senior economist, ties the area’s renewed housing demand to the AI boom, which is attracting highly paid workers and fueling homebuying.

As a senior data reporter, Dian uses data and quantitative analysis to tell stories about economy and real estate. She also builds databases and creates statistical charts that visualize data trends. Previously, Dian spent seven years as a senior data reporter at USA TODAY.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5554. How Buyers Can Tell if a Home Price Cut Signals a True Deal

More than one in five U.S. home listings received a price cut in August, but a lower asking price does not necessarily mean the property has become a good deal. Price reductions are becoming harder for homebuyers to ignore. In August, 20.4% of U.S. listings had a price cut, matching the rate recorded a year earlier, according to the latest Realtor.com housing report.

The median asking price fell 1.3% year over year to $424,500, marking the tenth consecutive month of annual declines. Meanwhile, pending sales slipped 0.2%, ending an eight-month run of year-over-year growth.

For buyers, the growing number of reductions may look like an invitation to start bargain hunting. However, a crossed-out asking price provides little evidence of the property’s actual value.

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says Jeremy Olsher, a principal at Mizner Residential Group. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.”

Olsher recommends three checks before treating a reduced listing as a deal.

Compare the new price with completed sales. Buyers should begin with recently sold properties that are genuinely comparable in location, size, condition and features. Active listings reveal what other sellers hope to receive, while completed sales show what buyers have accepted.

A $40,000 reduction may look substantial, but it has limited meaning if the home remains $50,000 above comparable sales.

“The percentage reduction is the part buyers notice first because it is easy to understand,” Olsher says. “The more useful question is whether the new price makes sense beside the homes that have actually sold.”

Read the entire listing history. The number and timing of reductions can reveal how the seller is responding to the market. A single adjustment after several quiet weeks may indicate growing flexibility. Several small reductions can suggest the seller is chasing the market downward without fully accepting current buyer demand.

Buyers should also check whether the home was previously listed, withdrawn and returned with a new price or description. A fresh listing date does not always mean the property is new to the market.

“Days on the market need context,” Olsher says. “I want to know whether the seller made one meaningful correction or has spent months making small changes that never addressed the real pricing problem.”

Account for condition and ownership costs. A reduced property can remain expensive once repairs, insurance, taxes, association fees and immediate maintenance are considered. Buyers should compare the home’s total financial exposure with competing properties, rather than evaluating the asking price in isolation.

A lower price may represent genuine value when the cost of resolving known issues has already been reflected. It becomes less attractive when the discount is smaller than the work or ongoing expenses the buyer will inherit.

There may also be room to offer below the revised price, particularly when comparable sales support a lower figure or the property has remained available after multiple reductions. Olsher advises buyers to base that offer on evidence rather than choosing an arbitrary percentage below asking.

“The strongest offer is not necessarily the closest to the seller’s latest number,” he says. “It is the one a buyer can explain with recent sales, property condition and realistic costs. A reduction opens the conversation. The numbers still have to hold up.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5553. Inside Billionaire Larry Ellison’s HOA Feud Over His 8-Home Buying Spree

Billionaire Larry Ellison recently spent nearly $10 million on eight homes for his staff in a gated South Florida community—but not everyone was thrilled about his buying spree.

Ellison, 82, co-founder of technology giant Oracle, purchased the properties in spring 2023 in Palm Meadows Estates, an upscale 288-home community in Boynton Beach, FL, known for its sprawling houses, manicured lawns, and lakefront views.

But the plan hit a roadblock when the neighborhood’s homeowners association adopted a new rule limiting owners to just five properties around the same time the deals were closing.

The amendment, obtained by Realtor.com®, was signed on May 30, 2023, and recorded with Palm Beach County on June 2, 2023—during the same period Ellison's eight purchases were finalized. All eight deals were closed between May and June 2023, according to property records.

However, the amendment appears to have come too late to stop the sales from closing, and property records show that a company associated with Ellison now owns the eight homes.

All eight homes were purchased for Ellison’s household staff, which included teachers, therapists, and chefs, according to his real estate agent Kimmie Cruz, who talked to CBS12 about how some of the deals were still in the process of closing when the HOA moved to limit the number of properties a single owner could acquire.

"They tried to stop it," Cruz said. "There were also some neighbors who felt that it was going to change the dynamic of the neighborhood."

The amendment to the HOA rules also requires a year of ownership before a property can be rented out, according to the document obtained by Realtor.com.

Attorneys became involved in the dispute, and all eight purchases ultimately closed.

The HOA did not respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

The identity of the buyer initially remained a mystery, with an LLC listed as the buyer on property records.

But Cruz later learned the purchases were being made for Ellison, who has a roughly $200 billion fortune. A year earlier, he had bought a $173 million oceanfront estate in nearby Manalapan.

Cruz, a local real estate agent with LuxeIQ who lives in the community, previously told The Wall Street Journal that she received an urgent call in March 2023 from another real estate agent about a buyer interested in purchasing as many as 10 homes.

The agent told Cruz that it would be “worth it” to arrange the last-minute showings, she recalled. A few days later, Ellison arrived to tour the homes and that night, Cruz received the first of the signed contracts for the houses.

Cruz said the homeowners walked away with sizable profits from the sales.

“Across the homes I sold, I secured sale prices averaging 20% above market value,” she said.

One couple, Paul and Yvonne Carozza, sold their three-bedroom, roughly 2,100-square-foot home to Ellison for $1.2 million, a home they paid $567,000 for in 2019, records show.

Ellison’s purchases highlight an emerging trend among the ultrawealthy who are buying properties to house staff who manage their multimillion-dollar estates on their behalf.

Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg has been buying up a number of homes in Palo Alto, CA, to create a family compound.

Wealthy newcomers to South Florida, including billionaires, tech executives, and hedge fund managers, have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into building out new private and charter schools for their children, according to the Journal.

Some, including Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, and real estate developer Jeff Greene, have even launched schools of their own.

#5552. Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of a Big Week for Inflation Data

In A Nutshell:  Mortgage rates are coming down as investors dial back expectations for rate hikes. But that could change: Key inflation data comes out this week.

Two highlights from a busy election week:

This week’s economics highlight is the CPI inflation data coming Tuesday, coupled with Friday’s PPI data. Together, the two will form a complete picture of the core PCE inflation measure the Fed uses. The consensus forecast has core CPI coming in at 0.2% month-over-month, down slightly from last month. Forecasters are expecting a small statistical distortion in the data due to last year’s government shutdown. A very low read for inflation might convince the Fed to hold off on hiking rates at the December meeting, but they could just as easily write it off as one data point. They would evaluate how broader financial conditions have changed since the last meeting, including any further improvement in rates.

Many Fed officials are holding speaking engagements this week. The ones to watch are Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan on Tuesday; Vice Chair Michelle Bowman on Monday, Tuesday, and Friday; Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Thursday; and New York Fed President John Williams on Thursday.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5551. Google DeepMind releases new advanced robotics AI model and next-generation gene prediction model

Alphabet Inc.’s artificial intelligence research lab, Google DeepMind, Tuesday debuted the next generation of Gemini Robotics, the company’s most capable vision-language-action model to date for creating an “AI brain” for robotics.

Separately, DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2 today, a next-generation AI model that can predict how DNA sequences and their variations affect human cell types, creating a powerful biological tool for fighting disease and drug development.

DeepMind said Gemini Robotics 2.5 enhances dexterity, reliability and safety to help engineers bring robots out of the lab and into dynamic, unstructured, real-world environments where they can coordinate alongside humans.

The company said that with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, the research division has been able to accelerate robot research and reach into physical AI. The new robotics AI model was tested across over 200 distinct tasks and the company said it anticipates scaling even further.

Argon, the company’s frontier artificial intelligence large language model, rolled out in late September, bringing advanced reasoning to the enterprise. Using the capabilities behind this new, flagship model, DeepMind said it allowed Gemini Robotics 2.5 to increase the breadth and speed with which robots can learn new skills and apply them to real-world scenarios.

The 2.5 version makes a significant jump in optimization and performance across three key areas. Boosted dexterity means robots running on 2.5 can perform more tasks with greater accuracy, including using everyday tools to handle delicate, flexible objects. With increased reliability, the new model successfully packed automotive parts with a 96% success rate during real-world proof-of-concept tests at Mercedes-Benz. Finally, DeepMind enhanced safety with improved physical steerability and introduced a new benchmark for testing against jailbreaks.

In evaluations, Robotics 2.5 now achieves a 30% to 100% success rate depending on the task and completes tasks 20% to 30% faster compared with the previous version’s baseline.

The company said that, like previous models, it natively works with many different types of robots, including Apptronik Inc.’s Apollo 2 humanoid robots and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers.

“This is what we built Apollo for: useful work alongside people in real industrial settings,” Apptronik co-founder and Chief Executive Jeff Cardenas said. “Pairing Apollo 2 with Gemini Robotics, we saw the models improve dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carry over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off.”

Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out today via DeepMind’s robotics partners, including Agile Robots SE, Apptronik and Boston Dynamics Inc.

AI models such as AlphaGenome help drug development and biotechnology companies turn genetic data into testable leads. By predicting how DNA changes affect gene activity and which cells in the body those changes act in, they can guide researchers to promising drug targets and help prioritize experiments.

Announced today, AlphaGenome 2 adds finer detail about specific cell types and states, potentially revealing disease-related effects that broader tissue-level models miss. These predictions guide research rather than replace experimental validation; the model is not approved for clinical or diagnostic use.

The problem researchers face is that every cell in the body carries the same DNA; however, different genes are activated at different times to differentiate cells and adjust their behavior. For example, a heart muscle cell or an immune cell fighting an infection may have the same DNA, but they use the blueprint to produce different proteins, enzymes and other tools to do their job.

DeepMind used global efforts from the Human Cell Atlas, a scientific consortium that mapped gene expression in millions of cells, to give the world an unprecedented view of how different cells use genes. However, predicting the paths and variations that drive activation and expression changes remains a major challenge.

Professor Sarah Teichmann, co-founder of the Human Cell Atlas and professor of Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge, said what makes Alphagenome 2 so powerful is “how it adapts directly to new single-cell data without retraining, predicting how DNA variants act in newly profiled cell states,” and that it can adapt even from very small samples.

According to DeepMind, the new model can predict core experimental readouts of DNA function as the previous generation, including gene expression, histone modification and chromatin accessibility – but also adds DNA methylation, which is a significant part of epigenetics, which explains how behaviors, environment and life experiences can influence gene activity.

#5550. This New Water Heater Gadget Could Turn Your Hot Showers Into Bitcoin. But Is It Worth It?

Your water heater already uses electricity to keep the showers hot and dishes clean. But what if it could also earn you a little money at the same time?

That's the idea behind Bitwater, an unusual new home appliance from technology company Heatbit that combines an electric water heater's heating element with a bitcoin mining computer.

Rather than purchasing an entirely new water heater, homeowners can install the device inside an existing electric tank, replacing a conventional heating element with one powered by computer chips that generate heat while mining cryptocurrency.

"We were actually looking for areas where electricity is turned into heat, where it's not seasonal," Alex Busarov, Heatbit's founder, told Realtor.com® in a phone interview. The company had already developed bitcoin-mining space heaters, he explained, but household water heating offered an opportunity to put the technology to work year-round.

It's an eye-catching proposition at a time when homeowners are looking for ways to offset utility bills. But can mining bitcoin really make heating water more affordable?

At first glance, Bitwater resembles an oversized heating element, the metal component inside an electric water heater that warms the water.

But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining.

But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining.

Those chips produce heat as they work. Bitwater transfers that heat into the surrounding water, cooling the computer hardware while heating the tank.

Unlike space heating, which is largely unnecessary during the warmer months, households need hot water throughout the year. That makes a water heater a potentially more practical home for computing equipment that generates heat.

The device replaces only the lower heating element in a conventional electric water heater. The upper element remains in place to provide additional heating when demand increases.

According to Busarov, Bitwater typically operates at approximately 400 to 600 watts, heating water more gradually than a conventional element that might draw several thousand watts for a shorter period.

Busarov said the device automatically stops mining when the water reaches its target temperature. He estimated that the mining hardware operates approximately 80% of the time, although actual utilization would depend on household demand for hot water.

Bitwater can reportedly generate up to 34 terahashes per second, a measure of the computing power used to mine bitcoin, which Busarov estimated could translate to roughly $30 per month in cryptocurrency under current mining conditions.

That would represent approximately $360 annually, although actual earnings depend on bitcoin prices, mining difficulty, operating time, and other factors.

At that rate, a roughly $900 device would require about 2.5 years to recover its purchase price, even before accounting for installation costs, mining fees, maintenance, or changes in cryptocurrency earnings.

There is an important distinction, however, between generating bitcoin revenue and saving energy. Bitwater doesn't eliminate the electricity needed to heat water. Instead, the company argues that the electricity can perform two useful jobs: powering a computer and producing household hot water.

In principle, that gives the homeowner some cryptocurrency in exchange for electricity that would otherwise have gone toward conventional resistance heating.

Busarov says the mining operation shuts down when the tank reaches its desired temperature, so the device isn't intended to consume additional electricity solely to mine bitcoin. It prioritizes heating water, with cryptocurrency mining as a secondary function.

At an illustrative electricity rate of 18 cents per kilowatt-hour, operating a 600-watt device continuously would consume about $78 in electricity each month. Bitwater is not designed to operate continuously, however, and that electricity would not necessarily represent an additional expense if the heat replaces what a conventional electric heating element would otherwise produce.

Heatbit's projected earnings are therefore not the same as guaranteed savings on a utility bill. The calculation depends on how much the device operates and how much cryptocurrency it actually generates.

Heatbit designed Bitwater as a retrofit for conventional electric tank water heaters rather than a complete replacement system.

The device is intended to fit compatible residential tanks equipped with standard screw-in heating elements.

Busarov said installation is designed to be comparable to replacing an ordinary water heater element.

"We really built it for DIY installation," he said.

That doesn't necessarily mean every homeowner should attempt it.

Working on a water heater involves electricity, pressurized water, and potential flooding hazards. Homeowners unfamiliar with those systems should use a qualified professional and check local code requirements.

Heatbit promotes several safety and maintenance features, including leak protection, overheating safeguards, and programmed high-temperature cycles intended to limit the growth of Legionella bacteria.

Busarov said protecting against leaks was a significant part of developing the physical product.

He also described a system that can periodically raise water temperatures to combat bacterial growth without maintaining those higher temperatures continuously.

The company says Bitwater also incorporates a powered anode rod designed to protect the tank against corrosion and anti-limescale technology intended to reduce mineral buildup. Both corrosion and mineral deposits can contribute to water heater maintenance problems, and Busarov saw these features as selling points even for homeowners who aren't interested in cryptocurrency.

However, homeowners should verify that the specific product they receive has the appropriate electrical and plumbing certifications, and that its temperature controls and other protective features operate as advertised.

Independent, long-term reliability data will be especially important as the technology moves beyond its initial testing phase.

For homeowners primarily interested in reducing utility bills, Bitwater faces an established competitor: the heat-pump water heater.

Unlike conventional resistance heaters, heat-pump models use electricity to move heat from the surrounding air into a water tank.

According to Energy Star, an efficient heat-pump water heater can save a four-person household approximately $550 per year compared with a standard electric water heater.

Those savings come from reducing energy consumption rather than producing a separate stream of income.

Bitwater takes a fundamentally different approach. It aims to create financial value from electricity already being used for heating.

That may appeal to homeowners who already have a functional electric water heater and don't want to replace the entire appliance.

But a homeowner considering a major water-heating upgrade should compare installation costs, electricity consumption, maintenance, and expected savings before choosing one technology over another.

For all its ingenuity, Bitwater still faces some crucial, fundamental questions—like does adding cryptocurrency mining to an everyday appliance actually save homeowners enough money to justify the investment?

Regarding the latter, Heatbit claims it tested the system in households in Miami and Rochester, NY, during January, according to Busarov. Both locations maintained adequate hot water despite their dramatically different winter climates, according to the findings.

"People didn't really notice the difference," he said.

Realtor.com asked Heatbit to arrange interviews with the homeowners who tested the devices to independently assess their experiences, but those interviews had not been arranged by publication deadline.

While the concept has generated enthusiasm among cryptocurrency enthusiasts online, others questioned whether the device's mining revenue could justify its upfront cost, particularly if its computing performance declines as the water in the tank heats up.

There is also the question of whether homeowners want to become cryptocurrency miners, even on a small scale.

Bitcoin's value can fluctuate dramatically, and mining profitability depends on competition from other miners around the world. A device generating $30 in one month might earn considerably less in another.

There are also questions about actual mining utilization. Busarov estimated the device can mine approximately 80% of the time, but that figure has not been independently verified. Because the mining operation shuts down when the water reaches its target temperature, households using less hot water may have fewer opportunities to generate cryptocurrency.

Long-term maintenance presents another uncertainty. A conventional heating element is relatively simple and inexpensive to replace, while Bitwater introduces computer chips, electronic controls, and other components into an appliance that homeowners generally expect to operate for years with little attention.

And while the company insists the early household tests suggest the product can provide adequate hot water, the item is still in pre-order phase right now with the first units slotted to ship in the first quarter, so there is no independent evidence of its performance and durability, and real-world earnings remains limited.

Taken together, those uncertainties make Bitwater an intriguing proposition, but not yet a proven way to reduce household expenses.

#5549. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5548. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. Need a place to start? Use Redfin’s conversational search to begin your homebuying journey.

#5547. Hurricane Season Is Over Early, but El Niño Is Not Done With Us Yet

In a typical year, the Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to the end of November. But 2026 has been anything but a typical year.

In fact, the meteorologists at AccuWeather have announced that tropical activity for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is over, three weeks before the official end of the season on Nov. 30.

"El Niño has played a significant role in limiting tropical activity across the Atlantic," said AccuWeather lead hurricane expert Alex DaSilva.

"While tropical storms can still develop this late in the season, the weather patterns we're seeing give us confidence that the United States will avoid additional direct tropical impacts this year. It's an unusually quiet conclusion to a season that defied expectations and broke a 121-year-old hurricane record.”

But while the hurricane season might be bowing out early, the country still needs to prepare itself for the coming winter months in a big way.

AccuWeather originally forecasted 11 to 16 named storms for the season last spring, but once El Niño arrived and strengthened much earlier in the year than usual, the forecast dropped to eight to 11 named storms and three to four hurricanes.

To date, only 10 named storms came to fruition, the fewest since 2014, when there were only eight storms. Only one reached hurricane status, with Hurricane Isaias making a destructive Category 2 landfall on the Florida Panhandle in October.

It was the first time since 1925 that there was only one hurricane in the entire season.

That’s not to say that the season wasn’t destructive. The first storm of the season, Tropical Storm Arthur, dumped more than 20 inches of rain in some spots across the Gulf in June and caused an estimated $4 billion to $6 billion in total damage and economic loss, according to a preliminary estimate from experts at AccuWeather.

While the hurricane season is over, homeowners across the country still have to continue with a deluge of wet weather on the way.

Again, all thanks to the Super El Niño still churning away.

Notably, the El Niño could influence winter weather across the United States, bringing warmer-than-average temperatures to Northern states and wetter-than-average conditions to the South and East Coast, according to NOAA’s U.S. Winter Outlook.

Wetter-than-average conditions are most likely across the southern tier, from the Southwest to the Southeast, and along the East Coast. But if the temperatures stay up, the likelihood of snow is slim.

But even without the snow, the storms could be significant for this area this year.

“As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Nino will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” said Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service.

“While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides. Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.”

Meanwhile, more snow than average is favored across parts of the Intermountain West, the Plains, and the Appalachians this winter because of El Niño's active storm track, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In fact, most models that were reviewed showed above-average snowfall across the Plains, from South Dakota to northern Texas, and a swath of the central and southern Appalachians.

#5546. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5544. Kubernetes had settled into quiet maturity until AI blew the doors back open

Kubernetes has grown from a maturing container orchestrator into the agent substrate that enterprises are counting on to run artificial intelligence. The shift revives old security ideas such as perimeters while raising the stakes for portability across clouds.

Infrastructure providers are racing to make that foundation simpler to deploy and safer to run. Broadcom Inc. used KubeCon to unveil two open-source initiatives, and the show marks a turning point for a project that had seemed settled, according to Dilpreet Bindra (pictured), senior director of engineering in the VCF Division at Broadcom.

“There were a few that were like, Kubernetes is becoming mature, and so things were stabilizing, and they were less energy, I would say. And this KubeCon just blasts those doors wide open because Kubernetes has become the foundation for AI,” Bindra said.

Bindra spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes has become the agent substrate and how Broadcom is adding security in depth and workload conformance to make it portable across clouds. (* Disclosure below.)

Agents are bringing back security concepts the cloud era had declared dead. Broadcom’s approach is security in depth, using its vDefend firewall at the network perimeter and deeper inside to cut off network access when rogue agents appear, Bindra explained.

“How do you then isolate them in a compute boundary in our vSphere Pods, which is a micro VM, so you can have a very secure runtime,” Bindra said. “You can employ things like Agent Substrate to be able to run within them.”

Portability is the other half of Broadcom’s agenda. The company is co-chairing a new working group on Kubernetes workload conformance, aiming to end the separate validations software makers run for each distribution, including VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, or VKS. It also contributed its VM API project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, bringing virtual machines into Kubernetes as first-class citizens.

“We want Kubernetes to be Kubernetes wherever it runs in any environment,” Bindra said. “You don’t have to do individual validations of VKS, and then do individual validations of other Kubernetes distributions. You can do it as one Kubernetes.”
